NOVEL DUTCH METHODS. Electricity bids fair to crowd the auctioneer off his pedestal. At least an electrical, system of auctioning eggs has been tried in Holland, and has met with such success that it might possibly be tried on other commodities. Poultry farming is one of the great indus,ries of Holland, and within the last ten years, through co-operative methods, the poultry raisers have greatly improved their breeds and become big producers. The eggs are sold at auction every Saturday in at least one of the centres of the chicken indnstry. and the noise aid confusion of the egg market on silts day did not go well with the Dutchman's love of Trace d quiet. Therefore the invention of the electrical auctioneer. The eggs are sold in lots of 2,500 and each lot is numbered. Each of the intending pur- chasers of eggs is given a number and a seat that has also a number. The presiding official stands before a large dial on which are placed figures representing prices ranging from a very high figure to one that is correspondingly low. Beside the dial is an annunciator which is connected with push buttons ( n the seats,each having one button. The presiding official announces the number of a lot of eggs with a statement of their weight, etc., and then sounds a bell. • At this souud a pointer begins moving slow.y around the dial, com- mencing at the high figures, and dropping to the lower. When the dial reaches the price a prospective pur- chaser desires to offer, the purchaser presses the buttnn on his chair. the pointer stops, a bell rings, and the purchaser's number flashes on the a anunciat There is no noise and no confusion': The sturdy Detch broker sits at ease atal waits for the point-3r to reach his price. When a sale has been made in this fashion, a new lot is announced, and the 'same process followed in dieposing of in—" Irish Independent Weekly."
Eggs, Poultry, etc.

Sir, Being a great lover of good music, I, among hundreds of musicians of our town. would be highly delighted if our couucil can see their way .5 provide a new organ for Parr Hall. lam rather surp.ised at Alderman Tinnion's remarks about " something for nothing," and I hope that mhers more able to write in reply will let him have it hot. Let us have a good. new organ, and some good organ recitals, and you will see Parr Hall packed at popular prices.— Yours truly, APOLLO.

Sir, May I again trespass upon your spaca in order to state the facts relating to the erection of the old ,rgan in the Parr Hall, referred to at the Council meeting. These facts are as follows :—Before the completion of the Parr Hall it was decided under an arrangtsuaeut with the Corpor ation,the Organ Trustees and Mr Parr, that the organ should be ertcted in the new hall in time for the opening, September 12th, 1893, the sociEty first having the organ overhauled,enlarged, and a new front—in kr eping ,ith tire hall vrovided. This was done at a cost to the Music a Society cf about £350. About thee years later, the Corporation wishing to determine the then existing agreement and having the option f purchase, fresh negotiations were entered into which ultimately resulted in the purchase being completed, the amount paid to the a. eiety by the Corporation being £lB2 Ifis 2J, out of which the halal cc of debt on the organ was paid, leaving the actual amount rt ceivcd by the Society at slightly under ..k;128. The organ is TlC)Vir almost useless, but it has still a considerable value which, it and when, a new organ is erected, could be realised and would nearly or pro- bably more than wipe off the original cost to the Ccr poration. lieferriug now to the benefits which a new organ would comer on the town, and especially the poor r classes, there is a real and strong need for a good up-to-date organ, quite apart front the facilities such an organ would give to the Musical Society in further- ance of its good work. I take it that the varir us institutions such as the library, technical schools, school of art, baths, gymnasiums, park bands, park and recreation grounds &c, are all established for the benefit arid well I eing of the town, and yet they do not pay Why then exclude music, which is essentially educational, and cannot fail to have a refining and elevating influence ? Given the good organ neces- sary, I maintain that there is no more valid reason against giving weekly recitals with free admission to certain parts of the hall than there is against carrying on many, if not all, of the above ins•itutions. Such ' recitals would, I feel sure, he well attended, be greatly appreciated, and be highly teneficial. Further than this, there are many occasions when a good organ in the Parr Hall would, if available, be used, and so far from its being used EO seldom as it was stated at the Council meeting might likely be the case, I maintain that it would prove a source of income greatly exceedieg cost of upkeep. I therefore again plead sttongly ,that such an organ be provided, and I t. ast that it may be done with ittle delayo, 83 that it may be available next winter. Yours truly,
JOHN P. REYNOLDS, Hon. TrPas. Wairiugton Musical Society. February 13:h, 1913.

Sir,—Music lovers will be pleased to observe that last week's discussion was so favourable towat ds the provision of a new organ. There is no question that a new organ is ardently desired by them, nor is there much doubt t hat the !town's musical progress is greatly retarded in its absence. Naturally, in the discussion, the M us'cal Society was often mentioned, .and though some of the remarks did not directly bear upon the organ question, per- haps I may be permitted to refer to them here Criticism is often hel?ful, but much of it at the Couiteil Meeting consisted of mis-statements. For instance, Councillor Pemberton said the society consisted largely of wealthy people. This may be flattering to the members, but unfortunately it is not correct. The Councillor fails to appreciate the dis- tinction between the concert sub,cribers and the ordinary members of the society. Again, be said that the society did not have cheap prices at the concerts. At every concert there are god sixpenny seats, and artistes of the highest repute can be heard for this modest sum in the varied musical works given by the society. Councillor Pemberton was also wrong in the statement that at the recitals given in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, the attendances are c-mparatively small. So recently as a few weeks ago the hall was crowded at a recital given by the recently appointed city organist. I believe that popular recitals at the Parr Hall would be appreciated, and the several successful recitals by Mr. David Clegg at the Bold-street Wesleyan Church will be remembered with pleasure by the many who attended them. Alderman Tinnion considers that the Society should be put on a more democratic basis. This may be so, but the criticism seems to suggest that it is not easy to bec.tme a member. New members are always welcome and are reqeired to pass but a simple test, and to pay a small subsci:ption. Indeed the Committee has many times considered the ways and means of increasing the number of male voices in the chorus. The Alderman is not convinced of the disinterested- ness of the Society in the organ question. The Musical Society cannot be other than very closely interested, but not in the selfish manner inferred. To quote horn its rules : "The society is estab- lished for the encouragement of local talent in the study and performance of vocal and instrumental music, and for improving and extending the musical taste of the town and neighbourhood," and the pro- vision of a new organ would further this object, and greatly help to maintain the excellent musical reputa- tion which the town has earned. Yours etc., GEORGE 11. SMITH_ Wilderspool-road.

Sir,—The debate in the Town Council upon the purchase of an organ for the Parr Hall seems to have been nothing more or less than an attack upon the Musical Society. I have never been connected in any way with the society, but as one who has spmt many an enjoyable and instructive hour at their concerts, I feel it my duty to protest against this unwarrantable attack. They provide a series of con- certs, which give us an opportunity of hearing music of a recreative and educational character at a very reasonable price. Works like the " Dream of Gerontius," Dvorak's " Stabat 1113ter," Berlioz's " Faust," etc., are not produced, without trouble and expense. Theee are very few towns in England, where such works can be heard in such comfort at the price. If a certain number of people do go to air their clothes and motor cars, their money is helping towards the cost of production and there is plenty of accommodation left at a cheap rate. The alderman who said that the poorer portion of the inhabitants could stand for sixpence was no doubt airing his wit. Evidently his love for music of classic form does nil take him to the concerts,',if it :were so he would find plenty of seating accommodation for sixpence. Perhaps he is one of those people who want "Something for nothing." The society has proved its usefulness in bringing talent forward. A great number of our lccal solo singers either ara or have been members of the society and in one case at least it has been a stepping stone, to what promises to be a brilliant professional career. . _

If the Council are so anxious to provide music at a cheap rate, they should not only buy an organ but should in addition subsidise the society. The main objection to the purchase of an organ seems to be that the society will have the advantage. Well, I suppose they will have to pay for it the same as any other user. To my mind any person who hires the hall for &meet t purposes has a legitimate grievance as it is not a properly equipped building.. No concert hall cf the size of Parr Hall is complete without an efficient organ. Very few persons can afford an organ or a building in which to place one, and it is therefore just one of the things which should be provided out of the public purse. There are not many fine organs in the churches or chapels as stated by one councillor, indeed they are singularly deficient in this respect. His remarks would lead one to believe that churches are built merely as concert halls. There are not more than two or three organs of any size in the churches or chapels and these can scarcely be class(d as recital instruments.

There is a distinct difference between a concert and church organ. The primary object of a church organ is not recital work and many organists object to ' playing certain classes of music on a church instru- ment. Of late years owing to the great improve- ments made in the action of the organ which has made the control of a large instrument comparatively easy, the organ has made great progress as a solo instrument. In my opinion, given a good instrument, a series of Saturday evening recitals could be arranged at little expense, occasi many engaging some player of note. There are also many meetings during the year at which the organ would be requird. The upkeep of the organ would not amount to a big sum per year, and if it was well managed tl- e burden on the rates would not be great, The C uncil are entitled to spend money ,in the intellectual improvement of the people by means of art gallery, museum, etc Sur&y the art of tflusic should be supported. If an organ should ever be placed in the Hall, let us hope its pipes will produce less discord and more harmony than that wh.ch prevails in the Council Chamber. _

div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY
FARMING.
[BY REDCAP.]
PEDIGREE STOCK.

Nothing is gained by starting a poultry farm with inferior stock birds. It is far better to make a beginning with a few good birds than a lot of znongrels. You cannot hope to build up a business unless your name is known as a breeder of a good strain of fowls. Once you have ciccided on the variety, stick to them ; improve them all you can ; weed out all the worst specimens, and breed cnly from those of proved merit. I could name you plenty of poultry men who have been known breeders of certain varieties f3r more than 20 years. These are the succcessful men, whose names are as familiar as the variety they breed. This then is what I want my readers to do. Get hold of a good strain of fowls to begin with, and once you have become known in one variety, you can add other varieties if you choose, and thus enlarge and extend your operations.

div.head: TOO MANY VARIETIES.
div.p: TOO MANY VARIETIES.

It is a mistake to take up too many breeds. Always go to the man who specialiees in a few vatietice. It is an ab.tolute impossibility for one man to understand all the different points and qualities of say, a dozen varieties at once, Not only so, but it is also a very difficult matter to find a farm with land that is suit- able for every variety of poultty. As a matter of fact, 83M0 of the Asiatic breeds would thrive where the Mediterranean breeds would ta:t. That brings me to another point of consideration.

div.head: BREEDS v. CONDITIONS.
div.p: BREEDS v. CONDITIONS.

One must thoroughly understand the breeds most suitable to certain soils. Of course all breeds of poultry thrive better on a light sandy soil than they do on soils of a heavy clay nature. But inasmuch as we are so much the creatures of circumstance and environment, we have to adapt ourselves to certain conditions when considering poultry matters. The breeds that can stand heavy soil best are found in the following list and perhaps best in the order n:imed : Barred, buff and white Plymouth rocks, white and partridge Wyandottes, all varieties of the Sussex fowl, white and huff Orpingtobs, Brahtnas, Faverolles, Croad Langshans and Rhode Island reds. Breeds that I would not recommend for heavy clay soils are the following :—Black Spanish, Black llitiorcas, Anconas and Brown Legtiorus. A,though vigor .us utility stock these varieties have been known to do well. But when bred for exhibition specimens, a dry soil is most suitable.

div.head: GENERAL REMARKS.
div.p: GENERAL REMARKS.

The subject of the selection of stock according to conditions has a great deal to do witli the immediate success of one's operations, and in concluding my remarks on this topic I would urge my readers, if they are at all uncertain about these matters to con- sult some practical adviser. Scores of people have given up poultry-keeping in disgust, for the simple reason that they made a wrong beginning. Get the best adi ice you can and act upon it. Do not experi- ment until you have had a little practical experience.

div.head: HOW TO SELECT GOOD LAYERS.
div.p: HOW TO SELECT GOOD LAYERS.

When purchasing fowls for laying purposes, it is men that you should understand their chief points Colour is a secondary matter, providing the fowl is in good hard condition. A good layer is known by the long body, bright eye and general alertness. Never select deformed specimens such as wry-tailed and roach-backed Head points nearly always indicate the usefulness or otherwise of laying stock. Therefore you should never be persuaded to purchase fowls that look dull and mopish. It only costs the same to keep a good fowl as it does an inferior one. Be wise in your selection and, if it is not possible to view the stock before pur- chasing, have them sent on approval, returning those specimen's which do not reach the standard herein laid (low n.
ones.

div.head: PRECAUTIONS.
div.p: PRECAUTIONS.
A few brief don't., often form a useful guide to the amateur poultry keeper. Therefore I append the following list :

Don't overcrowd. Don't leave food lying about. Don't forget the grit box. Don't forget the dust bath. Don't forget clean drinking water. Don't keep lazy old hens. Don't keep the chicks on dirty wet runs. Don't house poultry in draughty sheds. Don't feed your fowls at 10 a.m. Don't feed on maize evf ry day. Don't forget to kill and bury diseased stcck. Don't forget to clean the roosting quarters often. Don't forget green food in plenty. Don't forget to consult the poultry column. Cut out the above and keep it before you ; it wi save you a lot of trouble.

div.head: CHAMPION HENWIFE.
div.p: THE CHAMPION HENWIFE.

Mr W H Watton, in the February sth issue (I "Feathered Life," writes as follows :—We offer our congrhtulations to Mrs George O'Grady, of the Utility Poultry Farm, Coachford, Co. Cork, who is the fortunate winner of the fully equipped poultry farm which was olTered as a prize in a competition organised by The Pou'try World. The examination in practical poultry-keeping, which was held in London last week, and during the progress of which .our representative was present, was very thoroughly conducted - the questions, bDth written and oral, being of a very searching character. It says much for Mrs O'Grady'A abilities that she won in competition with men and women of undoubted capabilities, and, in many ca,es, of considerable reputation as poultry-keepers.

div.head: SPRING CHICKENS.
div.p: SPRING CHICKENS.

No time should be lost in getting a few eggs down from these mated for table purposes. Spring chickens fetch very good prices and this branch of p ultry keeping is very profitable. The following list includes the most use- ful crosses for table purposes. Indian game —Buff Orpington ; Indian game—Faverolle ; Indian game— Dorking; Old English game—Buff orpington and Old English game—Faw.rolle. There are of course many other useful crosses but the above list will furnish you with the hest selection. If you use a broody ben for hatching purposes see that she Is set in a quiet corner and free from draughts Remember that the duties are long and tiresome, therefore warmth and comfort aill assist her in bringing off a good batch cf chicks.
DISPOSING OF OLD STOCK.

A general clearance of all old stock hens should now be made. The space occupied by these can theretot e have time to sweeten ere the chinks arrive. There is nothing more detrimental to the health of young chicks than foul runs. After you have got rid of sur- plus stock, sprinkle ,ome powdered lime in the runs. If the rims are grass, simply let the rain wash in the lime ; if they are just earth runs, then fork the lime into the surface and sow a few grass seeds in the soil. By this process you will assist nature in her cleansing process.
TEMPoTZ.III,I" SIIELTERs.

While you await the arrival of the first batch of chickens, the time can be usefully spent in erecting a few temporary shelters. A fow wooden hurdles covered with wheat straw form a very good protection from cold winds and wet days. Of late I have noticed that wicker hurdles are being largely used. These are very good, and can be erected and removed very easily. At this time of the year some form of protec- tion from the vagaries of weather conditions is essential for the well-being of young stock. That is why I strongly urge my readers to have in readiness some form of temporary shelter.

div.head: LATCHFORD GARDENS.
div.p: LATCHFORD GARDENS.
A Promising New Society.

Latchford has now a promising garden society of its own. The new organization came into existence last autumn on the initiative of the allotment holdere, and a small show was held. With the approach of spring, gardening once more becomes a practical topic, and with the object of urging the claims of the society upon all nature-lovers in the district, a meeting was held in the Parish Hoorn on Wednesday evening. Despite the foggy weather, there was a good attendance and the enthusiasm augured well for the SUCCESS of the movement.

_ The Rev G C Bittocs, who sent a letter regretting his inability to attend, expressed the hope that it would be made clear that no opposition was intended to the Stockton Heath Garden Society. There was no reason why the two societies should not work side by side and be mutually helpful. It was obvious that a society with the title of Stockton heath would never" catch on "or make much headway in Latchford which consider‘ql itself, and quite rightly, an equally or even more important place than Stockton Heath. Mr F H Longshaw wrote advocating the formation of a tjuvenile section, pointing out that many of the prizes at the Beautiful ‘Varrington Society's shows had been won by boys and girls in the Latcnford district.

Mr W Tinsley presided and was supported on the platform by Councillor Ft Henshall, Messrs J Moore urray, l /-1 Turton, It Poulton, F Short, J Holt, and J S Burgess, the energetic hon. secretary. Mill Moore Murray gave a short address on the educational value of a garden society. He pointed out that Latchford was fortunate in having an excellent school which was not all building and playground, but where there was sufficient ground for the children to learn the culture of flowers and vegetables. linfortun• ately in the centre of the town,where such accommoda- tion was most needed, they were least able to provide it. The Education Committee were willing to arrange suitable lectures on horticulture provided good atteudances were guaranted. Referring to the sugges- tion that the prizes should be ()flared for the I_st, gardens, Mr Murray said that to-day everything must have a prize at the end of it. Was not there something Ley ond the winning of prizes to be gained for such a subject a 3 gardening ? Was there nothing in the delight of having overcome difficulties and produced a result which nobody else could obtain ? It was a weak- ness of all present day sports and hobbies, that there must be something to compete for. Councillor HENsHAet. referred to the great possibili- ties of expansion Latchford presented, under toe Town Planning Act, pointing out that practically every section of that district, had already been developed. There were 500 acres of laud in Latchford which could be laid out on town pl :nning lines and taking the low estimate of lO,houses per acre, that wouid mean at least 5,000 new houses, all of which would have gardens to cultivate. The outlook of the society was therefore most promising. Addresses were delivered by Messrs Turton, Short, and Holt, and a suggestion was put forward that tne society should have a poultry section. A resolution was unanimously passed approving the formation of the society and promising it loyal support.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL DEBATES.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL DEBATES.

Sir,— With reference to your report of the last i meeting of the Warrington -Town Council there are several surprising and contradictory statements about which ratepayers are entitled to -fuller information. Councillor Pemberton and Councillor Lashford think there is too much sect ecy and privacy in the purchas- iog of some pr,Jperty and that ridiculously high prices are given. On the other hand Councillor Broadhurst says the town has been saved thousands of pounds by purchasing secretly. What are the facts and who is speaking the truth ? Will Councillor Broadhurst support his statement by giving one or two cases in point or anything in the nature of proof? Is it a legal method which he aporoves of and did the Housa of Commons Committee s'anctinn it ? I think- many will agtee with C uncillor Lashford's letter in your last issue.—Yours W. CHRIMES.

div.head: 679, Knutsford-road, Warrington. THE PAINTING OF ELECTRIC STANDARDS.
div.p: 679, Knutsford-road, Warrington. THE PAINTING OF ELECTRIC STANDARDS.

jr,—l see in your issue of February 18th. a para- graph under the the heading of " Notes and Notions " le the complaint of our S.,ciely and the painting of electric standards. As this may impzess your many readers that the painters are complaining without reason, I should esteem it a favi.ur if you would insert the particulars in your next issue. The members instructed me to write the Tramways Committee and protest against conductors and drivers painting stattdat ds as they con- sidered it was no part of their duty: They claim that the work should be given to a master.painter or to one of the unemployed painters (and there are about thirty at present) in the town. This is not an isolated case, by any means, as it is often done in all our municipal departments, and has even been done on Sundays. • You will see there is a vast difference between a man painting his own gate post and public work. A man has a right ti do what he likes with his own gate post (whitewash it if he likes), but when it comes to municipal work, our members think they, as tate- pa3ers, should have a voice in it, mores() as the list of unemployed is heavy, and, lastly, it is a tradesman's job.
THOMAS JONES, Branch Secretary,
-National AnmOgaraated Society of Operative LIC)Use and Ship Paint,rs and Decorators, 2S, Algernon- treet, February sth. -- DRUNKENNESS IN WARRINUTON.

Sir,—ln your last issue ycu placed before your numerous readers the annual report of the Chief Constable, a hich I think affords food for grave thought and serious heart searching by every respect- alie citizen What are the facts? We are told that in spite of the vigilance of our excellent public force guided and controlled by one of the best of chiefs, and in spite of the numerous Acts of Parliament in opera- tion for the regulation of this traffic in intoxicating drinks, Warricgtort s ill ranks as the second most druiiken of ten towns in this part of the country. The leport states that there were arrested for drunkenness during the year 1912, 471 males, 101 females, total 572. Every tree is known by its fruits. The fruits of the traffic in Warrington are such as should bring a blush of shame to the cheek to all who have a true e gard for the •honour of ibis otherwise good old town. There would indeed be some consolation if the report pre- sented us with the aggregate of evil produced by the trade, but alas, we are afraid it only gives us a bird's eye view of the awful ravages wrought by this traffic, upon the lives and homes of the intemperate people ot Warrington. We can scarcely imagine the t3rrible amount of suffering which the children of drunken parents have to endure ; and to think that the per- petual wait of the children has not yet apparently reached the ear or attired the heart of the Churches. When will they with united voice demand that this rolling tide of Iniquity, which is leaving so much human wreckage in its wake, shall be stopped? Let us hope that in the near future we may see all good citizens, uniting with the Watch Committee, the palice and the magistrates in one great effort to change once and for ever the complexion of the future reports of the Chief Constable.—Yours respectfully, SOBRIETY. February 11th, 1913.

div.head: ANTICS OF A MOTOR-'BUS.
div.p: ANTICS OF A MOTOR-'BUS.

One of the new typo of the Widnes Corporation motor-'buses was proceeding along Albert-road, along- side an excavation made for the laying of granite setts, on Wednesday, when the front wheels of the 'bus skidded and the vehicle crashed into a lamp and mounted the footpath. Two men who were passing at the moment, Albert Morris, of Foster-street, and William Houghton, junior, of Peelhouse-lane, were struck by the falling lamp and badly injured about the head. After mounting the pavement the 'bus swerved across the road in the opposite direction and tra•,elled over a wide trench used for laying an electric cable, but remained upright. The passengers were badly shaken and greatly alarmed. Fortunately all the men who had been working in the trench had just got out. The springs and the front part of the 'bus were badly damaged'

Mts. Reed, of Saudown, writes as follows —"I: must tell you of the wonderful effect the Barkola pre- cription has had in the case of my mother. She is eighty years of age, and was attacked so badly with rheumati,rn, with great pain and suffering, that she could neither use her hands nor stand on her feet. Barkola did wonders for her, and caused the utmost surprise and satisfaction to all who knew her. Maby friends to whom we have given the prescription have also tried it with complete success." The prescription which cured this old lady was the well-known Barkola Compound, and is as follows : One ounce of syrup of rhubarb, one ounce Liquid Barkola Compound, five ounces syrup of ginger, and one ounce concentrated infusion of gentian. 'rake a teaspoonful after each meal and one at bedtime. It is believed that this prescription is at once the most effective and the very cheapest medicine of its kind in the world.

div.head: MESSRS. GAItTONS SEEDS.
div.p: MESSRS. GAItTONS SEEDS.

We have just received from Messrs Gartons Limited the well known firm of scientific farm plant breeders Warrington, an advance copy of their new publication containtng prices and particulars of their new and regenerated breeds of farm seeds for 1913. This publica- tion is tastefully got up and beautiiully illustrated throughout. The illustrations consist of views of the interior of the newly-erected Warehouses, as well as actual photographs of their new and regenerated breeds of oats, barleys, mangels, turnips, &c. There is also an interesting itlustration of two gold medals granted to Alessrs Gartons at the recent Brussels Exhibition, this being the highest award given to any English firm of seed merchants. Some remarkable results are record «1 obtained from Agricultural Colleges and other agricultural centres, of trials made which show the superior merits of these new and regenerated breeds over the old types. Copies of this interesting publics. tion which should be read by all progressive agricul- turists can be had post free on application to Messrs Gartons, head offices, Warrington.

£1,000,000 AN ACRE. The Oldham Corporation is making very slow pro- gress with its extensive scheme for improving High- street, one of the most congested parts of the town, owing to the great cost of property in the district. Two years ago the Yorkshire Penny Bank asked £6OO for 26 yards of land, but at a meeting of the Surveyor's Committee recently it was stated that the Bank now wanted £5,500 for the land, the reason given for the increased demand being the improved business done by the hank. A Councillor considered that the demand was extortionate, and that tha Committee should have Power to rate the land. It was decided not to give the price demanded.

div.p: FOURTEEN DAYS FOR CULPRIT.

At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday before Mr R T Fairclough (in the chair) and other magistrates, Albert Edward Bradley, 67, Lord Nelson-street,was sent to prison for 11 days on a charge of having stolen altirge quantity of property value £2 lfis 6d during the past 12 months, from the works of the R:chmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Limited. According to the Chief Constable Bradley had been in the employ of the company for ten years and had been a watchman for some time. He had, how- ever, been put on other work a short time ago. Information mils obtained by the police to the effect that the prisoner had been vilfering from the works with the result that Detec- tives Holland and Redo ington interviewed him in the presence of the managing director. He stoutly denied taking stuff, and Detective Holland said, " Well, if that is so, you won't object to your house being searched." Bradley said he did not mind, only some tubing would be found. When the house was searched a large num- ber of articles, tubing and pieces of metal, were found. I Bradley said he bad taken the articles, but not with the intention of stealing them. Thefts front works were becoming tar too frequent and ought to be checked. Bradley said he took the stuff for his own amusement. lie carried away the metal to make ornamental things simply as a hobby. He saw the stuff lying about and asked the men if he could have it. The Chairman raised a question regarding the value of the things which the prisoner had taken. The Cnief Coustable : You cut put the value down at is. The principle involved is exactly the same. fbe Chairman : It is a matter of opinion. The Chief Constable : This has been going on for twelve months. It cannot be a matter of touch opinion. The Chairman : We don't say hap hing about that. We are taking about the value of the articles. Bradley was sent to gaol for 14 days, without the option of' a fine. PRISONER'S STRANGE WAYS.
PREFERS STRANGE‘4IAYS TO LOCAL POLICE
bTATION.

Through long experience Patrick Richard Moran a well-known local character, has found that prisoners on remand get better treatment at Strangeways gaol than in the local lock-up. Patrick told us this when he was charged at the Police Court on Monday,before the Mayor (in the chair), and other iragistrites,with having wilfully broken a elate glass window, value .£l. at the Inland Revenue Offices, Arpley-street. The Chief Constable said that it was his intentinn to apply for an adjournment for a week in order to prefer another charge against the prisoner, thereby enabling the Bench to give him more severe punish- ment th,n was possible on the present charge. The prisoner would persistently break windows. The Mayor : He was here it short. time ago wasn't he. .

The Chief Constable : Yes, sir ; for the same thing. Ile has been frequeutly convicted, and has been to the police station to break windows. We can understand him having a grudge against us, but we cannot under- stand him having a grudge against Mr Lloyd George. (Laughter.) He went across the way from the police station and broke a window under our very noses. The Mayor: He got as near to you as he could, The Chief Constable : That is so (exhibiting lump of granite). Apparently, your worships, he made sure of doing it. There is a very grave question" as to whether he is sane. . _ _
The Mayor said the prisoner would be remanded for a week.

Moran : I want to go to Strangeways, and not stop here. The Mayor: You have got strange ways already. (Laughter,) The Chief Constable: Yes; he wants to put the town to all the expense he can. Nloran : A an is not as well treated down here (indicating the cells) as he is there tStran,,'ev,ays). The Chief Constable : I will ask for an ncljourhement

until Thursday, and will get another adjournment then. It's all very well this man wanting to put the com- munity to the expense of 25s to 30s. It's very satis- factory from his point of view. Moran : You will he getting on for a week soon. The Chief Constable : He's not so soft as I thought. Prisoner was remanded until rihursday. oran was sent to prison for two months with hard labour by the presiding magistrates Mr W Roberts (in the chair) and Mr .1 R,3mer Young at the Police Court on Thursday.—He was charged with being a suspected person, and loitering to commit a felony on the 9th February, in Arpley-street. The Cnief Constable mid that at 7.20 on Sunday morning the prisoner was in Arpley-street and cam across to the Police Station and said he had smashed a window at the Inland Revenue Offices. He had frequently been before the Court on different charges, but the one preferred against him that day was one of frequenting. P C. Howard said that when the prisoner was charged he replied "last's right ; I wanted to be locked up" Moran (sarcastically) : What was I charged with ? The Magistrates' Clerk : You were charged with wilfully breaking the window, but this morning you are charged under the Vagrancy Act. Have you any- thing else to ask the officer? s Moran: No, not on that charge. I hail no intent to commit a felony. If a man was going to commit it felony he would not come down to the police station and get locked up. The Chairman • What did you break the window for? _Moran : I did not know what I was doing at the

time. The Clerk : You often don't. The charge was reduced to one of breaking the window wilfully. The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been there 53. times previoasiy. tie thought they ought to send him away for some time aid in addition order Moran to find a surety which would keep him from bri aking windows wilfully. It WAS tuonstrowi, for there was no rhyme or reason why he should break them. He knew perfectly well what he was doing. Moran: I suppose I can speak to the gentlemen in dicating the magistrates) can't I? The Chairman: Von will be sent to prison for two months with hard labour. Prisoner : lam ving to make an appeal against that sentence. You cannot "land "me for two month:. on that charge and you don't forget it. Borough Police Court.

To Go TO WIGAN.—John Thompson, of no settled address was charged on remand with begging.—Thi Chief Constable stated that when the prisoner was first before the Court the police were not BKM:fled with tilt- statements he made. During the remand it had bee'. ascertained that he had recently absconded from Wien, where he was wanted for felony. He ran away with another man's wife and child and had since beer.

begginc. He suggested that the prisoner should be sentenced to seven days imprisonment commencing from the previous Monday so that he could be handed over to the Wighn Police. The prisoner had nothing to say and the Bench acted according to the suggestion of the Chief Constable.

A BRUTAL HUSDAND.—Peter Warburton, 10, Orford- street, was summoned by his wife, Mary Jane, for assault.—The wife's story was to the eff-ct that during the week end her husband took home a bottle of beer which he left on the table. The children asked for the buttle, and so she threw away the beer and sent the bottle back to where it had been obtained. On Sunday,. her husband asked for the bottle and before she could explain, her husband gave her a blow which blackened both her eyes. In the bedroom he bruised her all over the body.—The prisoner said what he did was done in self-defence.—The Chairman : You gave your wife two black eye 3 in self-defence !—Warburton was fined lOs and costs with an alternative of 14 days' imprison- ment, and his wife was granted a separation order with an allowance of 14s per wee% for the support of herself and five children. HANDS OFF THE LANDLADY'S FOOD.--Jonathan Barnsley, formerly lodging at 101, Bewsey-road, was summoned for having done wilful damage to the extent of 63 to two cupboards, the p operty of Mrs with whom he lodged. Mrs Mills said that the defendant and another lodger returned to her house about 11 50 on the Monday night, both being drunk. She had left his supper in the oven. Barnsley broke the locks off two cupboards and mixed jam, cake and other food- stuffs all together on the table. He wilfully spoiled all the stuff and when spoken to the next morning, argued that he had a right to do as ha had done,because he wanted something to eat, and he had paid for it, "and," added Mrs Mills," he has had five meals every day of his life all the time he has been with me. " The defendant admitted forcing open a cupb ,ard " because he wanted something to eat. Crackers were nothing for an ironworker to work upon."fle was fined 103., out of which the dam ige would have to be paid,and ordered to pay the costs-18s in all. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr J Hayward (in the chair)

Messrs C Jackson Holmes, and W T Williams. ALLEGED Til EFTS. —Joseph Reuben Ho 'sou, no fixed address, was charged with stealing on the 25th January an overcoat value Is, the property of Robert Connor from the dwelling-house 24, School-brow. He was further charged with steAling .E 3 in money and articles of clothing to the total value of .E 4 Os from 38,School- brow the property of Robert Connor. The Chief Con- stable said that on the day in question the prisoner went to Codnor's house where he had been lodging and took the overcoat from behind the door. He said he was only going to use it whilst he went for his wages. He did not return, however, until February Ist when he went in the house by taking the key from under the door and letting himself in. He went to the bedroom and stole the articles enumerated in the second charge. An adjournment was necesssary.—The case was adjourned for seven days. SEttrous ASSAULT CASE.—Thomas Hoyles' 3, Arnold's-yard, was charged with assaulting Nlary Jane Hennessy, 1, Arnold's-yard, on the Bth February. Com- plainant. stated that on Saturday night between S and 9 o'clock, the prisoner came to her house tor a chat and sat down by the fire. Without the slightest provoca- tion he went home and brought the poker suit struck her across the head with it. Ha was orunk at, the time. Prisoner said he did not remember as he was drunk. The Chief Constable said the complainant had bad to have five stitches put in her head A tine of 50s was imposed. WAS HE THE OFFENDER ?—Patrick Patten 2

Heatffla-square, was charged on a warrant with assaulting and beating Martha Burns, 20, James- street, on the 9th Februar), and also with assaulting Catherine Stretford. 21, Cockhedge-lane, on the same day.—Mrs Burns stated that at 10.50 on Sunday night she was standing at her front door when the prisoner came along with uis wile She (witness) had had some words with the prisoner's wile, and Patten asked what was the matter. She replied it was only over the :thildren. Mrs PAten tried to hit, her over the prisoner's shoulder. Patten struck her and thumped her in the face and then ran riv.ay with the remark " take that." She was rendered unconscious by the blow.—Mrs Stretford stated that she saw the prisoner so-ike the last, witness. She (witness) was going for assistance, when the prisoner struck her in the face tinder the jaw. When she was getting up he struck her again.— Prisoner said the women were rowing ant fighting between themselves.—Mrs Patten gave evidence on behalf of her husband and
said it was she who gave the woman the black eyes. he it was, who struck them both and not her husband.
—Prisoners' mother-in-law also said that Mrs Patten

struck the wornen.—A young girl witness said that alt the women were fighting in the hack. She did not see Mr Patten at all.--fhe Chief Constable: It is a case where something should be done to stop such disgusting behaviour on the streets.—Patten was ordered to pay lOs including costs.
THlTRsnA.Y.—Before Mr W Roberts (in the chair), and Mr.) Rymer Young.

A SPECTACLE CAE.—John Hayes. a pedlar, was charged on remand with attempting to ebtain 23 by false pretences from Detective-Sergeant Reddington.— The Chief Constable explained that on February sth Detective Reddington, when in Buttermarket-street, was accosted by the prisoner' who asked him to buy a pair of gold-rimmed spectacles for two shillings. He said he had found them on the road. The officer took prisoner into custody, and from inquiries he ascertained that the spectacles coulu be per_ chiised at 43 fici per dozen. The prisoner was unaware of the fact that Redding ton was a detective Prisoner said ho would not sell another pair of glasses. —The Chief Constable: Thera is one feature in the c,se, that apart from the selling of theee glasses and getting the money in that manner, he sold articles which would be injurious for anyone to wear. The Chairman : You have not imp ov,d Your case by the lies you have told. -Prisoner : I will go to Blackburn where I came from.—Considaring that he had been an remand for seven days, the in igistrates sent him to prison for a further seven days. A CRUEL TRlCK.—James Robinson (20) who is at preient unlerving a term of imprison- ment for an offence at Wigan, was charged with stealing on the 17th January, a lady's silver keyless water), lady's handkerchief and 33 Ild in money, from a bedroom of the house, 252, Nnutsford- road, the property of Mrs Mon agh-n.—The Chief Constable said that at 1.30 on January 6th, the prisoner scent to the house of the prosecutrix and represented to her that. be was employed by the Dunli,p lyre Co. He stated that be wanted lodgings and she said he could stay. He gave her is for a night's lodging and is 6cl for three meals. He went to a place of amusement and returned about 11 o'clock. He got up in the morning, had his breakfast and left. After he had gone, the things were missed.—Tho prisoner was undergoing a kind of semi-Borstall treatment at Walton gaol and it was suggested that the sentence he should receive that morning should be a continuation of that treatment.— He was sentenced to two months to follow the com- pletion of his other sentences.

The draw for the first round of the Northern Union Challenge Cup, to be decided on March Bth, was wade at Huddersfield on Tuesday, and resulted as follows: Broughton Rangers v Barton or Heyside. Swinton v Batley. Rochdale Hornets v Feathefstone. Barrow v Halifax. Pemberton or Wigan Highfield v Bradford. Wigan v Leeds Widnes v Leigh. St Helens v Huddersfield. hull v Seaton. Bramley v Hull Kingston Rovers. York v Hunslet. Elland or Rothwell v Wakefield Trinity. Normanton St John's v Oldham. lieighley v Warrington. Dewsbury v Runcorn. Coventry v Salford.

The cup draw has the same effect on the football enthusiast as a tonic on an invalid. He feels rejuvenated, the world is a better place, and he has 'something to look forward to. Of cow se he may feel 11+3Pressed if his pet team has to assail the walls of such Impregnable fortresses as Huddersfield or Wigan. But as a rule the approach of the cup-ties renews the -enthusiasm and eagerness of football followers in every camp.

Things have been decidedly dull in the neighbour- hood of Wilderspool, and the chance of seeing some cup-tie warfare has livened everyone up. Warrington's fate is to go to Keighley. It might have been better and it might have been a lot worse, but the omen could hardly be improved upon. The last time we went to Keighley we won the match and subsequently the Cup !

That was in 1905. Warrington had beaten Morecambd at Warrington in Round 1, and were drawn at home to Keighley in the second round. The match was looked upon as a "soft thing," and pro- -I)ably it would have been had not the Warrington Committee taken the opportunity of making one of their cup-tie experiments on this occasion. They Placed George Thomas at half back with Bate, and left Isherwood and Brooks out of the team. The result was almost a disaster, for bth halves and forwards made tgich a poor show that Warrington Were lucky to draw the match with a score of 3 points.

For the replay at Keighley, D Davies and Brooks took the hall-back positions, and Isherwood returned to the threequarter line. Warrington won 7-0 before c.h a crowd ai had never previously been seen round i‘eighley's narrow playing pitch. On a wider field, *Warrington would have scored more points, for they Were much the superior team. By the way, it is zather a curious coincidence that Berry was in the Warrington team on that occasion and that he should be turning out agaiu to-day after the lapse of eight Years. After polishing off Keighley, Warrington dis- Posed of Bradford and ran through to the final when they conquered Hull Kingston Rovers G-0, and brought tue Cup to Warrington.

_lyarrington's chances cf repeating their victory at la,‘-olghley are exceptionally promising. Keighley are „.°aving their worst season under the Northern Union -League, aid so lar have only won three matches out of 19. Only the other day they transferred their best three-quarter, Stacey —the man who scored at War- to Leeds. Now that Brooks and Bradshaw are in training again Warrington's resources are materially strengthened, and they should be capable of topping the first hurdle in the competition with •ease.

Last week they gave a display against Widnes which was anything but promising. The Chemicals -repeated their feat of last season by drawing the floatch in the second half and capturing a point. As a niattar of fact they ought to have won, but they did far too much punting in i_ srcond half—and punting does not bring points 'except by accident. Warrington should have made the match secure in the first half when the forwards were 911 top, and chances were frequent. But the .cmoombination was again very poor anu the attacking ther ver"nts lacking entirely in vim. Widnes were a toge a much more alert and nippy side.

--- I never saw the Warrington threequarter line slower tham on Saturday. Neither Tranter nor Renwick could raise a gallop on the attack and both tnen were pulled down with surprising ease by the :young Widnesians. Tranter is not fulfilling early expectations, except on the defence. He was better ou the attack in his first thre,r, watches than he has ever been since. Nowadays he kicks when be should tuna fatal fault for a centre-threequarter. If he would only remember how he ran through the Runcorn and Wigan teams in September be would ,kave more confidence in himself and do it again. ,41eowiok never seems to have trained on since his ,lejury and he is again resting. We badly want the 'ttenwick of last March for the cup ties.

It is a matter for surprise that Widnes have sus- tained such crushing defeats of late away from honr When they are cspable of giving such an energetic "Play as that of last, Saturday. The forwards are good arid the backs up to the average. In Redmond and Brassington they have two young players who a,re likely to make a name for themselv.s. Where Ina team is failing, is in combination. They were laing better football two years ago. Laws and winton are notable absentees.
_ The League table up-to-date is as follows :____

Te'dav the Warrington men journey to Wakefield, Where they I, n , ey usually play a good game but rarely finish .(..-- P. Seeing that the Trinity men won at War- , evltletory tn- __l,ngton they will probably be equal to repeating the day. Warrington have made some curious ?Pr4es in their thirteen the most remarkable of itch is tl introduction-' f Rushton at centre. It look . le o. - off" 8 like a big gamble with a man who has "come very few occasions. Brooks displaces Williams rii order to get in training again, and Brown earns the _eward of merit by displacing Daintith. The latter was f!. fdilure on Saturday. He seems to be at, home •only In the mud.

The selected team is: Jolley ; Brooks, Tranter, nl3slitoo and Davies, three quarters; Brown and 'Nicholas, half hacks • Thomas, Chesters, Fernley, Cox, Thomas and NaylCir, forwards. Shelhorn is injured.

The " A " team disgraced themselves by being beaten 26-0 at NN idnes with the strong side they had in the field. Bevan and Glitchley tnu•A have been missed from the pack, for the Widnes forwards simply overran the Warrington men, and Brooks, Bradshaw and Brown had no chance. Jordan was very much off form in the rear, and gave more than one try away.

The " A "team have a friendly at home to-day, and are putting an experimental side in the field against Flixton. Bardsley, Berry, Waywell and Bradshaw is a new threequarter line, and at half back a trial is being given to W. V. Morgan, a young ('umberland player who has been doing big things in junior football in the North. He is 21 years old and and weighs 12-s—a decidedly useful poundage.

The "A" team is : Brown ; Bardsley, Waywell, Berry, and Bradshaw ; Morgan and Daintith ; Arnold Bevan, Gibbs, Clare, Blundell, and Critchley. It is about time Clare appeared in the pack. He will have opportunities there of gaining the promotion that will never come to him as a threequarter.

Warrington were favoured with a fine day on Saturday and the result was a capital crowd of 6,000 to witnwis the popular return match with Widnes, about 1,000 people coming from the chemical town. Both sides were well represented, and a keen struggle was not only expected but expeptations were realised, the visitors equalising the score in the second half, as they did a year ago. The teams were : Warrington—Jolley, back ; Williams, Renwick, Tranter and Davies, tbreequarter backs; Nicholas and Dninteth, hall-backs; G Thomas, Ctiesters, Skelhorne, Fearriley, Cox and R Thomas, forw :rds. Widnes—Brassington, back ; Reid, Taylor, Redmond and J O'Garra, threequarter backs ; Noon and Lally, half-backs ; S Aspey, Gircoran, Cosgrove, Higgins, H O'Garra and Lloyd, forwards. Referee, Mr 1," Renton ( Hunslet). Touch judges. Messrs W T Chapman (Sv.intan) and A Roscoe (Broughton Rangers). Warrington won the toss and opened strongly with the sun and wind behind them. Nicholas soon had the ball in the Widnes quarter, and Brassington was hard pressed by the Warrington forwards, bat cleared with a celerity that marked him as a coming player. Noon and Lally were smart in their movements behind the Widnes pack, and a clever run by Lally narried play into the Warrington half, Jolley responding with a powerful punt. Skelhorne Cheaters, end Fearoley made a dashing raid on the Widnes line, which was supported by Renwick. The centre ran strongly and then passed wide of Davies when a couple of yards from the line. He might have gone on and scared. Warrington were now overplaying the visitors, and should have gathered points it the attack had been more finished. Tranter tried to burst through on the right but was grassed by Reid and Taylor, with Williams waiting for a pass. Then the ball was forced past Brassington by the Warrington forwards, and Skelhorne bad a glorious chance in front of the posts. An attempt to pick up instead of dribbling over resulted in him being tackled. It was a bad error of judgment. The Widnesians were penalized immediately after and though the shot was from a lengthy range, George Thomas made no mistake with the goal. Play con- tinued to be of a very strenuous nature and a useful

div.head: OUR 1 MPS' CARTOON.
div.p: OUR 1 MPS' CARTOON.
THE IMPS SNOWED UP.

breakaway on the left saw Redmonzt make a fine attempt to overcome the defence, Williams getting up at the opportune moment to save disaster. The Widnes meu were beaten back, and there being some fumbling with the ball Tranter nipped in, making good progress, he eventually sent the ball to the open, where Fearnley cross-kicked to Davies, who took the ball on the bounce, and, beating O'Garra, scored the first try of the afternoon. George Thomas missed the difficult shot at goal. Widnes were by no means disheartened at this reverse, for they rushed the sphere to the Warrington end, and exchanges between Noon, Lally, Redmond and O'Garra saw a desperate effort by the wing man to cross. Davies and Jolley, however, showed strength in their tackling, and relief came when Nicholas, Renwick and (Jhesters with soccessive efforts compelled the game to be fought out at neutral quarters. Widnes were very persistent, and at length a lofty kick was fumbled by Jolley, who lost possession near the line and allowed H O'Garra to dribble over with an easy try. The goal-kick was badly missed by Taylor, and Warrington wee still leading. Even play followed to the interval, when the teams crossed over v,ith Warrington leading by 5 points to 3. Warrington's chances were by fl) means rasp) n- resumption,and fine punting by Redmond atig Brassing- ton soon drove them to the line. Jolley had his hands full, and in saving one rush he parted with the ball when on the floor, and three Widnes forwards had the lire at their mercy. Lloyd dribbled over and was in the act of dropping on the ball when Renwick raced up and kicked dead in dramatic fashion. It was a lucky escape for Warrington. Strong forward rushes claimed attention for a long time, and in trying to stem one dangerous rush of the Widnes vanguard, Skelhorne was hurt and carried to the touch- line. Fortunately for the home club he was able to resume, but during his temporary absence the Waring- tonians did exceptionally well, wheeling the packs and forcing Taylor, Redmond and Lally to adopt saving measures to avert disaster. Eventually Widnes , took up a strong position, and after O'Garra and Reid had in turn taken up passing ' movements initiated by Noon and Lally, the last-named half back received from his partner, and, with a smart drop sent. the ball sailing over the hall, and the sides were placed on level terms. Following on the restart from the centre, the Warringtonians became more aggressive and the forwards appeared to realise that great responsibility rested upon them, using their feet to better advantage. Nicholas did some exellent work and only Taylor's superior speed saved Widnes when Brassineton was beaten and Fearnley looked like going over. Widnes played up strongly to the end,but kicked too much. Reid trade one great effort on the left, only to meet with a fine tackle from Williams. Final : Warrington, 1 goal 1 try (5 points) ; Widnes, 1 goal 1 try (5 points).

div.head: COMBINATION.
div.p: THE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A" BADLY BEATEN AT WIDNES.-

The Warrington men took a strong" A " team to Widnos,but found the locals in a very aggressive mood. Warrington were the first to become aggressive and 13,00kes early on had a futile shot at goal from apenalty Widnes responded, and, showing rare dash and determination, were not long before they had estab- lished a lead, Tench scoring a try, which was improved upon by Daintith. The visitors thad again an easy chance to record a tangible point, but, the kick from a penalty went astray. A fine save by Lawley from a dashing effort by Bradshaw was the next noteworthy item, following which,Reswick crossed for Widnes, the home team leading at half-time by eight points to nil. In the second stage Widnes were generally masters of the situation and tries in rapid succession were scored by Daintith, Farrell, G Aspey and Kinsella, Daintith being responsible for three goals. Result Widnes four goals six tries (26 points) ;Warrington nil,

div.head: SCHOOLBOY'S MATCH.
div.p: SCHOOLBOY'S MATCH.

An interesting match was played at Wilderspool on Sturdy before the seniors took the field, between Warrington and Widnes schoolboys. The Widnes lads had the wind behind them to begin with, and Cosgrove scored a try. Two penalty goal were kicked, and at half-time Widnes led by 7 points. On turning round, however, the Warrington lads showed smart football and tries were scored by Skelhorn and Parry after capital combination. There was a keen struggle for supremacy after this, and Walker settled the issue by dropping a smart gcal for the locals, who won by 8 points to 7 points.

div.p: ALTRINCHAM LADS V BOWDON VALE.

The " local Derby " took place at Stamford Park. Final: Altrincham, Lads, 2 goals ; Bowdon Vale, one goal. OU.HTRINGTON AMATEURS V. BROADHEATII. At lieatley. The visitors were the first to score, Kite partially saved a first time effort, but could not prevent Peacock from finding the net from the rebound. Mid- field play followed for a time, if anything, Broadhetith having the best of matters, but the home custodian was in great form and cleared all that came in his way. Before the interval the Amateurs were awarded a penalty, which they utilized to the full. Half-time, one goal each. In the second portion the Amateurs took the lead, Woods heading a very fine goal from a corner. Although the Heathens had slightly the best of matters they could not score until within fire minutes off the call of time. Quinn (centre-half), for Broad- heath, put in a terrific shot which Kite did well to get at in any case. Clegg secured from the rebound and once more equalized the scores. In the closing minute of the game Peacock was just wide with-a good effort. Final : Oughtrington Amateurs, 2 goals ; Broadheath, 2 goals. OUGRTRINGTON PARK v MORBERLEV.

LATCH FORD. At Weaverham the visitors were the first to press, Ford missing a good chance in the first minute. For a time Latchford had consicerably the better of matters and found the brothers Woodward and Vaughan plenty to do. They, however, were equal to all demands. Vaughan, in goal, making some fine clearances from Shakeshaft and Potter. Gradually the home players settled down to their work and began to have more of the game and made several raids on the Latchford defence. The uneven nature of the ground cAused the Latchford team some trouble, their backs making several miskieks. div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
SANKEY LADIES v. FARNWORTH LADIES.
Played at Fern xorth on Saturday, the home team winning a well-contested game by 3 goals to 1. Miss Devonport was the scorer for Sankey.
LATCHFORD.

The First Eleven lost by 10-2 against Manchester University at Fallowfield, but the score was no indica- tion of Latchford's form because after twenty-five minutes' play they were actually leading by 2-0, but at this point two of their players were accidentally injured and took no further part in the match. Pearson and Minards had scored and everything pointed to a com- fortable win for the visitors,butatter they were reduced to nine men, Manchester were able to attack strongly and the continual pressure told. Bruhl in goal played valiantly and kept out several nasty shots but had no chance with these which scored. Wilkinson and Knight were the best of the backs. For the University Boscolo, De Jong, Newton, were the pick. The Uni- versity have not done very well this season and so should not be begrudged their victory. They are a capital side when they once get into their swing. Manchester University" A " turned up at Latchford with a full side but were heaten by 3-1, although the home team were minus four of their regular players. The visitors were hest represented by their goalkeeper. left back, right half, and centre-forward. For Latch- ford, II Fletcher gave proof of his versatility by play- ing a right good game at centre forward, and scoring all three goals. lie was ably supported by Marsden, Gibbs and Morgan, and Eccles and Mull, the full backs were safe.

ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE)

The improvement in conditions last week led to more embers turning i,ut to try their kill. Three members in particular had more than the usual bag of fl,h caught within easy walking distan, e from town. Those who visited the Gowy returned with several roach, but nothing to mark up on the Board Still it was an improvement on the last. few weeks. Norton was visited but the returns from here were very poor indeed.

THE GOWN". Five merobFrs journeyed to Mickl. Trafford on Saturday last and found several meadows still under water. Sport was not good, the best being a catch of four roach, heaviest about 12oz. One or two again wade the journey on the Sunday and off feed was the verdict.

NORTON. The canal was tried by several members who seldom visit, this piece and they could not get the better if fish. All canals are not fished alike. Different methods used in different canals and members who visit these waters must acquire the methods recognised before they can hope for success. The secretary received a letter this week stating that five hundred roach from the Kentish fisheries have been twined in at Norton of an Soz. average. These- rhould make the length a better fishery this season and mem- bers who are new visitoi-s here will have something to compete for that will repay them for their trouble. GENERAL MEETING.

The general meeting at headquarters on Monday last confirmed the rults passed by the Joint Committees. It is now definitely decided that members who belong to more than one club shall pay subscriptions to each secretary, and not pay through one secretary for two or more clues, each seeretary I.)ing responsible for his own club's subscriptions only. Thus, it a man is in the Centre of another affiliated club, he shall take out his cards and pay his subscriptions at the Centre, and then pay in the club where affiliation has taken place to the secretary at the affiiiated club.

All se-ales from clubs shall be brought down to the Centre three days before any match and passed by the Joint Committees and taken to the match from head- quarters. The places for the matches are Rambling match, River Gowy, May 18th, opening match, New- bridge salt-works end ; annual match, Newbridge, locks end ; the officials' match was left over for the Joint Committee to decide at the Cooper's Arms at a date to suit secretary's convenience. All affiliated clubs to weigh in matches, clubs not affiliated, weights for matches not accepted. An Executive Council to be formed by selecting three delegates from each club and each club to nominate its own three.

All cards are now .to hand. Members who huve already paid subscriptions to the amount of Is. may apply to Mr k; Brooks at headquarters for them, no cards will be issued to members %sho have not paid in without applying to the secretaiy direct on Monday at 8 p.m. Members please note vre4lits of specimen fish will not be recorded at any club uclese they are in benefit with their subscripticn cards. A. S.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY FEBRUARY 15, 1913.

Once again in thelhour THE ANTARCTIC of triumph tragedy has TRAGEDY. -.7-brought sorrow deep- felt and pitiful. The terrLle news brought back from the Far South has plunged a nation, and, indeed, the world, into grief. In many ways the disaster t° Captain SCOTT and his gallant band in the icY wastes of the South Polar regions is 'the roost relentless of all the tragedies associated With the records of Polar travel and discovery Only the tragedy of Franklin can compare With it in magnitude and poignancy. Details of the terrible calamity are scanty enough, and there is left to the imagination the fill- ing in of much of the picture of the fearless explorers' fight with the malignant forces of nature in the hurricane-swept wilderness of the Far South. It is not difficult to imagine however, the spirit in which Captain SCOTT and his devoted followers faced the end. All through his career the man who planted the Union Jack at the end of the earth and Perished on his way back, almost in sight of safety, has given proofs of the qualities that have made the British Empire what it is. Re was a typical Britisher. He knew _the risks he took and the price which others before him had paid for their ambition to' °How out the tragedy-strewn trail to the Pole. He faced the dangers of the way with sPlendid courage and fortitude. He won his great prize, and paid the price. His last tragic entry in his diary tells us plainly that he was filled with no vain regrets at the end. He died as he had lived and worked—a hero. Nature, "red in tooth and claw," has once More, as in the case of the Titanic, asserted its supremacy over man. It must have athered up all its forces of frost and storm to overwhelm the little band which had Penetrated to its central solitudes, for what had they not previously endured of cold and hard toil, of numbing blizzard and pitiless Storm? How inconceivably terrible must have been that last icy- tempest which they found themselves without the strength and the resource to endure? The unadventurous and stay-at-home mind always asks the same questions as to such perilous under- takings as that of Captain Scurr and his e°roPapions—What is the use of it all? It might be possible to give a not wholly unsatisfactory reply on the merely utilitarian grounds. But who can conceal from himself the fact that if there had been more chance of of 'usefulness from the point 9f view, let us say, bringing back cargoes of blubber or ambergris, in the recent South Polar expedi- tion, there would have been less likelihood that they would have been undertaken? it 'Was something far above material advan- tage that was being sought. It was the exploring spirit of man which was seeking' a new outlet. It was another assertion of that deep human quality which will not rest While there remains anything that is assessable and unknown. It is such adventurous work which lifts humanity out of the rut. Lives and deaths like those of Captain Scow and his companions confer a new dignity on the race, and their names and their great achievement are, to quote the moving words of Commander PEARY, as imperishable and. as eternal as the icy heights under which they died.

Whim questioned in the House of Corn- as to whether he had seen Captain 4COTT's last message to his country, and Whether the Government will give favour- 131e consideration to the touching appeal With which the message concludes,the Prime ti4lnister answered, as was to be expected tr.°l/1 a mind evidently full of emotion, that e appeal of this great explorer will not fall ‘.'ll deaf ears. "Surely, surely," Captain f e°l7 wrote, as he, was looking death in the ijake at close quarters, " a great, rich country de otirs will see that those who are depen- ,iit upon us are properly provided for." vile trust is certainly not misplaced. Those 11° were dependent on the brave men who llave in their lives in the Artarctic will be Z,°Pted by the nation at large. There will 4.e B°lne substantial Parliamentary recogni- tion as a matter of course, but

't vastly larger movement of sym- PathY will find practical expression -through the public subscription that is •certain to be set on foot. Mr ASQUITH called Captain Scorr's last message one of the most moving and pathetic utterances in the annals of discovery. It could not be more fittingly or accurately described. "Had we lived," wrote Captain SCOTT, "I should have had a tale to tell of the hardihood, endurance, and courage of my companions which would have stirred the heart of every Englishman." The tale is already told with a deeply touch- trig, brave simplicity in the message that Was written with so much difficulty whilst death was gripping the hand that held the pen. And it is a story of which Englishmen Will be proud for hundreds of years to come.

It was very appropriate THE TORIES AND that Lord Middleton THE ARMY. should initiate- the House of Lords' debate upon the Territorial organization and Home Defence. Lord Middleton, better known to fame as Mr. Brod rick, entered upon his career at the War Office with high hopes and a favouring breeze of popu- larity from all quarters. That he was 1 one of the greatest failures that the War Office, that rocky shore upon which so many promising careers have been wrecked, has ever known, was due to the simple fact 1 that in his calculations he ignored the funda- mental difference between insular and Continental conditions in the problem of defence. Our first and second line of defence is the Navy. Mr. Brodrick proposed to create a Continental system of defence which the pressure of our insular conditions reduced to " paper " corps. Incidentally, Lord Methuen paid a well-deserved compli- ment to the great service that Lord Haldane has done for National Defence, and condemned the unfortunate " crabbing " of the Territorials.

Apart from the con- stituency he has so long represented there is probably no place where greater regret will be felt at the death of Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P. than in Warrington. He was almost a familiar figure here, for on numerous occasions he had occupied the pulpit at one or other of the Wes- leyan churches, and spoken at public meetings in Parr Hall on behalf of tem- perance and purity in civic life. To know Robert Cameron was to love and revere him. Few public men impress one with their transparent honesty and sincerity, their loftiness of aspiration, and their great humanity as did the veteran parliamentarian and social worker who has died this week in harness to the last, and full of honours. Though in his 88th year Mr. Cameron came specially to London and appeared for the first time for many months at Westminster to vote for the third reading of the Home Rule Bill. For weeks before he had been paired with Mr. Chamberlain, but before the Home Rule division he gave the required notice to break the pair, came up to London, and was brought from King's Cross to the House in the Chief Whip's car, just in time for the voting. 'Members crowded round to congratulate him, the greetings of the Prime Minister and the Irish leader being specially warm. Mr. Cameron came again for the Welsh Bill division last week, so that he was active to the last in his support of the causes of "Home Rule and religious equality," which he always stated were among his chief interests in politics.
THE LATE MR. ROBERT CAMERON, M.P.

Thankfulness for small mercies is the attitude of mind which the rate- payer is becoming accustomed to cultivate in these days of ever-increasing expenditure. A. general feeling of relief will therefore be occasioned by the news that Warrington's education rate for the coming year will not show an advance upon the present figure of is. 9d. in the £. Although the estimated deficiency is about £3OO more than for the year 1912-13, the Education Corn- mittee is recommended to make a call upon the rates for exactly the same amount £24,000. This will, at any rate, afford a welcome breathing space, for the committee undoubtedly inflicted a shock upon the towns- people last year when its requirements necessitated an extra 3d. in the £. A cursory survey of the estimates reveals savings under several heads. Last year £4OO Was set aside for the provision of meals for school children but the experience of the committee has prompted a reduction in the call for this purpose to £lOO. The opening of the Evelyn-street Council school has had the effect of 'educing the number of Warrington children attending schools in the Lancashire county area, and the pay- ment in respect of them are therefore estimated at £2OO as against £320. On the other hand, the committee is now in a position to accommodate more scholars from outside the Borough and the income from this source is expected to rise from £l2O to .£lBO. Last year an item of £2OO. appeared on the Sites and Buildings Committee's 'minutes in respect of the pros- pective employment of a professional architect to suOervise schobl buildings. This proiect, however, did not receive the con- firmation of the Education Committee, with the result that the £2OO is omitted from the new estimates.

If advocacy can win the day it should not be long before the Corporation capitulates and provides Parr Hall with an organ which will be a credit to the town. The Mayor set the ball rolling at the last Council meeting, and lovers of music have since been very energetic in their canvassing for public opinion. Mr J P Reynolds pursues the subject with an enthusiasm which seems bound to succeed. The balance of argument is heavily on the side of the " new organists." * This is the latest story from New York. A reporter of the " Herald " wanted to see a certain Roman Catholic dignitary very urgently to obtain some information. The Reverend Father was at confession and could not be intruded upon. By a happy inspiration the young man decided to join in the string of waiting penitents and get at the priest in his confessional. At last his turn came. * * "A great foreign export trade carries with it as a mathematical consequence a corres- ponding import trade; if it be desired that the export trade should be a •great trade there must be an import trade to pay for it. We must be paid in goods. We can be paid in nothing else . . . and we must not only be paid in goods for what we export, but we must be paid in goods for the interest on capital we have invested abroad. It would be unreasonable to be alarmed at the growth of manufactures in foreign countries. That growth is inevitable—like it or dislike it. Let us not grumble at what is really the result of inevitable laws."—Mr. Balfour, 1896. * *

Mr Chamberlain has calculated to a farthing the effect of his budget, of his pro- posals upon the food bill of the workingman. I observe that he has not taken into his calculations the enhanced cost of all those articles which the workingman cannot dis- pense with in addition to his food. He has not taken into account the enhanced cost of his house, of his clothes, food, shoes, house- hold furniture, household utensils, of every article which you find in a workman's cottage—every one of which will be enhanced in cost by his 10 per cent. duty upon foreign manufactures.—The Duke of Devonshire,l9o3

Mr. Wyndham spoke at the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, on Monday night, as Presi- dent of the Lancashire, Cheshire, and North- West Counties Division of the Tariff Reform League. In the "change of method" as to food-taxes Mr. Wyndham declared that there was " matter for regret, but none for recrimination." Is it tactics which has led to the change? Oh, dear, no! "It is not a tactical move, but a sincere effort to clear the Unionist Party in respect of Tariff Reform from any taint of the reproach which Unionists attach to their opponents in respect of Home Rule." This means, we take it, that the electors must know in advance at every stage what Tariff Reform " means." But we do not find (says the Westminster Gazette) in Mr. Wyndham's speech any indication of what the Tariff Reform taxes on foreign manufactures are to be. Possibly he thinks it etiquette to leave the "clear and intelligible" exposition to Mr. F. E. Smith, who promised it. 4:s *

The debate upon the working of the Insur- ance Act in the House of Commons at the end of last week has cleared the air. One cannot help feeling surprise that at this date, only three weeks after the coming into opera- tion of a vast piece of legislative machinery, an Opposition willing to wound is able to find so little to say in criticism. The case against the Act has completely broken down. As Mr. Lloyd George said, the British Medical Association (which spent £30,000 in its campaign against the Act) claimed that 8,000 doctors would be necessary to work the Act. We have got 15,000 on the panels. Already five thousand persons are being treated in the sana- toria, and Mr. Lloyd George testifies that the number of complaints received is infinitesimal. That is evidence of smooth working which we could scarcely have anticipated. The Act came into operation after a raging propaganda against it that has continued for months, and which had been conducted in part by one of the most powerful organisations in the kingdom. It has worked from the beginning because it was wanted by the people.

The Tichborne claimant's idea that as some people have plenty of money and no brains, and others have plenty of brains and no money, therefore the former are the legitimate prey of the latter,is well illustrated by the remarkable fraud known as the "Spanish prisoner swindle," which has flourished for many years in spite of innumerable warnings in tie Press. The method of the swindle was to pretend that a prisoner in a Spanish gaol was possessed of treasure secreted in some place not accessible to the owner whilst he was in durance. An offer was therefore made to share the treasure with someone from outside, certain advances being, of course, necessary. It seems strange that so obvious a trick should have deluded so many people,but the swindle was based upon a knowledge of human nature on its credulous side,and the powerful attraction of such a bait as hidden treasure. According to the " Daily News" correspond- ent in Madrid, the headquarters of the gang which worked the trick has been discovered, and the chief is said to have been arrested. But we fear that the people with brains who want the money will still contiime to exploit those who have the money without the brains. .

* * * In his speech on Friday night last, Mr. Bonar Law was led into further rashness in an attempt to answer Mr Asquith's questions categorically. Mr. Asquith's question No. 2 was: "Will you put on your tariff for the sake of revenue, or for the sake of Protec- tion?" To which Mr Bonar Law replies: We shall put it on for the sake of both, and we shall secure both.

We wonder what Lord Derby will say to this? For Lord Derby has expressly said that he will have nothing to do with any policy of Protection, the very thing Mr. Bonar Law admits and alleges the taxation of manufactured goods is designed to secure.
