div.head: CONGREGATIONAL P ROGRESS.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL P ROGRESS.
THE NEW CHURCH IN PADGATE LANE.

At a cost of 1'2,500 a new Congregational school chapel is to be erected in Elmwood-avenue, Pad- gate-lane, to replace the altogether inadequate and unsuitable Cockhedge Mission. The foundation stone of the new building was laid on Thursday afternoon in the presence of a large assembly by Mrs: Ziba Armitage, who acted in behalf of her .husband, who was unable to be present. The building about to be erected comprises a church hall 561 t. by 361 t., a guild room 261 t. by 16ft., six :large. class-rooms, minister's vestry, kitchen, and ample sanitary accomodation. It has been planned so that the hall and each of the class- rooms can be used separately, being approached by large, wide and well-lighted corridors, thus obviating using the large hall as a thoroughfare, a condition which was almost unavoidable in the old type of plan when the hall was surrounded by class-rooms. The site is a corner one, and sufficient land has been acquired to provide for the building of a church at some future date. The hall is lofty, and the ceiling broken with large gablets. The Renaissance type of architecture has been used for the building, and the boldly projective blocked cornices and gables will add to the beauty of the building. The inside joiners' work will be carried out in pitch and stained var- nished wood. The roof principals will be exposed. Ample provision has been made for ventilating the ,hall and various class-rooms and corridors by means of inlet and extract ventilators. The building will be heated by hot water on the low pressure principle by means of pipes from a fur- nace boiler placed in the basement. The build- ing, which will accommodate 350 people, is being carried out from the designs and under the super- vision of Mr. S. P. Silcock, F.R.1.8.A., and the builder is Mr. Joseph Dolan. ;There was a very largo 'attendance at the foundation-stonelaying ceremony, over which the new pastor, at Wycliffe, the Rev, T. T. James, presided. Among those present were: Mr. J. W. Slack (treasurer), Mr.. A. H. Crosfield, Mr. C. E. Parker, Alderman Bennett, Mrs. T. T. James, Messrs. P. T. Winskill; W. Knowles, J. W.-Jeffery, P. Silcock, J. Dolan, J. Pickton, A. Ashton, G. T. Rushton, A. D. Owen, C. W. Shaw, W. H. -Wallington, B. Farrar, J. Pod- more, A. Holland, J. Longland, G. 'Wallington, S. R. Armitage, W. Beswick, E. S. Garland, C. Eccles, R. Storey, J. Poole, J. Phoenix, H. Clayton, J. Derbyshire, E. Hough, C. H. Hibbert, F. Berry, and G. Parr, Mesdames Podmore, Gar- land, Longland, Walker, Winskill, Hawthorn, J. Hawthorn, Ball, Jeffery, W. Knowles, Edelsten, Batty, S. W. Jeffery, W. Knowles, Edelsten, J. W. Travis, Farrar, A. Podmore, J. Podmore, shaw, Pennington, F. Morrall, Molyneux, Berry, and Hibbert.

The speeches were most encouraging, and indeed from every quarter the mission has had a hearty send-off in its great undertaking. In his opening; remarks the Chairman said there was one feel- ing of real regret in which he knew they were all joined and united, and that was thy, regret that Mr. Armitage found it impossible to be pre- sent as he had hoped to be. They would all have been delighted to see him, and were keenly dis- appointed, but no one could be more disappointed than Mr. Armitage himself for having to be absent. It would have given him the greatest delight to have seen that large gathering that afternoon. They had Mrs. Armitage with them, who would take the part her husband should have taken. They extended to her the heartiest of wel- comes. (Applause.) That day was one of re- joicing for everyone, for they saw many years of hard work brought to fruition that day. He trusted it would be a day of real encouragement to everyone, and that the future of that building. to which they were all looking forward, would be full of the prosperous results of that scheme. He rejoiced with them on that step forward which was being taken, and he trusted it would mark the beginning of many days of happy work, which God would Mess, for the. extension of His King- dom and the happiness of His children. (Ap- plause.) He asked Mr; J. W. Slack, who had worked hard for the scheme, to make a financial statement.

In doing so, Mr.. Slack said the committee had as yet been cheered and encouraged in their work by the responses they had received to their appeal during the past twelve months, on behalf of that mission. It had not been an easy task ;.,they had met Month by month, and sometimes they had lost heart and said the scheme would not be carried out. They were, however, determined that some- thing should be done to alter the conditions at
WELL-KIMI CONTTREGATIONALISTS AT THE Front Row: Mr. J. W. SLACK (Treasurer), Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, Rev. T. T. Mr. S. R. ARMITAGE, J.P.

the .mission—friends having had.,Abower baths during services, and it would ntei doubt have affected some of the deacons at Wycliffe to do something if they had been under them (laughter) —and-at last the committee had arrived at some- thing tangible. The cost would be 1:2,500, and at first they had thought they would never raise the amount. Then they decided they would raise it, but instead of going on with the smaller scheme, which was about .4,200, they decided to make a bold venture and go in for the full scheme. (Applause.) They appealed to the Congregational Union and the Chapel Building Society, and they kindly promised £250 from each fund. Then their friends, Mr. and Mrs. Armitage, came forward very generously and put their names down for considerable sums. That encouraged them, and then they had friends who promised sums ranging from £lOO to £5, and even the humble half-crowns they had not despised. They had in hand and on promise £2,200, leaving them 4:300 short of the whole amount. They appealed now for 60 sums of £5 each. They had the first and last two promised, but they wanted the others in between. They were not going to open the building until all the money had been received. (Applause.) He Would like the expenses to have been covered and -.CIOO in the bank. (Hear, hear.) That was what he had set out to do, and he trusted that the , notes would come in readily, so that in July they would be able to say they were free from debt and that they had some money in band. Speaking with reference to the people at Cock- hedge, he said one of the chief things that en- couraed the committee was what the people of Cockbhedge, although only compartively poor people, had decided to do. They had decided to raise £2OO by half-penny subscriptions, and they had received more than half that amount already. (Applause.) Mrs. Armitage said she was very disappointed that her husband could not be present. Until that dinner-time he said be should come, but when the fog caine down he felt it would be foolish, so he decided to stay at home and not run the risk of a long illness. Now that the sun was shining be would be regretting he had, not come. He had, however, sent her a speech to read. He said the ceremony in which they were .there engaged pointed to the fulfilment and con- summation of the efforts and prayers of people associated with Wycliffe Church during the past 43 years, and the list of those who during that time had been actively interested in Cockhedge Mission included many names honoured in the records and dear to many Wycliffe people. The origin of the work had its inception in the War- rington Town Mission, an interdenominational society, which ceased its operations about the year 1869. Severv.l men prominent in the religious and municipal history of Warrington joined its committee and worked together with great public advantage; but it was found that the claims of their own churches drew them to transfer their interest to denominational schemes, and the War- rington Town Mission ceased to exist. Thereupon some friends of Wycliffe, discerning the need for some of the society's operations, engaged Mr. Jas. Stelfox to take up the work of vis'tation of the sick and destitute, and in the year 1870 Mr. Mat- thew Knowles was appointed to devote his whole time to the work under the title of the Wycliffe Town 'Misgion. The development of that enter- prise prompted the erection in. 1872 of the Mission Room at Cockhedge, and with their opening a Sunday school, an infant and day school, and a Sunday evening service were instituted in the name of the Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission, under which designation the work had been carried on until the present day. Other notable landmarks in the history of the mission were illustrated, and the speech touched upon the time of the Rev. W. R. Parry's appointment as minister in 1884. Great advances were being made, and the mission rooms were often crowded. Many of the events he had recorded should stimulate them to renewed energy and consecration. They all honed that in that new building they would have even larger congregations, and that the congregation which had worshipped for so lone in the old Brick Street rooms would be augmented by residents in that new district. (Hear. hear.) The Cockhedge friends were about to enter into a wider sphere of work, for which that new building would offer ample facilities. They had done, and were doing, their share in working up to that result, though he did not suggest there was no further call for effort. They had to bear in mind that while it was emnparitiyely easy to build a new church it was more difficult when the spur of excitement
!urrell.
CEREMONY. JAMES, M.A., Mrs. Z. ARMITAGE,

had passed to maintain all' its agencies in vigor- ous condition, during the following years, alike in prosperity and in depression. (Hear, hear.) It was in the firm belief that the added responsibility would inspire an impulse of liberal effort to supply its needs that so many of their friends were taking a willing part in providing the larger opportunity which that chapel would furnish. (Applause.) The past years,- with their fluctua- ti. . history of fortune and vicissitude, were gone beyond recall, but not without leaving their les- sons for them as they looked into the future, hoping with the Divine help and blessing that that house which they were rearing might be a harbinger of joy and peace to that district and its population, and the means of drawing the people to the worship and service of our Gracious Lord. (Applause.) Mr. J. Dolan then presented Mrs. Armitage with a beautiful silver trowel suitably inscribed, the gift of the builders. . In laying the stone Mrs. Armitage said: "I declare this stone Well and truly laid to the glory of God and His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, with the earnest prayer that many souls here will find comfort and man?, wanderers be brought back to their Father's home." (Applause.) Mr. W. H. Wallington proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Armitage. Having been connected with Wycliffe for a long number of years, he knew of the interest, both from a personal and genzral standpoint, that Mn. and Mrs. Armitage had shown in Wycliffe and Cockhedge. They also expressed their sorrow that Mr. Armitage was not with them. (Hear, hear.) _

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, in seconding, said the names of Armitage and Rigby, Wycliffe and John Yonge, had become household names to them in Warrington, and certainly, going back to his earliest recollections, one of the first things he could remember was a light in the sky when they were living at Lymm and his father brought his mind to it. That was the fire which brought down Cockhedge Mills. He had gone down the next day with his father, and they had seen Mr. Samuel Rigby, and he was struck by the calm- ness and philosophy with which Mr. Rigby faced what was a grave blow to him. They were all household'names, and he was sure they could only hope that Mr. James, who had come to succeed Mr. Yonge, would carry on the same fine work for the benefit of the whole town which was car- ried on for. so long by the Rev. John Yonge. (Hear, bear.) He regretted Mr. Armitai.,!e's absence, but was quite sure be was with them in spirit, for no one had more at heart the success of that good Cause than he. (Hear, hear.) It was a great pleasure to him to second that vote of thanks to Mrs. Armitage, whom they all highly, respected and esteemed. Referring to the su-n having dispelled the fog just as Mrs. Armitage laid the stone, Mr. Crosfield said it was a most happy augury for the future when "Old Sol" came out just at the right time. (Applause.) Mrs. Armitage, in reply, voiced her willing- ness and gladness to be able to do anything she could for Cockhedge. . Mr. Rigby Armitage spoke of the connection between the mission and the works, which had been 'extremely close. They had been allied all his time and long before that, and they could not part with a mission like that from such close connection with the works without some amount of feeling. They were all delighted that they had decided to build that large building, which would mean increased accommodation. He offered his heartiest congratulations to them for the way they had brought that about; it was .really a wonderful work. (Applause.) The Chairman had received' apologies for non- attendance from the Rev. A. J. Viner (secretary of the Lancashire Congregational Union), the Rev. John Yonge, and Miss Bessie Dutton.

div.head: Election of Guardians.
div.p: Election of Guardians.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, it was announced that the triennial election of Guardians of the Union would take place on April 'th. Nominations must be received not later than 12 o'clock noon on T,hursday, March 13th.

Warrington Photographic Society. Mr G H Walker presided over an enthusiastic gathering of friends and members on Tuesday to hear the ever-popular Mr J 11 Kirtland give his new lecture on " Aberystwith." Starting from Llandudno he took his hearers round the coast of Bangor. Clynnog and 13armouth to the University town show- ing charming views of inland scenery all the way. The choice of many bits showed the eye of the artist, as the excellent technique showed the hand of the careful manipulator of the plates. Many happy holidays must have lent each their contribution to make up the large number of pictures (nearly 200) shown ,and the lecturer well deserved the compliments that came from all hands for this delightful addition to this season's list of lectures. After the lecture the secretary mentioned the gratifying fact that no less then ten of the season's items are by the Society's own members. He was also able to announce the visit of the Photographic Convention of the United Kingdom to Bangor early in July, and hoped that many mem- bers will be able to arrange a visit thereto.

Is there a German Menace ? ['ha fortnightly meeting of the Philomathic society was held at the Old Acadeiny,Bridge-street,on Wednes- day night, when an interesting debate took place on the subject of "Is there a German menace to English- men ?" —The President (Mr. James Ball) was in the chair, and there was a good attendance of members.— Mr. F. Chadwick, who opened in the affirmative, stated the .real menace was, perhaps, not to be found in trade —as fortunately commerce was not dependent upon the whims of politicians—the real menace, he con- sidered, was to he found in the military spit it of the governing classes of Germany, in the rapidly increas- ing population of a country possessing few colonies, and in the intense national aspiration of the German people to a larger " place in the sun."—Mr. A. I Newton. in the negative, claimed that there was no foundation for the so-called Cr-o-rnan menace. England's vast commerce continued t exp md,hernaval supremacy was still unquestionable, and itur inter- national relations were such as to negative in a great degree German military preppiaderance, the Triple Entente acting as an effective curb on the ambitions of the Triple Alliance. Germany's impoverished finances, too; had to be considered, and he contended that the firm attitude of our statesmen, irrespective of party, to vas rds the maintenance of our Naval Supremacy was evidence, not of any serious German menace, but of an intention to render foreign aggres- sion hopeless.—A discussion followed, in which Messrs E G Burgess, N Nield, Dr Mellor and T E Knowles took part. On taking the opinion of the meeting. the affirmative was carried by four votes.

div.head: CONCERT IN BRICK STREET.
div.p: CONCERT IN BRICK STREET.

In aid of the funds for the new chanel, an excellent concert was held,in the Independent Methodist School- room Brick-street (kindly lent for the occasion) on Thursday evening. The attendance was a large one and the chairman was Mr J W Slack. The various items were well received and the function provei be a popular one. The Rev T T James addressed the gathering and had a word of encouragement for the workers in the great venture they had undertaken and honed their efforts would be crowned with success. Mr W 11 Wallington was respinsible for the whole of the arrangements which were of a most pleasing character,

div.head: Concerts by Crosfield's Band.
div.p: Concerts by Crosfield's Band.

Attention is called to the announcement of two sacred concerts to-morrow (Sunday) by Cr)sfield's Band and the unique Quartette of Trombones. The object is a most deserving one of charity, and the band welcomes the assi,tance of the general public in making the affair as great a success as possible. The band is in very fine form and music lovers should not miss this great treat. The quartette of trombones has met with great success everywhere. The players represent Foden's, Shaw and Crosfield's Bands, and the fine rendering of most difficult selections has earned a splendid reputation.

div.head: WOMEN LIBERALS. LATCHFORD AND STOCKTON HEATH DISTRICT.
div.p: WOMEN LIBERALS. LATCHFORD AND STOCKTON HEATH DISTRICT.

In connecti,n with the above, the Annual Tea and Meeting were held last evening in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Lat.diford. About 100 were present at the tea, which was in charge of Mrs J Walker and Mrs O'Brien, the district captains, and their helpers. At the after meeting Mrs A H Crosfield presided and was supported by the officials and committee of the Women's Liberal Association. Speeches were delivered by Mrs Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Mr A H Crosfield, Mr O'Brien, and Councillor Henshall. An excellent musical programme was contributed to by Miss Dodds, Miss Wilkinson, Mrs. Sanders, Mr Knowles (humorist), and Mr Tanner (accompanist).

LANCASHIRE PATIENTS AND PANEL DOCTORS.
NO SOAP WAR. MESSRS, BRUNNER MOND'S DENIAL.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday Viscount! Wolmer asked the Chancellor of the Exchcquer whether be was aware that the Lancashire Insurance Committee have refused to allow insured persons to choose their own doctors ; and whether that committee is carrying out the wishes of the Government in this respect. Mr Masterman (by written reply).—Every insured person has a right to choose any doctor on the panel in Lancashire, as elsewhere, and I am not aware that the Lancashire Insurance Committee have taken any action which would deprive insured ty4rsons of this right. An Insurance Committee, in allowing or refusing to allow an insured person to make his own amtngement for treatment by a doctor who is not en the panel must exercise its discretion in accordance with the Act and the regulat ions.

Statements have appeared in London newspapers regarding a probable soap war between Messrs.Brunner, Mond and Co., chemical manufacturers, and Messrs Lever Brothers. A Northwich correspondent inter- viewed the directors of Messrs Brunner, Mond and Co. on Tuesday and was officially informed that there is labsolutely no truth in the report. He was given authority to contradict the rumour. As is well known Messrs Brunner, Mond, and Co. have assimilated the soap businesses of Crosflelds and Goss.ages, both concerns using large quantities of chemicals. Brunners and Levers (adds the corres- pondent)) are much too good business men to engage in industrial war.
The Examiner, Saturday, February 15 1913.

to ensure this measure of justice being placed on the statute book." He said the speeches which were being made by the opponents of the measure were remarkably similar to those which were delivered when Mr Glad- stone proposed the Disestablishment of the Irish Church. btatements were made at that time that he intended to ruin the Church and all the horrors which bad been prognosticated recently with regard to the Welsh Church were predicted in those da3s. They had, however, been falsified in the event. The Disestablishment of the Irish Church had proved a great blessing to that Church, and when Welsh Disestablishment had been carried out, Church people themselves would in years to come be glad that that reform had been effected. Continuing, the speaker expressed the thanks of the workers to Mr Crosfleld for heralding the advent of the Insurance Act in Warrington by his gitts of silver spoons to the parents of the first bounty babies. He was sure the recipients would agree that the Act did not come into operation one day too soon. (Laughter and applause.) It was a matter for regret that

THE VOICE OF WARRINGTON in the House of Commons had been heard against that beneficent Act. Mr Harold Smith promised to look alter their interests, but surely a large measure of social reform like that of health Insurance was entitled to better treatment from him, if be really had the welfare of the workers of this great community at heart. Alluding to municipal topics, the speaker touched upon the proposed motor 'bus service in White- cross ward. The chief argument brought against the scheme was that it would not pay, and it therefore rested with the inhabitants to give it their full support. (Applause). '1 he resolution was carried unanimously. Mr A H CROSFIELD, who had a great reception, expressed the delight of the meeting at the re-appear- ance among them of Alderman Evans, who appeared to he quite in his old form. (Applause.) Referring to Welsh Disestablishment, Mr Crosfield said he had been long enough in democratic politics to have an old- fashioned belief that majorities, rather than minorities, should rule. (Hear, hear.) He did not care whether they were dealing with the question of Disestablish- merit in Wales or of self-government for Ireland, it was THE NEGATION OF DKAIOCRACY if they were going to allow a minority to lay down the law and say that, in fact, the tail should wag the dog. Such a system would not work in our orderly, modern, democratic progress. Councillor Hawthorn, who had proved such an acquisition to the Town Council, had alluded to the blessings of the Insurance Act. There was another indirect benefit of that Act, so valuable that it actually compared in importance with the direct, purposes of the measure in relieving sickness and suffer- ing. He referred to the effect of the Act upon health and housing—one of the most pressing problems which could concern a gathering of workers like that. Mr Lloyd George and those ,ho had hacked him up bad conferred incalculable benefits upon millions of our people by insuring Vz.ern against ill-health, but what the nation had not yet recognised were the wonderful subsidiary advantages of the Act. If in any locality the fair average of illness was exceeded by JO per cent, the cause of that illness was traced back to those who were responsible, whet' er individuals or public authorities. They were not allowed to tolerate insanitary conditions and if, for instance, bad water was found to be productive of excess of sickness in any neighbourhood the landlord or public authority could be penalized in a proportion of the cost of dealing with the cases of ill-health. The Act was so framed that he did not see how any guilty pereon, who was found to be responsible for

SLEAI CONDITIONS, could escape. In Mr Lloyd George they had a man who, having risen from humble circum- stances, had come forward to grapple with these realities which so closely concerned the people of our country, and above all, the women. The Insurance Act and old age pensions were, as the Premier said in Scotland, the most monumental and splendid piece of social reform that we had ever seen carried in this country. (Applause.) A party which,in addition to those constructive Acts of social reforro,had the proud privilege of defending the great and good system of Free Trade, with the purity of public government ad the freedom of opportunity to manu- facturers which it gave us, had every reason to hold its head high. (Applause.) Mr Crosfield concluded with a story about Mr John Burns, who, on leaving a meeting at the las.t, moment, had to ride to the station on a hearse which he happened to overtake. At the station he was hailed by a tariff reform lecturer who shouted : "Hello, Mr Bnrns. What have you got there ?" " " replied Mr Burns Inside here v.e have got Protection stone dead—(laughter and applause)—and tariff reform is pretty nearly as bad. (Lhughter.) We shall have that inside very soon." (Laughter and applause.) By way of giving the unfortunate lecturer a third shot in the eye, Mr Burns smacked himself on the chest and said " Here on the box you have got Free Trade triumphant." (Applause.) Wherever he (Mr Crosfield) went, he found the Liberal party in great fighting form, and he had never addressed a finer meet- ing in that ward. (Applause). Councillor PEACOCK proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Crosfield, the ward captain and helpers. Having referred to the good example set by Whitecross Ward in its allegiance to Liberalistn, he said his only regret was that Mr Crosfield was not the Member for Warrington. However, he felt sure—and be spoke with a knowledge of what was going on in arrington—that the next time the Liberals of Warringtfin would have a better chance than ever they had had W that, with the assistance of Mrs Crosfield, they would he ahle to pull Mr Crosileld through and keep him in Parliament. (Applause).

BONAR LAW'S BLUNDERS.
MRS. A. H. CROSFIELD ON FALSE
PROPHECIES.
MR. CROSFIELD ON THE SLUM PROBLEM

The Warrington Women's Liberal Association resumed its activities on Thursday evening, when a tea meeting for the members in Whitecross Ward was held in the Thewlis-street Schools. Mr and Mrs A H Crosfield and Miss Crosfield attended and were accorded a remarkably enthusiastic welcome. Excellent arrangements for the gathering had been made by Mrs Delaney (ward captain), assisted by the workers in the ward, the members of the Committee of the Association and Mrs E Osborne (hon secretary). About 300 sat down to tea, and the usual concert and meeting followed. Mrs A H Crosfield (president of the Association) was in the chair, and others on the platform included : Mr A H Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Alderman James Evans, Councillors Hawthorn and Peacock, Miss Agnes Kennedy (Central Campaign Committee for Welsh Disestablishment), aid Mrs Osborne. Mrs E A Sanders had arranged a most enjoyable musical programme, consisting of songs by Miss Elsie Wilkinson, Miss Eva Tanner and Mr McArthur, and humorous sketches by Mr J H Knowles. Mr Tom Tanner was an efficient accompanist. It was announced that a prize for the best knitted pair of child's socks had been awarded to Mi es Evans, Elizabeth-street. Mrs CROSFIELD, who was very cordially received,said that since she last had the pleasure of addressing them, a great many important events had happened in England. First of all, she must allude to THAT MEMORABLE DAY

_ January 13th, 1913—(applause)—when a certain number of babies were born with silver spoons in their mouths. (Laughter and applause.) Having referred to some of the ancient superstitions attaching to the numher 13, particularly in the East, Mrs Crosfield said that personally she regarded it as her lucky number and she was certain that those present would agree with her that the year 1913 was a lucky one. (Applause.) She hoped it would bring them every sort of good luck arm happiness. (Artilause.) Another notable circumstance was that they were holding their first ward tea in the new year on February 13th, and she hoped that augured even greater successes in the future. with regard to the Insurance Act, she did not know whether any of them remembered MR BONXR LAW'S PROPHECY

in the House of Commons on the first day of the session: "I venture to express the belief that although the hon. gentlemen on the benches opposite are very proud to have called it an Act, because it has become law, it will never come into operation." (Laughter.) They could all afford to laugh at that prediction, but was it not pitiful that a leader in such a responsible position should make assertions of that kind, which only rendered him ridiculous ? (Hear, hear.) Not only was the Act now in operation, but there were 14,000,000 people insured against sickness and 2,250,000 against unemployment. On January 13th there was £8,000,000, ready to be paid out for health insurance. (Applause). Money was flowing into the Treasury at the rate of £33,000 a week to meet the claims for unemployed benefit. After that, let Mr Bonar Law talk about the Act not b,?coming a law. (Applause.) She hoped all Mr Boner Law's prophecies would meet exactly the same fate. He had recently declared that there was every indication that Ulster would fight and he that could not, blame Ulster for fighting. 'Ale Home Rule Bill had how- ever, passed its third reading in the House of Commons by the large majority of 110. Then it was sent to the House of Lords, and of course they knew what happened there. Laughter). The Lords threw it out, but what did they Liberals mind ? They could

SNAP THEIR FINGERS-AT TIIE LORDS now. (Applause). In two years time they hoped the Bill would receive the Royal assent and be placed upon the statute book. (Applause). If Ulster sat down to think,she would not g‘,t up to fight again. (Applause)• In whatever direction they turned they found the Tory party in the same sad plight ; they really did not know which way to go. They reminded her of a feather that was being blown hither and thither in a gale—although she did not want to suggest that they were feather. headed. (Laughter.) Mr Bonar Law himself said some years ago : " I remember hearing of a man who was seen following a band of robbers and was asked Why are you following these men?' I most follow them was the reply, ; I'm their leader.' " (Laughter.) She was afraid thaL was poor Mr Bonar Law's condition. Hel was to follow wherever others chose to direct, because be was their leader. (Laughter.) Now, how- ever, they bad a new policy—they were going to have Tariff Reform, but they were not going to tax food. At the same time they were going to give Colonial preference—which was quite impossible, because every- body could tell them that they could not possibly give the Colonies a preference if they did not

div.head: TAX FOOD.
div.p: TAX FOOD.

The bulk of what the Colonies sent us was food ; the rest of the things they exported to England were in such small quantities that they were really of DO importance whatever. She had recently been staying in Paris and she had noticed that vegetables, butter, meat—in fact, every single article was not as good but dearer than were to be obtained in London. That, she maintained, was the effect of taxes. At the present time the rca.nufacturing interests were clamouring for higher duties, but their demand was not shared by the poor people who had no desire to pay further enhanced prices for their commodities. The workers must there• fore give no credence to the stories they heard from the Tories about tariffs not meaning higher cost of living. Mrs CItOSFIELD made a fieling reference to the terrible calamity which had overtaken Captain Scott and his intreped hand in the Antarctic regions. She wes sure all present would join with her in expressing their deepest sympathy with Mrs Scott in her irreparable loss. They need not pity the captain or his comrades, for there was nothing more glorious than to die for one's country andlto die so heroically as they did,facing deathlwith unflinching courage. But it was a lameut- able thing for those who were left behind and every- one must welcome the Premier's statement that pro- vision would be made for the dependents of the dead heroes. Finally Mr Crosfield asked the audience o join with her in extending a hearty welcome to Alderman Evans whom they were so glad to see looking fit and hearty, and quite recovered from his recent long ill- ness. (Applause.) Alderman JAMES EVANS briefly addressed the meet ing. When be was fist attracted to politics he said, such a gathering as that would hardly have been countenanced. In these days, however, women were increasingly realizing how closely politics concerned them and many of them were insisting on equality with the men in regard to electoral power. (Applause). He was glad there were signs of better social conditions for the masses, and it was for them to rise to the occasion and show their appreciation of the advantages won for them in political warfare. The high road to progress and position, once barred to the humbly circumstanced, was now open to every boy in the country. (Applause). Mrs CROSFIELD informed the gathering that the next day was Aldeman Evan' s birthday and they all heartily wished him" Many happy returns of the day." (Applause). Miss CROSFIELD gave an interesting address on a subject which s',e said did not receive the attention it deserved—the

div.head: WAGES OF WOMEN WORKERS.
div.p: WAGES OF WOMEN WORKERS.

The number eds-v-O-rnesi; between the ages of 20 and 25 who earned their own living in any capacity worked out at 66 per cent. Taking the average of women of all ages, throughout the country, 34 per cent. were wage earners. That meant that a third of the women sup- ported themselves by their Gan work. She supposed it was common knowledge that, with a few exceptions, their wages were very much less than those of the men. She was proud to think that one great exception was to be found in their own native county of Lancashire. In the cotton industry the men had received the women into their trade unions and the consequence was that they received equal wages. There were women in the north of Lancashire who received from 25s to 35s a week—excellent wages—but in the other textile industries, the average wage of women was much below 15s a week. Having touched upon the extensive employment of girl labour in London jam factories, and to the work done at low wages by women in the clothing and warehouse industries, Miss Crosfield said one remedy for such conditions was the protection of the vote,as Mr Lloyd George and Lord Haldane had told them. Another was better training for the girls, beeause much of the work referred to was unskilled labour and if only the girls could be better trained they would command higher wages. A Bill ought to be introduced to limit the work of boys and girls alike and they would then be able to continue their education at the technical and evening continua- tion schools. (Applause.) Miss KENNEDY then delivered an interesting address on the question of Welsh Disestablishment. In a general reference to the achievements of the Govern- ment, she said its work came nearer the teaching of the Sermon on the Mount than that of any Government since the world began. As to the Welsh question, she referred to the overwhelming preponderance in numbers of the Nonconformist., pointing out that there were four Nonconformist full members to one communicant of the Church of England in Wales. Counting all Nonconformists, the proportion worked out at ten to one. She contended that the Church in Wales would be more prosperous after Disestablishment, as it was not good for the life of a Church that it should be, bounty-fed. Touching upon the ancient endowments she contended that when the Roman Catholic Church ceased to be the Church of this country that money should have been handed over to the nation for the benefit of the whole country. Councillor HAWTHORN moved the following resolu- tion :—" That this meeting heartily welcomes the Bill for the Disestablishment and Disendowment of the Church of England in Wales as giving effect to the long expressed desire of the overwhelming majority of the Welsh nation, and pledges itself to do all in its power

div.p: WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION
ELECTION OF MAY QUEEN.

At tho electic n of Queen for the coming May festival for which all the societies affiliated with the Union are requested to nominate one of their members, Miss Maud Kirkland was unanimously voted for this position of honour. Miss Kirkland has been a member of Hill ClifTe and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope for 12 yews and is a very devoted worker in connection with that society. She has also taken part in each of the preceding May festivals and last year occupied the position of fairy queen and her selection for the premier position will be very popular amongst the workers and members of the Band of Hope movement.

div.p: WE PUT NO DROPS OR DRUGS IN THE EYES
Wycliffe P.S A. Society.

There was a good meeting on Sunday last presided over by Mr B Farrar, who spoke upon " I Will " as bearing upon the future work before us. Given the "I will," its perfect work in our home life, our daily life, our social and religious efforts, and we shall accomplish much.—Mr G H Langton gave the address upon " Satirs vision by the way," and what it enabled Paul afterwaris to do for Christ and his fellow men. Saul's whole life past was male plain. The grett light he saw on the road to Damascus, exposed all the black spots of his life and his present purpose. Mr McEachern and Mr A Healey also tiok part in the meeting.—The President proposed a vote of sympathy with Mr R Lewis in his long illness ; also with Mr R ,tcliffe in the sickness of his wife.—The meeting was very interesting throughout.

div.head: Missionary Work in Africa.
div.p: Missionary Work in Africa.

Mr. D. Crawford, F.R.G.S., the author of the book I entitled "Thinking Black," which deals with Missionary work in Africa, gave a graphic account of his twenty- three years' labour as a missionary in South Africa, in a lecture in the Gospel Hall, Forster-street, on Tues- day evening. The Lecturer has also translated the New Testament into the Luba language. The LEcTrItER said missionary work in Africa seemed to be a very practical thing. Everything was thrown into the missionary's bag. He was the doctor, the teacher, the road end bridge builder, and above all, the house builder. He was proud to say be had been t/,e means of gutting out many tropical slums of Central Africa and lining out the natives in long one-street villages. Be had a hank of twine, which, he asserted, had lined out more than six miles of house frontages. The greatest part, however, a miesionary had to play in that lone country, after the Gospel of love, was the , settlement of tribal troubles. For centuries the African tribes had been playing at" Cain and Abel," cutting each other's throats for no cause at all. Here it was a missionary played many a noble part,getting in amongst them with only a walking-stick. The result would be a long two days' palaver when the sheer stupidity of the thing was borne in on those wild men's brains, and they buried the hatchet again and again.

div.head: International Peace Movement.
div.p: The International Peace Movement.
Rev. H. Dunnico's_ Appeal to Bishop

At Kensington Chapel, Liverpool, on Sunday-night the Rev Herbert Dunnico, who is closely identified with the international peace movement, referred to the noble words of Admiral von Tirpitz in the German Reichstag. During recent years, said Mr Dunnico, pacificists had had much to gladden as well as to sadden them but no event had happened in big recollection half so important as the intimation of the. Secretary of State for the German Navy that they were willing to call a halt on terms laid down by our own Government. Only a few months ago it had been his privilege to visit Germany and to enjoy the hospitality of several municipalities, and he was at that time deeply impressed by the more than generous feelings entertained by all classes towards Britain. Mr Crooks, M.P., bad said to them at the time. "If the Germans don't love us, then they are the greatest hypocrites have ever met." They knew now that it was not hypocrisy but genuine regard that lay behind that German welcome. In past years the Christian Church bad played a most ignoble part. in the peace crusade. It had been either criminally silent or vulgarly blatant and obsequious in the presence of the military spirit ; and what was she going to do now ? Her testing time as well as her opportunity was at hand, and if she failed in this hour she would cease to count among the moral forces of the age. The Bishop of Liverpool had demonstrated on more than one occasion that be could lead it in a worthy cause. Might he (Mr Dunnico) appeal to the Bishop to call the Christian people of the city together in order that Liverpool might play a worthy part in a great crusade for establishing the world's peace?

div.head: Colborne-street Baptist Church
div.p: Colborne-street Baptist Church

The Rev H Ogden preached at Golborne-street on Sunday night upon " a week and the Gospel." His text was from John xii.. " The poor ye have with you always." He declared that imposing buildings may he built upon flimsy foundations. An amiable prelate in a cosy palace, or a minister secure in an income of £l,OOO a year, or a piously disposed capitalist were comforted with the assurance that the poor we should always have. It is so much easier to build a church than annihilate a slum, easier to sign a cheque than clean up a district. The poor are thriftless and to remove them would only create a slum elsewhere. Evidently God intended there should he poor and poor there will always be. That view is a comfort to a conscience that is quickened by evident social inequalities. However social life advances there will always oe bearts i to cherish whilst the days are going by, but poverty s a product of man and too often a cloud between man and God. What has the Gospel to say about £1 a week in our present day? £t a week of course is purely a relative term. £1 a week might have been a salary to our grandfather.,but not a living wage to-day. The Gospel points to life that is ideal in mind, in soul in body. Its like leaven which leave us the whole lump. Does a£l a week make an ideal life in body, soul or mind ? The landscape is crc wded with block- houses of bricks and mortar and the field is strewn with dyine consumptives. Coneestion of cities and towns is all a matter of £s d. Drink never did make our slums. It accentuates their horrors. £s d made the slums and now drink exploits human misery and makes the solution almost thrice impossible. Where must the unskilled labourer reach when he leaves or is ejected from his cottage to find a home in a great city? His pay is at the rate of soiled goods. His labour value is almost nil. Whatever be his morel status or spiritual attainments there is only one spot for him, the place where food and rent are lowest. His £1 a week, if he has it ; buys him misery. Does the Gospel sanction that? The Gospel denies it and opens out the better way. The Gospel intends man to live the fuller life. £1 a week is a celibates income and not the pittance of a married man. The Bible advises marriage and the replenishing of the earth, and a railway porter may be permitted to replenish on a£l a week. Australia is said to be the Paradise of a single man, and the tariff of it married man. That is equally true of England. If a man would live in decent house ; if he would live upon decent food ; if his wife is to be decently attired, and his bairns are to hold up their heads with th9rest of the street, £1 a week is impossible. The empire demands that our youth should be married. Fatherhood and motherhood are eulogised, but they are impossible on a £1 per week. The man who does it is a hero. The woman who does it is a heroine ; she is a Grace Darling all the way. The Gospel opens out to man the fuller life. .£1 a week narrows, limits, dehumanizes. The Gospel must prevail.

div.head: INSURANCE ACT. HEALTH COMMITTEE AND THE SANKEY
div.p: THE INSURANCE ACT. HEALTH COMMITTEE AND THE SANKEY
SANATORIUM

Speaking at a ward meeting in connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Association on Thurs- day evening Councillor Hawthorn alluded to the operations of tile Insurance Act in Warrington. He pointed ( ut that many of the patients recently admitted to the SankAy sanatorium were insured per- sons, and the Insurance Committee paid the Health Committee so much per week in respect of them. The accommodation at Sankey had already proved too small and in the course of a week or two the com- mittee wruld bring before the Local Goveri.ment Board a scheme for enlarging the sanatorium, so that they would be able to treat all the people in War- rington who suffered from consumption. If ever evidence were needed of the usefulness of the Act, it was to be found in the great demand for sanatorium treatment. (Applause.

HEAVY MOTOR VEHICLES IN LANCASHIRE In the House of Commons, on Monday, Mr Higham asked the President of the Local Government Board whether his attention had been called to the repre- sentations from municipal corporations and urban district councils of Lancashire as to the vibration and damage being caused to houses and shops adjoining main thoroughfares by heavy motor vehiclas, daily increasing in number ; also the splashing and squirting of mud on pedestrians, shop windows, &c. Mr Burns : I have rec-ived representations from various local authorities on this subject. The regula- tions contained in the Heavy Motor-car Order were based upon the recommendations of a Depirtmental Committee, and I do not see my way at present to modify the particular provisions referred to by the hon. member, but the matter is not being lost sight of. The compulsory provision of mudguards appears to me to be within the scope of regulations und .r the Motor-car Acts, but I am not satisfied that an effective mudguard has yet been invented.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
" Cinderella."

Mr. James Kiddie's pantomime " Cinderella," which has drawn large houses to the Hippodrome this week is a capital operatic, spectacular and genuinely funny p'rcductiou and the management are to be congratu- lated upon securing such an able company of smart dancers, refined singers, witty comedians and clever actors to amuse and entertain their patrons. The scenic effects are carried out on a lavish scale and the music is of a most enchanting and captivating nature. Chief amongst the many laughter provokers is Mr Leo Bliss the amort‘us page, Pimples, who, during the ibtervals of leve-making with the charming Cinderella, keeps the audience in one continual state of Jr dsterous merriment. Miss Queenie Mayor thoroughly capti- vates the audience as Cinderella with her grace and beauty, combined with her flexible voice, which is heard to decided advantage in duets with Miss Lily Ennis who is a dashirg Prince Perfect. The latter has a choice stock of catchy songs and is at Once popular with the audience. Mr Will Kirk and Billy Wesley are very successful as the ugly sisters and share equally in the honours as comedians of merit. Mr V. illie Barratt as the bibulous Baton Shiphtalotte has the happy knack of causing laughter just at the right time, the while scheming that the Prince shalt marry one of his ugly daughters. Miss May Grayce greatly rleased the audience with her singing in the role of Dandini. Miss Bessie Willow was a charming fairy godmother, Sunbeam and Miss Bertha Irving was also successful as Marquis de Cadie. Specialities are given by the Sisters Mayor and The I.isando Brothers, the former being smart American coons who dance cleverly and the latter marvellous and dexterous equilibrists, hand to hand balancing being a special feature. There will be a matinee to-day at 2.30 and two performances to-night. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

"Wakes Week"and "Perkins M.P" will be presented by Fred Kai /l.'s London company of clever comedians next week, Mr Tom Nelson appearing as " Joe Waddle" and Perkins. Nelson is truly described as the inimitable comedian and patrons of the Hippodrome are in for a good thing. Other turns will he The Sisters Gilbey, musicians and dancers ; Charburn's Young Stars, in vocal and dancing scena ; Jimmy Athlone, Sandow's lecture model; Russell Brandow, coon comedian.

Si'. HELENS TRAGEDIES. COLLIER'S WIFE BURNED TO DEATH.

Mrs Mary Barton, the wife of a collier, living at 33 Binney-street, Sutton, died at the St. Helens Hospital on Sunday morning, under exceedingly distresing cir- cumstances, from burns received at her home. About eight o'clock last Thursday morning, it appears, she was looking about for some money she had mislaid. Her husband was sitting in the kitchen, when she went into the •front room with a candle Soon afterwards she rushed back into the kitchen with her olothes on fire. The husband at once wrapped a cape about her, but the poor woman was burned from head to foot. Dr It Cook had her removed to hospital. At four o'clock on Friday morning Mrs Barton was confined prematurely, and her cmdition became hopeless. After the accident the husband found that a paraffin lamp that was on a shelf in the room had been knocked down, and it is surmised that the oil had spread over Mrs Barton's clothes. She was thirtv-six years of age.

div.head: MERRIE ENGLAND.
div.p: MERRIE ENGLAND.
COLOUR AND MOVEMENT OF LIFE IN THE MIDDLE AGES.
THE GROWTH OF TRADE UNIONS.

Continuing his series of lectures on " The Guilds of the Middle Ages " at the Socialist Hall, Wilderspool Causeway, on Monday evening, Mr J Dalby took for his subject "Organization and conditions of work in the craft guilds." He pointed out that in the early history of the guilds, the feeling that to them was entrusted the honcur of a trade, a profession, was a great spur towards good workmanship. As the guilds became wealthy, that fine spirit of honour rather degenerated and, instead of inspiring the actual workers with £l. motive for the best workmanship, blossomed out into a mania for display, the several guilds competing among. themselves as to who should produce the most magnificent pageant shows. The lecturer also referred to the great dramas, on the story of Christianity, which were supported by the guilds.

div.head: EIGHT HOURS A DAY.
div.p: EIGHT HOURS A DAY.

Thorold Rogers, had stated his belief that,to wards the close of the middle ages, the average labourer worked only eight hours a day. He said : "The artisan who is dernanciing at this time an eight hours day in the building trades is simply striving to recover what his ancestor worked by four cr five centuries ago." Never must we forget that anything like the modern speeding up of labour was absolutely foreign to the whole system of things then. Setting aside the middleman of the richer crafts, master craftsmen and servant would work together at whatever task was in band,whether it was a piece of work which the master in his capacity of small retailer WaS making to stock, or whether it was work on material supplied by the customer. In Belgium the proportion of wages was fixed as between master and servant. In his first lecture he quoted the regulation against work by candle-light, introduced at first no doubt in order to guarantee good workmanship and per- haps to protect the worker against excessive hours. Afterwards, like most of the restrictive enactments of the guild, it became is defensive weapon, used to pro- tect the guild in a state of society into which was steal- ing more and more the baneful competitive principle. In later times the guild worked to secure for itself, or rather for its richer members, that monopoly which was so sought after by our modern trusts. MOItE COLOUR AND MOVEMENT IN LIFE. As regarded the number of holidays in the year, Thorold Rogers, whose method was always striotly scientific, stated that whatever might have been the good fortune of the foreign worker, the English work- man had very few days of holiday in the year outside Sundays. Though he (the Lecturer) had no first hand 1 knowledge on the subject, he did not feel convinced, by the evidence he brought, that things were so bad. It was not taken for granted then, as it is now, that the preservation of good trade was the great purpose which should inspire all good and true men. Alter all, magnificent as that ideal might be, it left life rather a dull, grey thing for the geuerality. Now it was his opinion that, in spite of telephones, railways and even picturedromes, there was much more colour and move- ment in the world for everybody to see and feel in the middle ages, than there is now. There were royal visits, visits of foreign ambassadors,Church processions and pilgrimages and, according to contemporary accounts, the pupulace was always in evidence on those occasions. Why should they not have been? There was no machinery then; steam was not up, which might he wasted if work was stopped. Then there were pilgrimages to make, lairs to attend and, if one had the music-hall gift, one could do very well as a wandering minstrel. At anyrate, there was always the chance of some fighting. Life was much freer and one did not abstain from healthy human enjoyment for fear lest one should be inefficient for the next day's work. So that he thought the holiday allowance worked out much better than it does now.

div.head: TRADE UNION RESTRICTIONS.
div.p: TRADE UNION RESTRICTIONS.

Dealing with points of resemblance between the old English guild cud the modern trade union, Mr Dalby said every effort was made by the guild to get such powers as would enable it to forbid those outside the guild to fullow the particular trade practised by that guild. No guild member could be arraigned about trade matters before any other judge than the one appointed by the guild. Some attempt was made to restrict the output of wares and the prohibition of night work aught have been laid down pray to that end. No guild associate was to entice away a brother's customer ora brother's servant. Frequently we found restrictions as to the number of servants and apprentices allowed to an individual. Guild statutes forbad further working for a customer who was still indebted to a brother. As long as members of the guild were out of work, no member was to work with non-members. lhe last prohibition reminded us, too, of the treatment meted out to blacklegs in the strike to-day. On the other hand, a member was always allowed to employ his wife, children and maid in work. Later that led, of course, to a family caucus. Newcomers to the town were kept out of the guild and employed only an servants, whilst admission into the select circle was made as easy Us possible for relations of the members themselves. Refusal of any of the members to pay entrance fee and mdouveesmesnotmesetitmeisn resulted in their tools being taken away. Towards the end of the period, a towards amalgamation. The more powerful guilds were often naturally amalgamated through the Town Council, which they controlled ; and the inferior guilds were forced to come together in their own interest. REGULATION OF TRADE.

Mr. DALBY touched upon the very large part a hich the guilds in their corporate capacity played in the regulation of trade. They drew up regulations, aimed at the prevention of fraud and insisting on the observance of certain standards of size and quality in the wares produced. Of course, the tendency towards centralization was always going on, More and more, the State by its officials was taking into its own hands the fixing of standard measures. Even when the crafts had the watter in their own hands, they only laid down their restrictions when the town or Government allowed them and, although the early guild theory might have laid the stress on the honour of the craft which must be kept at all costs, the towns looked upon those regulations as protecting the interests of the con- sumer. Then, too, it was a handle of power, by no means to be despised, as the crafts grew more wealthy and anti-social. Referring to the growth of the power of the Central authority, Mr llalby said that although in the great battle between town and guilds, which took place in England durirg the early part of the fifteenth century, the guilds generally won, it was only is victory in appear- ance, for the officers of the guild were transformed into the officers of the town, and the town in turn was brought under the strong hand of the State. The stronger guilds had law courts of their own which they clung to as marks of their independenne, in the same way as the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge clung to thelr Court of the Vice-Chancellor and his assistants.

THE APPRENTICESHIP SYSTEM. One of the most interesting things about the guilds was their system of apprenticeship which made every trade into an industrial school. At first, before the guilds had become exclusive Corporations, there was no system at all, no fixed period of bondage for the youth and no great insistence on apprenticeship at all. In the beginnit g of the 15th century the apprentice seemed to be looked upon as a 3 outh destined soon to be a master, as against the servants who had no chance of ever being free workers. They would see the modern parallel, of course, in the case of the manager's son or relative. Later still it appeared that some masters were employing apprentice labour on a large scale in order to avoid employing adult survants or journeymen, and a statute of Elizabeth laid it down that at least one journeyman most be employed for the first three apprentices, and at least one journeyman for every additional apprentice. The usual period for the apprentice in England was seven years ; in Scot- land he was given full wages in his last year. Abroad the period of apprenticeship was not so long, but once out of his time, the apprentice had to travel to seek work for a few years and in Germany, unless he happened to be a relative of some guildsman, he had to produce a "masterpiece" or fine specimen of work, before he would be granted the full freedom of the guild. The apprentice was also given a certain training in arms and when,as happened in London on more than one occasion, war was declared between the companies, the streets rang with the battle cries of the rival prentice bands.

A PURITANICAL NOTE. Finally Mr Dalhy referred to the Puritanical note in some of the guild documents, because he regarded it as a symptom of a very grave defect, which lay very near to the root of things. In one record the brethren were exhorted to take very stern measures against any com- rade who was given to lying in bed in the morning. They were to fetch him out and se 3 that he went to his work. Then in a contract between one John the master and Walter his apprentice, it was laid down that " the aside Walter shall he none ale goer neyther to no la b 31d nor sporte during the said vii. yeres without the licence I of the slid John." We must remember the difference in the times. It was really very much as though a! business man, in taking in a lad in his office, were to demand that he should never go to a football match, ' nor visit a cafe or theatre. Now, of course (concluded the lecturer) I am act saying that such a demand was always made—l am sure it was never kept—but over and over again we come upon that note of restraint. I am one of those who believe with William Morris that "No work which cannot be done with pleasure in the doing is worth doing." The more 1 study these guilds the more 1 feel that though they had got hold of the principle of co-operation, yet they held it in a fixed and stilted way. And if we are to recover it in the future—and I see no hope for humanity unless we do—we shall have to have it in an altogether freer and finer way. Then, if I may be allowed a Theological reference, it was the Law rather than the Gospel. No system of co-operation is any use in which all kinds of restrictive regulations have to be made by one Guild as a protec- tion against another, or by one lot of Guild members as against the evil nature of their brothers in the Guild. It is this hardness, this fixity which appears to me as the one fatal defect in the Medireval Guilds, and it is my belief that the centuries that have passed since those times have not gone for nothing, but rather in them a type of humanity has been moulded which will be able to found and use a co-operative Commonwealth in all I the full freedom cf that glorious ideal.

div.head: MR. W. P. RYLANDS ON TAXATION. ---- ITS RELATION TO SOCIAL REFORM,
div.p: MR. W. P. RYLANDS ON TAXATION. ---- ITS RELATION TO SOCIAL REFORM,

Mr W Peter Rylands touched upon the relation of taxation to social reform in an interesting paper on " The theory and incidence of taxation" before the members of the Literary and Philosophical Society in the Patten Hall on Monday evening. Mr Oswald Loftbouse presided over a fair attendance. Mr RYLANDS endorsed the maxim of Adam Smith that the subjects of every State ought to contribute towards the support of the Government as nearly as possible in proportion to their respective abilities. That principle in its highest interpretation Feenied to demand not only a contribution in proportion to the individual's ability to pay, but also that his sense of contribution should be real, and that he should thus tool a personal interest in good government, and be inclined to check rather than encourage extravagance in public finance. While all tavation was borne by the producers, all expenditure of public revenue by the governing body, provided it was spent at home, flowed back again ultimately into the pockets of the producers in the form of rent, wages, or profit. The whole burden being borne by the producers, the weight of that burden varied in proportion to the 'amount of unproductive labour which it supported. The economic soundness or otherwise of taxation depended upon a comparison between the method in which the governing body spent the money and the manner in which it would have been spent had it been spent in the discretion of the indivi- dual members of the community._

The essential test was the probable effect upon the productive capacity of the State. It was at that point that social reformers met with tv wave economic difficulty. A wealthy community, however' could afford for social reasons to incur expenditure, which, in the case of a poorer natioa would be dangerously unsound. Every measure of social reform providing, for instance, for the support of the population in times of sickness, accident or old age, infringed every economic con- sideration already enunciated, except so far as support in sickness rendered people more capable as workers when in health. The fact, however, remained that money spent in those directions roust inevitably prove an added burden upon the shoulders of the producer. No one, however, in a wealthy country like Great Britain would hesitate to express approval of such social measures, but it was none the less of the utmost importance that the economic effect of a policy of that kind should be appreciated to enable them to realiise that it was a policy which carried with it economic objection, and that there must be some point beyond which it could not be safe to go. If the proportion of unproductive labour was, by the action of the State, increased to any substantial extent the consequences must be an advance in prices and reduced rent, wages and profit derived from productive industry. While the subject was full of complexity there were certain guiding principles which anyone of intelligence could understand and apply, and while on the one hand the nation was wealthy enough to stand much, on the other hand there must be some limit to the burden of unprodactive labour which it could sup- port. Taxation fell largely upon labour through what- ever channel it was collected, and while it was right that the heaviest burden should fall first upon those most capable of bearing it. they must not deceive them- selves into a belief that the burden could not and would not be shifted on to the shoulders of others. The Rev. E. C• E. CA RLEfON, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr Rylands said that, in his opinion, there was a tremendous amount of economic heresy abroad to-day, and be was afraid, a great that of economic ignorance. He agreed with all Mr Rylatids had said, and especially with the statement that taxation was certain to fall upon productive labour if principles which were now being popularized were put into practice. It was usual to say that everything came from the land, but it would be much nearer the question to say that everything came from labour, and that nothing came from land except which was put into it by the labour of man. By itself laud was worth nothing, it was simply raw material, and until labour was brought to hear upon it, it was practically worthless. In every field of taxation we dealt with commodities very different from the way in which we dealt with land. The idea in other spheres was to tax the profits yielded, but in the matter of land it was expected to pay a tax without labour being brought to bear upon it. Mr A FetosT seconded the proposition. _ _ . .

Dr MANSON said the old t;coLiomists appeared to overlook the fact that the laws of political economy unlike the laws of chemistry and physics, were undo r the control of man. Mr Rylands had cksssed officials among unproductive labour. In one sense they might come withia that category but, if they looked at the nation as a living organism, he was inclined to think that the officials represented, to some extent, a kind of supporting structure. They could hardly say that officials, if they were rightly placed and had proper duties to perform in the interests of the nation, were unproductive individuals. Mr H Grosvenor said it was a fundamental principle that representation should go with taxation. We had not got beyond the theory at present,but in time he sup- posed we should attain more efficient system of govern- ment and have better control of our representatives. The people had a right to say what services should be rendered to them and in what way the funds should be obtained. It was a very unjust thing that any man should escape his proper share of taxation by being a teetotaller or non-smoker. (Laughter). All partici- pated in the services of the State and, therefore, all should pay according to their abilities. The speaker advocated a universal income tax as being easy of collection and just to all. Mr W ROWLAND said that by an income tax system we had definitely abandoned the theory of equality of payment, recognizing that the wan who had £2OO a year was not in the same position to meet taxation as the man with £2,000. It would be interesting to have an address on the ethics of taxation. Surely there was a very real reason why taxes should be placed upon the less necessary rather than upon the more necessary things of life. Referring to the suggestion made in New Zealand that amusements and football matches should be taxed to meet the cost of old age pensions, the speaker said it was an extremely useful proposition to make that the people who were suffer- ing in some way or another in the State should be paid for by the people who were giving themselves a certain amount of enjoyment. On the continent vast sums of money were raised by State forestry. He did not say that we could compete with great countries like Germany, with its immense natural forests, but there were possibilities of dealing with the question here, and, as it was an industry which could not be compared with ordinary competitive undertakings„ it seemed to be a proper one for the State to take up. The vote was heartily carried.

div.head: WOMAN WHO WAS.
div.p: THE WOMAN WHO WAS.
