div.head: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
THE
INDIANS AND THE FRYING PANS.

A good story has come from America. It will be known to most of my readers that Red Indians still live and flourish in America' and the Government takes an interest in them, giving them all sorts of tools and implements from Government stores. Among the things sent out to one of these stores was a supply of large frying pans with good long handles. But they did not appeal to the Indians and at the end of a year not a single pan was sold. Thinking it might be of advantage to the natives the agents pressed the frying pans upon them. At first they showed no interest,, but by the time he had given out about two dozen there came a sudden change. Not a day passed in which the agent did not have applications for at least a dozen, and some days he disposed of twice that number.

When the supply was nearly exhausted,he noticed among the applicants some to whom he had previously given pans, and naturally enough he became curious to know what use they were making of them. He questioned several of the men to no purpose, but at length a young buck, more communicative than the rest, gave him to understand that if he would visit a certain part of the reservation, not far away, he would find his inquiry answered. The next day, the agent rode out in the direction indicated. About two miles from

the agency he noticed on the crest of a narrow spur of the mountain three or four Indians who suddenly disappeared on the opposite side of the ridge. At the same time he heard,faintly, the cry of many voices. On turning the point of the ridge, he saw a ciowd of several hundred Indians, who were shouting as if greatly excited. He noticed also .several objects, which he at first supposed to be boulders, descending the side of the mountain toward them with frightful rapidity. Instead of fleeing from these moving objects, the Indians simply applauded and shouted. Soon he saw other objects, like the first, descending. In a short time the whole situation was plain to him. Having selected a long, smooth slope of the moun- tain, where there were no stones, the Indians had converted it into a sort of earthen toboggan slide, and were utilizing the frying pans as toboggans. Seating them- selves in the pans, they grasped the handles with both hands ; then, crossing their legs over their arms, they went spinning down the slide with great rapidity. The agent let them have the few pans that remained in the stotehouse, but did not order a new supply. THIS WEEK'S STORY.

In connection with recent celebrations at Delhi the Middlesex Regiment stationed in India was ordered to take part in a cere- monial parade. The Commander decided hastily to fit out the men with new boots and telegraphed to a Calcutta firm to send several hundred pairs. His telegram said "Send 500 pairs of boots for Middlesex by next train."
Many hours passed and the Commander became very anxious. At the other end the Hindu manager was

in a state of terrible axiety. He could make nothing of the telegram and finally wired in reply; "Order received, but not compre- hended. Male sex we know, ditto female sex. Middle Sex not known. Please send sample."

WHAT'S IN A NAME? My big doll is called Hildegard° ; little one is Marjorie; The paper dolls are Evelyn, Bettina, and Elaine The rag dog is named Claribel ; The baby I call Gwendolen. l've different taste from my mamma— She named me Susan Jane.

div.head: TANNING TRADE IN WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT.
div.p: THE TANNING TRADE IN WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT.

Although new tininess comes along in laggard fashion, we have had a full busy week ; contract deliveries have been taken up fully and to time, and in many cases consumers are asking for deliveries to be expedited, so that together with prompt sales (which continue numerous, the " quiet " time notwithstand- ing) practically everything which came down from the sheds had gone by the week-end. Stocks in tanners' bands continue very small, which naturally breeds an independent spirit, and nothing is changing hands except at fullest quotations, and in several quarters a determined effort is being made to push on a further advance. Unfortunately for buyers, it is of little use protesting they cannot pay more, for the tanner's obvious retort is that he can get his price, and as his depleted warehouse affords silent confirmation, argument is of course futile. A prolonged run on all low-priced bends lits been going on, and Madagascars, Mornbassas, and low-grade Capes have gone out as quickly as ever they might be found ; as to the relative cheapness of this class of stuff there may be two opinions, for a branded Cape at 18d. against a good secondary English (clear, of course) at 19d. and 190. seems t, compare rather poorly. Presumably the scarcity of American sides causes the demand for this bottom stuff ; meantime, of course, producers are not complaining. At the risk of being monotonous, I must again refer to the financial situation. Nearly everyone is "jumpy," and fears are general that there are many disastrous realisations to come ; as a consequence accounts are rigidly scrutinised, and credits are curtailed very largely. It is reported that one of our leading local firms has despatched a representative to South Africa to cultivate the market there, and the experiment is likely to be watched with much interest, as hitherto tanners have not done a very extensive direct foreign trade ; it has, however, been growing of late, and if the present venture is successful, it is sure to find imitators. SOLE LE ATITER.—Bends have been in regular good demand, but without much animation. English have sold up to full production' and heavy weights show considerable improvement. Some little business is reported in Army selections, and high prices have been made. As mentioned earlier, there has been com- petition for common grade lines. Shoulders continue to move very strongly, and all selections moved out very rapidly; bellies were very satisfactory in all classes, the briskest demand being for heavy goods. ROUGH LEATTIER.—S trap butts are urgently demanded, and it is no exaggeration to say that if deliveries could be doubled the market could still take more. Rough shoulders and bellies are absorbed as quickly as produced.—" From the Leather World."

div.head: COUNTRY HOUSE FIRE PROTECTION.
div.p: COUNTRY HOUSE FIRE PROTECTION.

Tha large number of serious fires, which annually ccour at country mansions,couclusively prove that there 's need for more adeq .ate fire extinguishing arrange- ments and in many insthoces improvements are being made in this connection. " Wentworth" Virginia Water, the vest of the Countess de Morella is a case in point. The fire protective arrangements at this country mansion, which are under the c'turge of Mr A Luff, have just been placed on a more satisfactory basis, by the acquisition of a Merryweather " Valiant " steam fire engine. This engine which pumps 100 gallons per minute, is mounted on a light two wheeled carriage, and can be readily wheeled about by a couple of men. Steam can be raised from cold water to working pres- sure in six and eight minutes, from the time of lighting up, so that the engine can be very quickly brought into action should occasion arise. The " Valiant " engine has been extensively adopted for country house fire protection, and in addition to its services in this con- nection it is also a very useful machine for carrying out various pumping operations such as are likely to be needed on a country estate.

div.head: TERRITORIAL DINNER.
div.p: TERRITORIAL DINNER.
THE ROYAL VISIT TO WARRINGTON.

At the invitation of Captain G R Crosfield, the men , of "A" Company,4tli Battalion Prince of Wales Vo:un- teers (South Lancashire Regiment) were entertained at dinner in the Men's Dining Hall at Messrs Crosfield's works on Tuesday evening. The function was arranged in celebration of Captain Crosfield's promotion to the rank of Major in the Battalion. For many 3-ears he has most energetically and successfully commanded the A Company which is drawn from employes of Messrs. Crosfield. Ile will now take charge of the Newton detachment and no doubt he will train them to that high standard of efficiency to which he has brought the men of "A" Company. At the dinner Captain Crosfield presided and he was sup- ported by Lieut.-Colonel B Fairclough (commanding the battalion), Captain and Adjutant Elgood, Lieut. Ingram, Second Lieutenants Robertson and Seymour , Jones, Sergt.-Major Newall, Instructors Hackett and ' Russell, Colour-Sergeant Ryder and ex-Colour-Sergt. Ashworth.

In proposing the toast of 'The King, Queen and other members of the Royal Family" the CHAIRMAN said that in view of the forthcoming visit of their Majesties to Warrington they had cause to drink the toast with greater pleasure than usual.

Speeches of an interesting character were made during the evening and the following artistes coot, i- buted to a capital programme :—Messrs W W Ray, J Newns and J Harrison, Sergeant Tynan, Private Hewitt, Private Lamb and Mr Brobbin. Mr R E Lee was an efficient accompanist and pianoforte soloist. Captain ELGOoD prop,sed the toast of "The Imperial Forces"and emphasised the great possibilities which lay before the Imperial forces. They had only got to think of what some of our largest Colonies had done for the Empire quite recently. (Hear, hear ) It seemed to him that was only the beginning of it. (Hear, hear.) Referring to tie" A " Company assembled that night, he said it had always seemed to him that they were worthy of considerable congratulation, for it was an ideal company. It was an example to any town and any works in any town that a Territorial Company should be formed entirely, from the officers downwards, from mearbers and employees of one firm. He did not think anyone could hope for anything better. A great deal could be said on the Territorial movement which was being discussed very generally at the present time. Every member should realise that, whilst they were members and wore the uniform, LS surli,they should put what they had rend In the papers at the back of their minds. Their " job " should be to make every particular unit a complete success. That was the only way in which any company or battalion could do any good, and also the only means of obtaining the right stamp of recruits and keeping them together. Whilst they were doing Territorial work, they must be in it heart and soul, and eo the thing properly. He had great pleasure in proposing the toast and coupling with it the name of Colonel Fairclou,gh. (Applause). Colonel eAIRCLOLIGII responded, and had an aband- ance of good advice for the men. They were members of a great force and, although they were called slackers,and useless, by the Little Englanders, they had plenty of hard work to do. They did it, knowing that it was for a good cause. (Applause.) Referring to the KING'S 'VISIT TO WARRINGTON,

he said it was a great honour which was going to be conferred upon the town of Warrington, and incident- ally upon Messrs Crosfield, as their Majesties intended to inspect their works. Incidentally, he hoped the "A" Company would worthily represent their battalion by turning up in full force as a works com- pany. He would do his hest to help the company to do credit to themselves and the town that day. (Applause.) He took it that the " A " Company's place would be somewhere near those kuildings. In conclusion, be said they were " playing the game" and, although some people might consider it a farce, they knew it was something worth workiag for and giving of their best for., (Applause). Captain CROSFIELD proposed the toast of the" A Company and expressed the sorrow he felt that he had to leave them as their commander. Hs was glad to know they were going to soldier on together in the same battalion. He might not be so intimately con- nected with them, yet they would still be all together. He wished to thank his subalterns, colour sergeants and their own colour-sergeant Ashworth, the non- commissioned officers and men for the way they had supported him and backed him up, and also for the way they had played the game. Ho hoped they would 'support Captain Layton as loyally as they had supported him. (Applause.) Reference had teen made to the rough time Territorials were experiencing at present. All Lhat lie would say to them was " stick to your Company and stick to this battalion of which we are all so proud." (Hear, hear.; Whatever theemight do in their private capacity, they had got to play the game whilst they were with the battalion, for the battalion. They all agreed when they came back from camp that they were better for having been there. There was in their attalion a fine esprit tic corps. It had an atmosphere—he dii not mean the atmosphere they f mind in the tents some mornings,which they could cut with a knife—(laughter) —lt was the spirit created by a body of men who threw themselves in the work and thought only of the efficiency of the corps. All those present could do their utmost t) create that spirit, develop and foster it by playing the game whenever they donned His Majesty's uniform. (Applause.) Lance Corporal Wright having spoken, Colour Sergeant Ryder responded. Ile deeply regretted they had lost such a good officer as C,ptain Crosfield but he hoped the conipany would work together quite as happily as they had hitherto done and do their best to help it along. Carvain Crosfield had been a great help to them whilst in camp and when they had been out for a five or six mile march he had taken out a map and given them some valuable information about historic battles which had been highly interesting. (Applause). In conclusion he proposed the toast of Captain Crostleld.
The toast wa-9 received with musical 'honours.

Colour Sergeant Ryder on behalf of the company presented Captain Crosfield with a handsome lurnin ,ai prismatic compass. In reply Captain Cr sfield said that if ever the country was so unfortunate as to be engage d in war and he had to use that compass, he would always think of tlie jolley fellows he had felt it ta great pleasure to command. (Applause).

div.head: SHORTAGE OF TEACHERS.
div.p: SHORTAGE OF TEACHERS.
PROFESSOR CONNER'S WARNING TO CHESHIRE.

Reference was made at the Cheshire Education Com- mittee, at Crewe, on Monday, to the dearth of teachers. A resolution was passed that in the case of uncertifi- cated teachers appointed since June, 1912, and to whom no allowance on account of past service was made in fixing their commencing salaries at the time of their appointment such allowance up to a maximum of four years at .£2 10s per year be made from April, 1913, provided that such allowance shall not raise the revised salary above the maximum salary allowed under the county scale. Professor Gunner warned the committee that they would have to take up the question of the salaries of certificated teachers as weil as uncertificated. That matter had not been before them, but he feared it ' would do so before long. One knew that the training college entrants showed a very remarkable variation, and that there was a dearth of teachers. The usual remedy was to reconsider the scale of remuneration, but ho was not anxious to press that at the present moment.

In reply to Colonel Dixon, the Chairman (Dr IIodg- son) said they had more applicants for admission to their own training college than they could satisfy. In a year or two the whole question of the remuneration of teachers must be considered ; hut the materials at their disposal at present were not sufficient for them to deal with the question. The successful venture of the National Union of Teachers in persuading parents that It was no good entering their children for teachers because there were no vacancies had had influence, and had no doubt led to the dearth of candidates which the training colleges were more or less feeling. It was the experience of school authorities, and certainly of the Board of Education, that in the near future there would be some distinct pressure felt with regard to the obtaining of teachers. Mr J Hinchcliff (teachers' representative) said he understood that there were only four male bursars from the secondary schools applying for admission to their training college next year. He was afraid that the whole trend of events seemed to point to their colleges becoming colleges for females only. He hoped they would be able t'o get a certain number of male entrants. The resolution regarding the salaries of uncertifl- cated teachers was adopted.

div.head: RUNCORN CRICKETER'S DEATH.
div.p: RUNCORN CRICKETER'S DEATH.

The death has taken place of Mr John Roberts, who was prominent in the Runcorn Cricket Club, being an excellent fast bowler. Two years ago he played with the LancashirVColts on the invitation of the County Committee. He was also a prominent chorister.

div.head: LEGAL DISADVANTAGES OF WOMEN
div.p: LEGAL DISADVANTAGES OF WOMEN

It is not often realized, by the general public, how handicappei women are. If husband and wife are in business jointly--and these cases are by no means rare although the wife may be an actual necessary factor by her acumen or skill in the success of the business, still she has no claim ; the business is legally her husband's ; she has no claim to share or salary. Married women who have separate property, and whose income has Income Tax deducted therefrom, cannot claim any return,even though the amount of income may be such that a claim is allowable. The claim must be made by her hus- band despite the fact that he may be entirely depen- i dent on such incetne. The returned tax will be paid to him only In caFes of intestacy, a mm's widow is harshly dealt with by the law. If there are children she takes one-third of the personal estate (that is broadly, property other I.han land or houses) and none of the real estate (houses and land). If there are no children she first takes £5OO. Beyond that she has none of his real estate, and one-half of his personal estate ; the other half reverts to her husband's relatives, and fail- ing any, to the Crown. On the other hand,in the case of a woman's intestacy the widower tdkes the whole of the personal estate and enjoys a life interest in the real estate. An unmarried woman who becomes the mother of a child is in a very unfair position as against that of the father of the child. The child is hers and not the father's. She only is responsible for the child's welfare. Against this, the children of a marriage are the children of the father, and the mother has no claim to them.

The laws of divorce operate largely in favour of the husband. Unfaithfulness en the part of a wife is suffi,•ient to enable a husband to obtain relief, but a woman must be able to prove cruelty in addition to infidelity to obtain a divorce. Won3en workers have been told by their Parlia- mentary representative that their grievances could ut be urged with any degree of success because they had no vote.

With regard to salaries, as school teachers they receive about two thirds of the salaries of their brothers, though they are required to qualify as highly as the male teachers. As factory inspectors, their maximum salary is £550. Male inspectors maximum is .f.. 1,200. Similar disparity applies to clerks, factory employees, shop assistants and others. Those employed by State contractors are often badly under- paid, to wit tailores,les. The possession of the vote will not interfere with women's duties as wives and mothers, and not cause them to neglect household duties. They pay taxes, they manage the household and look after the children. They become the parent of the children when the father dies and thereby take over the man's obligations. The countries that have extended the vote to women find that it works admirably.

div.head: EPISCOPAL MOTOR IN COLLISION.
div.p: EPISCOPAL MOTOR IN COLLISION.

The Bishop of Liverpool (Dr Chavasse) preached at Haydock on Sunday, and on his way back to the Palace in Abercromby-square, met with a somewhat exciting experience. It was about 9 pm. when his lordship, with his chauffeur in charge, was spinning along the highway from the place indicated. It was dark, of course, though there was the usual modicum of lights along the road, which is traversed by a county tramcar system. At a certain point on the homeward stretch the chauffeur was 'Anxious to pass a tramcar which then came up. The motor was manipulated so as to pass the end of the larger vehicle. Unfortunately, however, there was a misjudgment of proximities, the result being that the episcopal car struck the ' step of the tramcar, wrenchiug it with some force. There was a jolt of course, and halt, and a hurried scramble of people insidh the car to see what wag wrong and to help if necessary anyone who might be injured. The bishop was not greatly alarmed, but he as well as the chauffeur got out of the motor to see what had been the effect of the collision. His lordship took a head lamp and held it aloft while the chauffeur was making a m nute examination of the parts. It was found that the engines were not damaged, and beyond a few scrapes here and there the motor did not appear. to have sustained damage. Willing workers lent a hand to get the bishop out of his temporary difficulty.

THOMAS CARLYLE.
ELOQUENT APPRECIATION BY THE
REV. DR. MELLOR.

At Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday evening, the Rev Dr Mellor began a course of special sermons on "The leaders of revolt." The subject was "Thomas Carlyle and the gospel of might." The preacher dealt first with Carlyle's personality and then suggested the main outlines of his message. Sketching the career of Carlyle, he stated that poverty was his nursemaid ; the severity of Calvinism his foster-parent. By those he was reared and nourished, and the influence he drew in from them never left hitn;he never lcst the note of sternness and intensity,nor was he ever without the hardness of an ascetic spit it, almost, one might say, loving those trials of the body which purified the soul. He carried with him also to the end of his days a certain ruggedness of disposition a kind of wild grandeur of spirit, which was his heritage from generations of Puritan ancestry and fitted well with the scenery of his earliest years. Amid the
TURMOIL AND THE THUNDERS OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION

Carlyle was born, and from the streets of Paris to the countryside of Ecclefeehan the revolutionary spirit passed into the soul of the boy, whom his schoolfellows scoffed at because he rebelled against their usual ways, and there helped to form the man who was to go about the world, like a lion, devouring, and denouncing, and destroying idols. By his parents intended for the ministry, Carlyle's spirit revolted and he became a writer of books, the mightiest with the pen of all his generation, utterly loyal to his calling. "Of all that is written," said Nietzsche, "I love only what a man bath written with his blood. Write with blood and thou wilt find that blood is spirit." Well nigh every line that Carlyle wrote was penned with his blood; into his written words he put all himself. They were verily bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh, the essence of his being. Being a maker of books, he wrote about books and their writers. He wrote about ideas, of morality, of religion, of social life, all that men called philosophy. Ho wrote history and made dry records throb and glow witt life. He stirred the dry bones in the valley, BO that from the dust spirits arose and vanished heroes walked the earth again. Above all he loved to write about

div.head: GREAT MEN AND STRONG MEN
div.p: GREAT MEN AND STRONG MEN

and of his chosen ones—Cromwell, Frederick, Napoleon, Dante, Borne, John Knox—he wrote in such a way as o leave little for anyone else to say. Ile seemed to have a veritable passion for those in whom the divine spark of personality had blazed into flame ; his own fiery soul was a sort of beacon which answered to the lire of great souls through the ages. When he wrote history what he grasped himself and strove to give the world was not records and enactments, dates and slumbering facts, not even clicumstunce and destiny impelling her human pawns, but living, breathing, active men and women, making history by the play of their thoughts and passions, their whims and fancies and passing desires, as well as their lofty dreams and aspira- tions.

His record of the French Revolution was it long succession of living pictures, and behind the confusion, the disorder, the hoer ,r of the time be laid hold upon the quivering hearts and throbbing thoughts of human creatures, more or less like ourselves, who, by what they attempted, rightly and wrongly, made the time what it was. No one could read Carlyle's "French Revolution" without reflecting seriously and earnestly upon THE SOCIAL WRONG AND SOCIAL INJUSTICE of his own day, without seeing how, in human history, again and yet again, the lessons of eternal righteous- ness had to be learned, perhaps even " in a horror of great darkness and shakings of the world, and a cup of trembling which all the nations shall drink." We forgot sometimes that history was the record of human living and human acting. Not so Carlyle! Always he wrote with his eye fast fixed upon the individual. What he saw was personality, masterful and triumphant, or struggling blindly to express itself, to get the chance for expression. When Carlyle urged, as he did over and over again, the Gospel of Might, he meant always the might of genuine and sincere personality, not, mere physical strength, nor what we called simple brute force, but that interior might and majesty of the soul, spiritual might, in which were inherent all the intense values of life, justice, truth and goodness, the splendour of angels and the glory of God, in the presence of which 110 merely natural might, whether of physical nature or of law and custom, or of environment, had any justifiable claim. If his passion for great men led Carlyle often, as it did, to some contempt for tbe mass and the majority of mankind— were not the twenty miliion of his fellow-countrymen mostly fools ?—if it led him to set upon supremacy and leadership a value which, in so-called democratic times, men were apt to overlook, if it caused him to turn

div.head: HERO WORSHIP
div.p: HERO WORSHIP

not only into a religion but into a political creed, what then ? Did it make the truth of the man less real, did it alter the value of the idea for whica he strove so bravely, the idea that it was the spiritual part of a man that counted—what he called his personality, not his clothes, nor his wealth, nor his positio,:, nor his acci- dental place in the world, but himself, the true man, as he is ? In a world of illusion, of clothes, what we should be for over seeking was genuine personal worth and greatness. "Happy he who can look through the clothes of a man into the man himself and discern, it may be, in this or the other Dread Potentate, a more or less incompetent digestive apparatus; yet also an inscrutable venerable mystery in the meanest tinker that sees with eyes." Suppose we made that the test and standard in all our judgments, suppose we did go about thus stripping away the clothes and getting at the real man, neglecting the surface and the show of things, all the monstrous conspiring tricks of social life, for the sake of the real heart and soul,

div.head: WHAT A GRATEFUL AND SUBLIME MESS
div.p: WHAT A GRATEFUL AND SUBLIME MESS

we should make of the things to which we were accustomed, the distinctions we so loved ! What a falling and crashing down of dignitaries and so-called great men there would be ! What a debacle of Cabinet Ministers and members of a Parliament, municipal councillors and mayors and justices of the peace, bishops and ministers of religion and officials of all kinds ! What Carlyle believed passion- ately in religion. He preached faith in that which was wider and deeper and higher than we were ourselves, and loyalty to thr,se values of truth, beauty, justiae and love which we did but dimly grasp yet whict, if we grasped at all, we could not feel as other than eternal. Carlyle had no belief in creeds and dogmas—they were not religion to him—and in organised Caristianity he had no faith at all—" all manner of pulpits are as good broken and abolished " he said—but in genuine, spiritual religion, in the idealism that made life rich, tie did believe. If we believed one-half the things that Carlyle preached there would be nothing for it but promptly to turn the world upside down. What is man himself," he cries, but a symbol of God ! Is not all that he does sym- bolical, a revelation to sense of the mystic for Gcd- given force that is in him—a gospel of freedom which be, the messenger of nature, preaches, as he can, by act and word ?" Man had in him an infinite as well as a finite, a soul as well as a stomach. Grasp that soleien tact and all their philosophies of mechanism would blow up in smoke. Grasp that fact and they would no more sit content beneath a sysitem which degraded them and their fellows into machines and crushed the divinity within their soul. Let them not inquire too circumspectly into the details of Carlyle's teaching. Lie had, heaven knows, as inched all great men had, inconsistencies enough. But consistency was the fault of servile minds, and any way the were letter mattered but little. What they did need, and what they could get if they would, was the spirit of Carlyle's gospel—which was the spirit of the man himself—an utter confidence in freedom ; and in the personal power of humanity to mould its (fan destiny, coupled ivith the assurance that in the end the only right was might And the only might was right—that shams and pretences would go and truth remain.

div.head: OLD MAN'S SUICIDE.
div.p: OLD MAN'S SUICIDE.
PAINS IN THE JAW DISTRESSED HIM.

Depressed through illness, Joseph Jones, aged 66, who tor the past 14 months had been an inmate at the Workhouse, ended his life, while on a visit to his niece in Fitzberbert-street, by cutting his throat with a razor. Tue inquest was conducted at Warrington on Monday, by Mr F A Jones, the deputy coroner.

- Annie Moores, 39, Fitzherbert-street, sal4 the deceased was her oncl3 and was formerly an ironworks labourer. Until quite recently he had always been of a cheerful disposition. A short time ago he began to complain of a pain in his jaw. About six months ago he had two teeth extracted and since had suffered from neuralgia. It was her uncle's custom, when he had a day out, to spend it at her home, and he visited her on Tuesday. January 28th. She went out and returned about 1.15, when she found her uncle sitting by the fire in the kitchen, and he then complained of severe pains in his jaw and appeared distressed. About three o'clock she went in the sitting-room and found him lying on the carpet nrar the fire. She asked him to rest on the comb, but he refused, and asked her to cover him with a jacket as he wanted to sleep. She returned about twenty minutes later and noticed her uncle's head lying in a pool of blood, and a razor was lying on the floor by his side. A doctor was called in and her uncle was removed to the Workhouse Hospital where he died on Friday night. Inspector Stuart said Dr Megaw had informed him that the deceased suffered from a cancer in the jaw.
The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide Whilst of unsound mind."

fled with the return, and it would hope to lay " that very unpleassnt bogey." The CHAIRMAN said the officials never entertained their friends and relations at the expense of the rate- payers. div.head: ENTERTAINING FRIENDS.
div.p: ENTERTAINING FRIENDS.
ANOTHER DISCUSSION BY THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
REV. A. M. MITCHELL IN CONFLICT WITH THE CHAIRMAN.

The question of the entertaining of friends by officials of the Warrington Union gave rise I o another lively discussion at the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. In the absence of the chairman and deputy-chairman who,along with the Clerk, were attend- ing the Central Poor Law Conference in London, Mr 0 Mather presided, There were also present :—Mrs Simpson, Mrs Collingwood, Miss Broadbent, Revs. 1' R Matthews and A M Mitchell, Messrs A Brooks, W Houghton, W C Brooks, W Furness, J A Hughes, G A J A Rushworth, M W Seton, T Ritchie, it I Partridge (assistant clerk), W J Brown (master) and C E Lawrence (superintendent of Cottage Homes).
VISITORS TO THE WORKHOUSE. THE MATRON'S DENIAL.
With reference to the complaint made by Mr W C Broks of an alleged statement by the matron to a visitor, the Matron attended before the House Com.

mittee and, after the minute of the previous meeting had been read by the Clerk, stated that she was abso- lutely innocent of the charge made against her. She had nut spoken to any woman in such a manner, and she knew her position better than to lower the dignity of any Guardian by such a remark. The, committee were of the opinion that the matter having once been noted in the minutes, should, if possible, be conclusively dealt with, and invited Mr W C Brooks to request the attendance of the visitor referred to before the next meeting of the Council. At a subsequent meet- ing, the Clerk reported that be had received a communication from Mr Brooks to the effect that he regretted inability to attend the meeting, owing to other important engagements. The committee expressed their regret that Mr W C Brooks should have been unable to attend the meeting and decided to invite him to arrange for the attendance of the visitor referred to, before the next meeting of the committee.

div.head: NIGHT CHARGE SISTER.
div.p: NIGHT CHARGE SISTER.
Miss C A Hese!dm, of Tranmere Infirmary, appeared before the Board and was apF ointed to the poition of night charge sister ht the hospital. ENTERTAINING FRIENDS.
REV. A. M. MITCHELL IN CONFLICT WITH THE CHAIR. "HEATED ATMOSPHERE."

The Rev A M MITCHELL moved :—That a Return he prepared showing (a) the number of guests entertained by officers in November and December 1912, and January 1913 ; (b) the amounts charged for hospitality and when credited in the bonke of the Union, He said credit was due to Mr W C Brooks for having mooted the question in the first instance. He opened what promised to be a brilliant campaign, but ended by adopting the motto that" He who fights and runs away will live to fight another day." (Laughter). How- ever, Mr Brooks was present that morning and he (Mr Mitchell) hoped the other fighting day had actually arrived. It was the desire of every member of the Board to make the lives of the officials as happy and bright as possible and, to that end, they ought to have the opportunity of showing reasonable hospitality to their friends. It was, however, their duty to the Board and to the public to ensure that the number of guests entertained by officials should be known. A return should be sub- mitted periodically, showing the number of people who were enterti.ined by the officers—who he supposed would be the chief officers—and also what amount was charged for their hospitality while they remained in the House. .They had had a statement from the Finance Committee—that immaculate body—(laughter)—that they were confident that everything had been done in due order. He would, however, like the Finance Committee to be able to refer to the books and state definitely what amounts had been debited as money received from the officers who bail entertained friends, and the occasions should be enumerated. It something of that kind were not done, there would always be a suspicion that the Union was being charged for the entertainment of friends, and it would be very unwise to allow such an impression to get abroad. Mr W C BROOKS seconded. In reply to Mr Mitchell, he wished to state that he had not yet run away. It was through circumstances over which he had no con- trol that he bad not been able to pursue the investiga- tions, hut he hoped to do so, on the lines of his own resolution, in the immediate future. The ASSISTANT CLERK said that in the Case of friends who spent the night in the institution it was quite possible to get the information sought,from the records in the porter's book. With regard to guests casually entertained at meals, it would he impossible to com- pile the return from the records and the only way to obtain the information would he by questioning each officer who would have to trust to his or her memory as to whether a friend had received a cup of tea or any- thing like that. No food was issued to the officers except the ordinary rations. The Rev A M MITCHELL said his resolution had reference only to those who stayed over-night. He was not thinking about the other trivial matters. Mr ItusHwowrit said it was foolish to proceed with the motion, when no extra rations had been issued and nothing had been interfered with. It was a waste of time. _

Mrs Stmrsos: said one did not like to he too narrow in these cases and, looking at the matter from another point of view, the Board might make an allowance to the nurses or officers who w eat away for the week-end or got meals outside the institution. The Bev A M MITCHELL : It is not quite the same thing. The Rev T R MATTHEws agreed that they ought not to take too narrow a view or to scrutinise such cases too closely, especially in the hospital. Miss BROADBENT : Get hold of good officers and trust them.

The CHAIRMAN: Any amendment? Mrs COLLINGWOOD : 1 would like to move an amend- ment that we waste no more time. The Rev A M MITCHELL said he did not think there was any narrowness in the motion at all. He hoped be had risen quite above the accusation of narrowness in any of his dealings. The CHAIRMAN : It all depends what people think. The Rev A M MITCHELL said that when the books showed that officers had had friends staying with them a few days, he did not think it was businesslike that no further information should be given. It was not using the ratepayers' money conscientiously. When members talked about narrowness they were overlook- ing their duty to the ratepayers. They had no right to spend money from the rates on entertaining. Mr FURNESS said the Board ought to look at the matter from the broad standpoint. Unless the officers of the institution were allowed a certain amount of liberty in regard to the entertainment of friends, they were leading little better than prison life. The Board ought at least, instead of being too parsimonious, to give them some opportunity of entertaining their friends and relations. The position had now become so acute and the officers were placed in such an unpleasant position, that something ought to be done to rreike their conditions tolerable and to give the Board a clear know- ledge of the facts. He suggested that the Board should empower the master to keep a record of visitors enter- tained by officials in a book which should be open to the inspection of any member of the Board. Miss BROADBENT : it is very unnecessary, Mr Chair- man. Mr Mitchell overlooks the fact that when the officers entertain visitors,it does not cost the ratepayers anything. He has been told over and over again but he does not seem to believe it. The CHAIRMAN : That is the accusation that Mr Mite 101 l has brought against ',ha officials. The Rev A M MITCHELL : I have brought no accusa- tion against the officials. he CHAIRMAN : That the officials-- The Rev A M MITCHELL: I have brought no accusa- tion. (Cries of " Chair "). Tne CHAIRMAN : That the officials here entertain their friends at, the expense of the ratepayers.---You say that. The Rev A M MITCHELL : I never said it. The CHA.IRMAN : I leave it to you, ladies and gentlemen. The Rev A M MITCHELL : I ask for a return show- ing the number of people who have been entertained and whether or not any charge has been made for their hospitality. You have the presumption to say I made a statement accusing the officers of doing certain things I never made any such statement, sir.
Mr W C BRooks : Nothing oi the kind. You (the Chairman) have no right to put words into Mr Mitchell's mouth which he never used.
The CHAIRMAN: I will leave it to the Board.

Mr FLANAGAN : This thing is getting intolerable. Mr W C Brookes says you have no right to put words into Mr Mitchell's mouth. Why should Mr Mitchell put words into other people's mouths? It is all assumption. Neither Mr Brooks nor Mr Mitchell knows that there have been any entertainments here— that the officers of this Union have entertained any persons whatever. It is all assumption. You want to get to know things of which you have no knowledge. The Rev A M MiTettELL : That is an untrue etate- ment.

Mr FLANAGAN : You have no knowledge of the system in this institution. You intend to get hold of information by any means, whether straight or crooked, so long as you satisfy your own ideas and your own ends.

Mr FURNESS : The atmosphere is getting very heated. Mr W C BROOKS : It is Mr Flanagan who is blow- ing off a bit. Mr FURNESS said he thought lfr Mitchell was quite justified in bringing forward the resolution. whetber for his own information or for that of the Board. It was not often he (the speaker) stood up for " his reverence," but he did not think Mr Mitchell ought to be treated quite in the way he was. Any member had a right to ask for returns to be made. He believed that if the information wore given, it would be found that there was no ground for any suggestion of impropriety ; but that the officers had been very reasonable in their methods of entertainment. The Board would be satis-

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARY.

The salary of Mrs E Jones, foster-mother at the Cottage Homes, was increased to £22 per annum with the usual emoluments.

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT AND COMMERCIALISM.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT AND COMMERCIALISM.
THE EFFECTS OF MONEY WORSHIP ON ART.

According to Alderman Bennett the duty of the Museum Committee is to try to fan the flicker of art in the town into flame. Judging by the large number of people who assembled in the Co-operative Hall on Saturday evening, to hear the first of Mr J E Phythians' series ot lectures on" Florence and its art " given under the auspices of the Ogden trustees, the Committee are meeting with success in their endeavour to promote a love of the beautiful:amongst the people of Warrington. Alderman Bennett presided and the lecturer dealt with the" Churches, palaces and sculpture " of Floreece Many beautiful pictures were thrown on the screen and one was made to realise something of the surpassing lovliness of the famous Italian town. At the outset the chairman referred to the increasing popularity of the lecturet3 evidenced by the tact that they bad been obliged to meet in a larger room. He was pleased to see so many young people present. It had neen said by a critic of their town that art seemed to be dead in Warrington, and one sometimes felt there was a certain amount of truth in the statement, but the presence of so many people as that lecture showed it was not absolutely dead, and that there was still a flicker of life. It was, therefore, the duty of the Museum Committee to try to fan that flicker into a flame. Warrington WBB a town of' artistic traditions, which, he hoped, would be surpassed in the future. Unless thy could revive the love of the beautiful in the hearts of the citizens and make them proud of their towes in the direction of beauty and art, as well as in commerce and wealth, they would never get these " cities beautiful," of which they had been dreaming all their lives. (Applause.) One of the best was to rouse them from their stupor and fill them with the love of beauty was to stow them the examples of some of the old cities,so that they might IT enabled to judge themselves ty comparison, and, if they did that he felt sure they would feel somewhat ashamed It had been said that the one god they seemed to worship in the North of England was money, and they were looked upon as lunaatics, if when building a new school, they tried to make it artistically attrictive. He contended that money spent on beauty, adornment., making life really pleasaut, rind appealing to the higher instincts was money well spent. (Applause.) They had a noble church in Warrington, but it was almost hidden by the slums about it, and they had another beautiful church in the centre of the town, which quite a number of their local administrators would like to see pulled down and a bacon shop or something of that character erected in its place. (Laughter.) All the continental cities were proud of their sculpture. What had they in Warrington? A statue of Cromwell at. the Bridge, and one of Colonel O'Leary in the Queen's Gardens, and they knew how they had to beat the drum and flog a dead horse to raise that monument to their great Military hero. fle hoped the lectures would awaken a love of the beautiful in the hearts of the younger generation. (App?ause). Mr PHYTHIAN soon condemned the conditions under which the people lived and worked in the so-called successful places in the country, as not far short of hideous. Through that, the people had lost the sense of beauty. Continuing his lecture which he made highly interesting and instinctive, he said. Florence was a great commercial city of the later middle ages, but, like other old Italian commercial towns, was exceedingly beautiful. Those old cities had two great advantages. In the first place they had no machinery worth speaking of, and that was an advantage on the side of beauty, and the other advantage was that the wealthy people lived in the towns, as it was safer than outside, owing to the fighting which went on con- tinually. He believed that if every manuf.cturer was compelled to live within the shadow of his own mill chimney their towns would not be as ugly as they were now. Their towns were hideous places, where people scrambled for money, and those who got on best in the scramble lived outside the town. It was con- demnable and unchristianlike. (Hear, hear).

div.head: SOBERER BLACKPOOL. PICTURE HALLS, SAND SERVICES, AND BAD WEATHER.
div.p: SOBERER BLACKPOOL. PICTURE HALLS, SAND SERVICES, AND BAD WEATHER.

At Blackpool Brewster Sessions, on Monday, the Chief Constable reported that last year only 215 persons were convicted of drunkenness—a decrease of 26 per cent, as compared with the previous year, and the lowest since the year 1890. lie attributed this improve- ment to the increased number of cheap amusements in the way of picture halls, which provided attractions for many persons who otherwise might spend their evenings in public-houses, the earnestness of the appeals of ministers at largely attended services held on the sands during the season, and the bad weather during the holiday months of the year. This last- named although a recognised factor for increased drunkenness in most towns and pleasure resorts, appeared to have the opposite effect in Blackpool. The Chairman said that, compared with the returns of 1875, the convictions showed a decrease of no less than 90 per cent., and if that continued drunkenness would soon become one of the extinct vices.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Women and Local Government.—Women have done admirable work in local government in the Metropolis, and elsewhere, particularly as guardians of the poor but they are very sparsely represented on the London County Council.—At present there is only one vvoir an Councillor, Miss Adler ,eSlio represents Central Hackney and very few lady candidates are coming forward for the triennial election, which will be held on March 6th. This is a matter fo, regret, because women are particu- larly fitted for the administration of much of the social legislation of recent years, and which is in tne hands of the local authorities. There is an immense amount of work of this kind under the Infant Life Protection Act, which requires the registration of everyone who undertakes the care of young children for payment and involves periodical inspection. There is also a good deal to attend to under the Employment of Children's Act of 1903, the Shop Assistants act, and the control and inspection of employment agencies and i registry offices. It s important for the social welfare that all this work should be efficiently carried on, and there is much in it that could be better undertaken by women than by men,

An Octogenarian Suffragist.—Among the early supporters Of the woman movement, is Miss Emily Davies, one of the founders of Girton College' Cambridge. As a friend of Miss Elizabeth Garrett (Mrs Garrett Anderson) she helped to draft the petition to the House of Commons, which was presented by John Stuart Mill, on June 7th, 1866. She also knew Charles Kingsley, who at that time advccated the feminist cause, and in 1869 attended the first women's suffrage meeting held in London. He afterwards changed his opinions, because the better worren of his acquaintance were against him, and those who supported the move- ment did so "in a noisy and demonstrative may." One hardly knows what Kingsley would have thought of the present day militants. Miss Davies, who is eighty-two years of age, says however, that the general attitude towards women has mostly changed for the better, in the last forty or fifty years, and she quite expects to live to see the extension of the Parliamentary vote to women.

A Domestic Servants Bill.—The Insurance .Act has made a start in bringing domestic service. within the scope of social legislation, and there is little doubt that it is only a beginning. Already there is talk of bringing the vast army of domestic women workers under the Shops Act, as regards the compulsory weekly half-holiday, and of further legislation affecting the conditions of employment. That, in a very large number of cases, the servant has grievances from the ht gienic standpoint, long and irregular hours, no definite meal times, and in some instances inadequate food, is undeniable. At the same time the vast majority of domestic servants are much better housed and fed than the factory worker, and with wages now almost double what they were in mid-Victorian times, they are upon the whole much better paid. Their main cause for discontent is, that unlike the trained nurse, they have no definite part of the day off duty, when they can do as they like. The compulsory weekly half-holiday for servants is pretty sure to come before long, but it would cause something like a general movement to do without help of this kind, if it is followed by a statu- tory nine hours day for domestic service, and the intru- sion of sanitary inspectors to see that the bedroom, the kitchen and scullery arrangements, the food and environments are sufficiently good for the health and well-being of Mary Jane. This Season's Sleeves.—Fashion is as fickle a jade as Fortune. She never tiros of change nor of evolving new ideas from old. She adopts the fashions of former periods to the exigencies of the present and never fails to receive a mode with a difference. She is also infinite in her variety, as the ne, sleeves for this season will easily prove. To describe half the shapes in vogue for this important part of the corsage, would require a great deal of space, therefore to mention the most striking must suffice. The coming sleeve promises to be the bell. Its introduction has caused a surprise, but as the season advances its vogue will increase, for experts predict that it will be extensively used for tailored suits, especially in silk. In some instances it is finished with a cuff of cream lace, which sometimes is carried up the outside seam. The leg of mutton sleeve comes in at regular intervals of about five years. This year it hss been revived and differs slightly in shape from its predecessors. It is tight at the wrist, the "leg " coming above the elbow, in addition it has a band of fur at the top, a piping of braid, or even stitching being also used.

Sleeves for Blouses and for Evening Dresses. —Loose , bishop sleeves are to be seen on some of the newest not and chiffon blouses. These are very loose and full, but have a long tight wristband, which is finished with a pleating of net or chiffon falling over the hand. For day wear and more especially on afternoon frocks, the long tight sleeve is very much in evidence. This is tight round the hand, loose at the elbow, and still looser at the shoulder. This shape requires the most careful cutting and fitting, but when well-made is most becoming to the hand, which it improves. There is the sleeve made of a different material from the dress which from just above the elbow may be of brocade, silk, chiffon, or heavy, where it may be pointed or rounded. In order that it may flt tightly, it is fastened at the wrist as it is too tight to be drawn over the hand. Three-quarter sleeves are still seen on magyar blouses and are becoming to the fortunate possessors of pretty bands and arms. The newest sleeves for evening wear are of the loosest, lightest description. On some low-necked models the fichu is arranged to form a sleeve, which, when cleverly manipulated has a graceful effect.

The Jibah Frock.—Never was the clothing of tiny babies more elaborate and costly than in these days, and many lobes for the little strangers are decorated with priceless lace. Early spring flowers in wonderful stitchery add to this embellishment in the newest christening robes. Borders of capes and hoods, are most delicately, and exquisitely embroidered, and quilted silk and satin protect from draughts, whilst silk kimonos, also most elaborately decorated with coloured silks, aroused over long or short dresses indoors. But these extravagances are only for the few,and the jibah, and sweater, are the usual dress of the average child. rho former come to us from America, and in common with the greater number of ideas from Yankee- land, is eminently practical, and yet so simple, that given a pattern the merest amateur can build it success- fully. It also lends itself to all sorts of adaptations, and embroidery ; a little originality and inventiveness therefore producing numerous variations. It takes very little stuff, and can be made from short lengths of serge, velvet, satin, net, chiffon, or lingerie. In the latter it shows to advantage any delicate embroidery, often to be bought in short lengths cheaply as remnants.

The Knitted Coat.—The newest thing in knitted coats reach to the waist from which a basque of a contrast- ing colour depends. The collars and cuffs match the basaue in shade. These coats are decidedly smart and are made almost exclusively of home-woven silk, or, as it is most improperly called " mercerised silk." The woollen knitod coat appears to hive lost its once unassailable position, since the introduction of the woven silk which is noA first favourite.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMMITTEE'S REPLY TO
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMMITTEE'S REPLY TO
COMPLAINTS.

To the Lancashire Insurance Committee, on Monday, the clerk reported that the scheme submitted for dividing the county area into districts for administra- tive purposes under the Insurance Act had been approved. Answering questions, the Chairman (Mr J Travia Clegg) said the county medical officer was trying to provide 150 beds for sanatorium treatment,which would no for the use of insured persons in the county area. Mr Blundell drew attentien to the refusal of O. Medic:a Benefit Sub-Committee of a number of applies tions from insured persons to be allowed to make arrangements with a particular doctor for medical attendance by him. He knew for a fact that in three cases the doctor had said that unless he continuad to treat the patients as he bad been doing for years paste they might die. This doctor was not on the panel, and the applicants, who were old patients, desired him to continue to treat them.

l'he Chairman said that a simple way out of the difficulty was for such doctors to come on the panel for the particular cases they wished to treat. They were at liberty to refuse any other cases they did not wish to treat.

A lady member said that to allow these people to choose doctors who were outside the panel was getting the thin edge of the wedge in, and was calculated to wreck the Act. She proteuted strongly against ail arrangements outside the Act. Another member asked why there was so much delaY in giving out the maternity benefits. Some womeo were up and about again before they received anything, and some had had to apply for parish assistance since the Act came into force.

!dr Hallsworth said that unless they were deposit contributors, various societies were responsible. The committee decided to write to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, asking him to receive a deputation on the subject of the payment of members of the committee.

div.head: ANNUAL DRINK BILL.
div.p: THE ANNUAL DRINK BILL.
Lancashire and Cheshire Fiitires.

The annual meetings of the Lancashire and Cheshire' Band of Hope and Temperance Union were held in the Onward Buildings, Illanchester, on Saturday. At the afternoon session the chair was taken by the president' of the Union (the Hon. Lady Barlow) and an address on; " Belief in Ideals ; an Essential to Practical Work" was given by Professor A S Peaks. Lady Barlow said that this was the 49th annual meet-' ing of the Union, but while much good work had beee' done during the past 3ear, she had seen no cause to believe that there was any excuse for slackening their efforts. In her journeys about the country she had been' constantly impressed by the awful power the' drink traffic still had over us, and the immense need for the work of the temperance societies. In the area of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union the' amount spent annually on drink was £3 lls 10d per man, woman and child. The population of the district covered was between five and six million' s and the totsli amount annually spent in drink £21,000,000. There wasi one licensed house to every 304 people and 1,624 clubao To deal with the trewenduous problem suggested bSY these facts the Union needed more sympathy, mot* power and more money. It was necessary to reach out, to classes never touched by the movement, and 'co gather in a greater harvest than had ever yet, IY3eO dreamed of.

Professor Peake said the ideal they bad set. 'before them l% as that every child born into the world should have opportunities of the happiest, fullest, and richest possible life. And it was this idealistic principle which supported them in their struggle even more than Oa thought of the immediate evil and disorder In the woad which had to be remedied.

The Northern, senior and junior championships are set for decision at Stockton, on the Ist prox. and the keenest interest is being shown in the doings of the clubs and individuals considered the most likely to be concerned in the strenuous part of the racing at the head of affairs.

To qualify for these races it is necessary for a club to finish as one of the first four teams and for an individual to be one of the first six men home (unless he qualifies as a member of a placed team' in the divisional championships of the North Eastern Counties East Lancashire, Yorkshire. and West Lancashire Associations, aid of these trial races the North Eastern and East Lancashire were decided on Saturday last with the following result :
NORTH EASTERN SENIOR. 1, J W Breed, Durham City H ; 2, .1 McCluskey, Consett and District H; 3, T Spiers, Durham City ; 4, G Lee, Durham City ; 5, R Lee, Saltwell H ; 6, E Wren, Saltwell H.

Teams-1, Durham, 39 points ;2, Saltwell, 58 points; 3, Darlington, 109 points. NORTH-EASTERN J UNIOR. 1, S Metcalfe, Darlington 11 ; 2, P` W Carrigan, Darlington 1-1 ; 3, E R Thompson, Heaton H ; 4, A ; Swainston, Darlington H ; 5, T Umpleby, Heaton H 6, J Lyons, Blaydon H, EAST LANCASHIRE SENIOR. 1, G C L Wallach, Bolton United H ; 2 C J Bryant, Bolton United H ; 3, T Fennah, Crewe El; 4, A Wyatt, Bolton U H ; 5, E Owen, Broughton H ; 6, W C Fay, Broughton H. Teams : 1, liolton, 86 ; 2, Crewe, 99 ; 3, Broughton, 101 ; 4, Salford, 125 points. Wallach won as be liked and experienced little difficulty in shaking off the ex-Birchfield Harrier J H Massey, whose chances were highly esteemed by Broughton, yet Massey was the only serious challenger and he eventually finished seventh in 61min. 56secs. Fennab, who won the two miles handicap at Warrington last August, did well to finish third. It having been repeatedly stated recently that Bolton have not lost a race this season, whet about November 16th at Leigh: —Wan ington : Vose 1, Shadwell 6, Gregson 7, Nurse 9, Walters 12-35 points. Bolton :! Bryant 2, Grantham 3, Horan 4, Chilton 14, El rington 19-42 points. Jeffrey Watson finished within inches of his clubmate Walters and both were 150 yards ahead of Chilton, so that on a count of six a-side, Warrington won more easily than the points represent. The Yorkshire and West Lanca- shire clubs run their races to-day, when Hallamshire (E Glover), Warrington (C Vose II Holbrook), and Wirral A.G. (S Franoom) are expected to qualify.

div.head: LOCAL.
div.p: LOCAL.

Antrohus gave a glimpse of his real form whilst leading the senior pace over a nine-mile course, with W Bolton clinging in characteristic style. C Vose brought It Burgess through at a useful pace, and F Shadwall's style of moving suggested that he is recover- ing his form. II Holbrook, who started after the pack, came through at a great pace, J Nurse accompanied the seniors and did splendidly. A Gregson made the pace for the Junior division over about six miles of splendid country. .1 Hanson moved nicely in bringing W Walters, H Woods and N Stafford through at a last pace.

div.head: TO-DAY.
div.p: TO-DAY.

Train leaves Bank Quay at 11.42 a.m. for Lancsster. and despite several drawbacks and the many strong fancies, the locals are very hopeful about holding their own with the opposition in the Senior anu Junior Championships of the West Lancashire Association. P Scott (Wallasey) is considared a very strong order in the Junior.
CHURCFI LADS' BRIGADE (CADETS) COMPETITIONS.

The annual cross-country race for Non-Commissioned 01 ricers of the Battalion was held by kind permission of the farmers, Messrs Ward and Walker, on the Ist inst., near Latchford. The course was about 1,1 miles with a fair number of water jumps. The result was as follows :-1, Colour-Sergeant Bradshaw (Christ Church Latchford Company), 10 minutes ; Lance-Corporal Woods (St. Paul's, Warrington Company), 10; minutes) ; 3, Corporal Holloway (St. Paul's, Warring- ton Company. Eleven-minutes prizes were given to each of the above as well as a small statuette ot himself (before and after the race) to the last lad in who shall be nameless, by the Commending officer. February Bth, Battalion Inter-Company cross-country team race (Battalion Shield Competition). The com- petition consists of Company teams composed of one sergeant, and one corporal and eight privates and the winning team is that which completes the course with its full number of competitors in the shortest time. Sergt-Major Newall and Sergt-Instractor Russell 4th South Lancashire Regiment kindly acted as judges. Result :-1, St Paul's Warrington Company, 8 minutes 155 marks; 2, St Elphin's Company Warrington, 9 mins, 150 marks, towards shield. Lieut Johnson acted as clerk of the course on both occasions assisted by Sergt- Major 133ttomley and the tea arrangements were sat is • factorily carried out by Quarter-Master F Bunch.
