div.p: LYMM.

THE MAY QUEEN DATE.—According to the adver- tisement for hand tenders that is piven on our front page the Lymm May Queen Committee are hoping to hold their testival next Whit Thursday. BANK DEVELOPMENTS.—The legal formalities relating to the purcha,:e of the two shops at the corner of Eagle Brow end Bridgewater-street from Mrs Pickton by the directors of the Union Bank of Manchester having come to a successful termination, workmen have commenced alteratiens on the property. When completed the new branch will afford relief to the Heatfey Bank where several of the Lymm authorities have their account, which they will be able to transfer to the nearer branch. LENTEN CELEBRATIONS.—In connectiun with the Lenten observance at the Lymm Parish Church, the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, M.A., is to give devo- tional addresses at the Wednesday evening services. whilst the following ar.i7 the special preachers arranged for the Sunday evenings :—Feb. 16th. Canon Willis, rector of Warrington ; Feb. 23rd. Rev J C Turner, Knutsford Parish Church ; March 2nd. Rev the Hon. C e Cross, vicar of Stretton ; March 9th. Rev W J Stanton, of Thelwall ; March IG.h. Rev T F Rods, vicar of Bolllngton. The Rev H B Firth, vicar of St James's Latchford preacher] at last Sunday evening's service after which Mr W Cooke F.R.C,O. gave an organ recital.

At Oughtrington Church the first of the special Wednesday evening's Lent Services was held this week, the preachcr being the Rev J Edwardes-Evans, M.A., Vicar of Ringway.—The following clergyman are appointed to take part in the succeeding services : February 19th, Rev W Bracecamp, Vicar of St Paul's, Warrington ; February 26tb, Rev E H Edwards, Chaplain at High Legh ; 'March sth, Rev A Svmones, Vicar of Over Tabley ; March 12. th, Rev T F Royds, Vicar of Bollington.

HIGHER LANE BAPTISTS.—The members of the Higher-lane Baptist Church held their annual tea and concert in the schoolroom on Wednesday night. There was an excellent number of persons who participated in the sumptuous tea that had been provided by the lady members of the church. After tea the room was pre- pared for the concert over which Mr J H Clarke pre- sided. The programme was opened with a hymm and prayer after which Mr Greenwood, and at a later stage, Mr Scragg (student-pastors-in-residence) gave brief addresses on the work of the church. The rest of the programme, with the exception of Mr Harry Perrin's recitation " The unprepared sermon," and the dialogue "The insurance agent" given by Messrs E Donaldson and H Poyner was of a musical nature, being composed of a pianoforte solo by Miss Wright ; violin solos by Mr Fred Randall songs " Dear heart "and " Annie Laurie," by Miss C Rigby ; "Abide with me" (encored) by Miss Wright ; "It's just like being at home," "The village black- smith," and encores by Alaster Fred Ingham ; whilst Mr McArthur's sonorous bass voice was heard to advantage in "The trumpeter," " When I think of the happy days,'" and " The sergeant. of the line." The succesqful proceedings terminated with the Doxology and Benediction. The duties of accompanist were shared by Miss H Brundrett and Miss Wright.

div.head: COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP. RESULT OF THE INQUIRY.
div.p: THE COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP. RESULT OF THE INQUIRY.

As a result f the inquiry held on Tuesday, December 17th, at the Council Chambers into the Urban District Council's application for an additional member for the Statham ward a sub-committee of the County Council recommend that the Council be increasel by one mem- ber, to be assigned and allocated to the Statham ward. It is further recommended that one of the members to be elected for the ward shall .etire from oflice each triennal period, and the remaining members for the ward each second year, the order of retirement to be determined by the number of votes obtained by each candidate, and that in the event of no election being held the order of retirement shall be determined by lot by the returning officer. The recommendation was approved at the meeting of the County Council on Thursday, and now only requires final formal ratification at the next meeting.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

THE WESLEYAN CONCERTS.—Tbe series of entertain- ments held during the present. winter and last, towards the reduction of the outstanding debt on the new premises of the Wesleyan Sunday School have proved highly successful. The latest of these entertainments were held I,tst week-end and were given by the famous Fisk Jubilee Trio. That their first visit, about a year ago, had established their popnlrity was proved by the large audience present on each occasion, the large room being filled with an appreciative assembly. It is impossible in a brief report to detail the items in the programme, but it can honestly be said that they were one and all received with great favour. Saturday evening's entertainment was folloned by short sacred concerts on Sunday afternoon and evening, and on Monday evening there was an another crowded " house " and a most enjoyable programme. Apart from its distinctive negro associations and characteristics which, of course, are its chief claims upon our notice, the singing of the party is strongly rearked in one particular—they know how to pianissimo and they not only know how, but they do it. One might go a long way and live a long time without hearing anything to tqual the sustained, tuneful, graduated softness of the simple songs " Steal away to Jesus," "The winter will soon be over children " and the imitative " Hear them bells!! In closinrj, Mr Eugene McAdoo paid a warm tribute ot thanks to Mrs Draper who had assisted them by accom- panying on the piano, to Dr and Mrs Bennett who had entertained the ladies, and to Mr and Mrs Proffitt whose hospitality he had personally enjoyed.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

HILL CLIEFE AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OE HOPE SOCIETY—On Monday evening the fourth entertainment of the session was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. An interesting programme was given by the members of Cairo-street Band of Hope Society, entitled 'A dream of nursery rhymes." The children acquitted themselves very creditably, thanks to the careful training of Miss Monks. Several of the mem- bers also contributed recitations, much amusement being caused by Master David Plinston, who recited " The Christmas stocking." Miss Ada Hamer sang "The Better Land " and " Father pray with me tc- night," very sweetly. Miss Amy Spencer (an ex-May Queen) and Miss Maud Kirkland gave recitations with much taste and expression. Miss Monks, Mrs Mellor and Mr P Fletcher ably played the pianoforte accom- paniments. A vote of thanks was accorded to all who had taken part in the entertainment, on the proposition of Mr G Whitfield (secretary), seconded by Mr II Brereton.

LICENSING SESSIONS.—The annual Licensing Sessions for the Daresbury Petty Sessional Division were held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday. Mr F A Frost presided and the other magistrates present were : Messrs A H Talbot, Roger C Parr, .1 Hepherd, L Greening, G Dakin, W Fletcher, H G Robert., C Jackson Holmes and J A Ransorne.—ln his annual report -uperintendent Ennion stated that there were 20 licensed victuallers and three beersellers in the division, giving an average of 545 of the population to each licence. No licensed victuallers or heersellers had been proceeded against during the sear, nor were any proceeded against last year. Eleven persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness during the year, all of whom were convicted, which was the same nu mber as last year. The eleven persons prosecuted during the year ended 31st December were all males, which showed an increase of one male and a decrease of one female as compared with the previous year. Eight of those pro- ceeded against were residents and three strangers, and they were all classified as being of the labouring class. The Chairman said the report seemed satisfactory as far as it went. One would 'ether have seen a diminu- tion in drunkenness, but so long as they were not going worse it was better than it might have been. Tbe only difference was that one female less was convicted and one male more, but, perhaps it was as well the sins should be put on the shoulders of the males.—All the licences were renewed.—The adjourned sessions will be held on March llth.

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

WESLEY GUILD.—On Wednesday evening, a lantern lecture entitled "Condemned to death or a story of the Civil war," was given by Mr Moss of Lymm, it being an illustrated story of an incident in the American Civil War. The slides were of a very high order and were ably shown by Mr Mess's son who acted as lanternist. Mr Meldrum presided over a very good a ttendance.A vote of thanks to Mr Moss and his son was proposed by Mr I Lawton and seconded 14 Mr J II Cattwright.

div.head: MR. P. M. OLIVER'S VISIT.
div.p: MR. P. M. OLIVER'S VISIT.

In connection with the Enntsford Division Liberal Association, a meeting was held in the Infant School, Moore, on Tuesday evening. The speakers were Mr P M Oliver, the prosspective candidate for the division and Councillor Grindle,of Eccles, the chair being taken by Mr John Jackson. After a few introductory remarks Mr Jackson called on Mr Oliver to address the meeting. Referring to the chairman's r?marks about recent work done by the Government, Mr Oliver said : " For a short time I am going to turn from what the Government is doing to what the Opposition has been doing or trying to do. During the last few weeks the dropping of the food taxes from the opposition programme is, I claim, with the exception of the Insurance Act and the passing of a Home Rule Bill one of the greatest achievements of the Liberal party.We have compelled our opponents to give up the idea of taxing the food of the people. Let us just look into the history of these food taxes. It has been a rather strange and long history. In the January election of 1910, the Conservative party if they got in, were going to introduce food taxes as soon as they possibly could, in the December elections they got a little bit frightened and they said before they introduced taxes "we will have a referendum and then introduce food taxes later on." Last December they got a little bit more frightened still and intro- duced another plan. Then Mr Boner Law changed his coat a fourth time and said" We won't introduce food taxes until we win two General elections together." Tell every Literal member that if the Conservative party is not to win two General Elections the best way to prevent them is not to allow them to win one. I want to turn away from our Conservative friends with all their shuffling about food taxes. The Liberal party have stood their ground in this, as I think I might say they have in most other matters. Some of the things we have advocated have not always been popular. The Insurance Act was not as popular as some of us would have liked ; it met with a great deal of opposition, but we did not throw it over because it was unpopular—(hear, hear)—because we believe it to be right whether it is popular or not. Be we Liberals or Conservatives do like a man to stick to his guns like Mr Lloyd George. (Applause.) Continuing Mr Oliver said : I just want to say a few words with regard to some of the legislation the Liberal Government has been able to get through. We have read in the papers to-day that Capt Scott and four companions have perished in the antarctic regions after having reached the South Pole. In his last message written in his diary he said that in a rich country like ours he was sure their dependents would be pro- vided for. Mr Asquith said in the House this afternoon the appeal would not fall on deaf ears. I want you to remember that after all that is what the Liberal Government has been trying to do. We have seen that in industrial life many people fall by the way-side. either through accident, sickness or old age, and the Liberal Government have said that they can "ate for these people and will see that they do not suffer for their misfortune." Mr Oliver quoted the following figures, relating to old age pensions in Cheshire, to show what a boon this measure had been to the aged section of the community. Cheshire population 676,000 of whom 11.065 are receiv- Old Age Pension, estimated annual cost of which is .£133,000 equivalent to a tid. rate. As might be expected the introduction of Old Age Pensions has brought about a reduction of pauperism especially in the number receiving out-door relief. The figures for Cheshire are as follows :—During the period from 1906 to 1912 the number of indoor paupers was reduced from I,OUO to 786 and in the same period the number receiving outdoor relief was reduced from '1,157 to 286. Concluding, Mr Oliver said the Liberal Government has a reputation for solid work and he honed they would receive from the people the support which they deserve. (Applause). Councillor Grind's then addressed the meeting. He said wa had been told by our opponents that the benefits of the Insurance Act would never come into operation, but they had and in his opinion, come to stay, and he pointed out the following extra benefits which are to follow latter viz.: Medical attendance for persons dependant on insured persons, dental treatment, payment for partial disablement,and on increase in maternity benefits Ile then went on to show how the Government has provided for the welfare of the people right from child- hood, to old-age; by the Childrena Bill, White Slave Traffic Bill, Workmen's Compensation Act, 'National Insurance Act, and Old-age Penison. The meeting was well attended and very enthusiastic.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

NEWTON DIVISION LABOUR PARTY.—On Tuesday evening the Penketh Branch held a most successful public meeting in the Labour Club, Stocks-,ane, Penketb, when this pirty were favoured with a visit from their friend and prospective Labour candidate for the division, Mr J A Seddon. Thera was a record attendance. Mr Seddon had a most hearty reception and dealt with the various items of political interest at the present time, particularly with the Trade Union No 2 Bill, and ridiculed the idea of the Tory party being the friend of the trade unions. He mentioned Lord Wollner's attitude in Grand Com- mittee on the Bill in question. Trade unionists in the Division would rememr.er his work against them at the next election. Ile also said that he had lately had the honour of conveying to the United States trade unionists the fraternal greetings of the trade unionists of this country. Mr Seddon promised at the annual social of the party on March 15th to give a discourse on his visit to the United States, especially on the question of Protection. The Chairman of the Branch, Mr G Faulkner, presided.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " Dick Whittington."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " Dick Whittington."

When one has visited the theatre and laughed right heartily over the good things provided in Mr Richard Nightingale's new and up-to-date pantomime "Dick Whittington," one does not wonder at the popular Ity lands-street housa being crowded from gallery to stalls each night. An outstanding feature, palatable to all, is the excellence of the genuine wit and humour which is kept up all through the "show." The sing- ing is very refined, the artistes possessing highly modulated and well-cultured voices. The ballet is an exteasive one and the groupings are carried out with unmistakable taste for the artistic. The proprietors have been most happy in their choice of Miss Dolly Boss as dauntless Dick Whittington," who works most assiduously, always endeavouring to please and amuse the audience. Her catchy rendering of "Alexander's Rag-time Band " thoroughly captivated the audience. The tit-bit of the evening was undoubtedly the duet " Take me back to the garden of Love," rendered in such a sympathetic manner by Miss Nellie Mascot as Fairy Sunshine and Mr Fred Preston a really clever baaltone as Koke-Hi-O. Another pleasing number of their's was "Your eyes have told me all.'' Both of these items were received with uastinted applause which was well deserved. The comedians are clever, witty and smart, their gags and witticisms being clear of vulgarity but charac- terized by commendable smartness. These mirth- merchants are Tew and Lea, who as Captain Salts and Bobbs are excruciatingly funny, in addition to ~ne of the couple being a tricky dancer. They are aided by Jimmy Goode as Alderman Fitzwarren, Bob , Stevens as Idle Jack and Billy Fauder as Caroline the cook. The latter was an expert dancer as well as a racy comedian. Gocde, in no way belied his name for he was really clever and to say the least, good. Stevens also worked hard in keeping the ball of humour rolling, although he was styled as Idle Jack. Miss Gladys Henderson was responsible for the success of the character of Alice Fitz warren and Miss May Beaumont was a captivating Maudie McSplash. The part of Bertie De Jonks could not have been placed in more able hands than those of Miss Frances Henderson, whilst Barbendo who took the part of Thomas, the cat, proved himself to be a clever contortionist and acrobat. Pleasing specialities were given by The Dancing Durhams, and the Sisters Beaumont and Henderson. The Scenery was beautiful, the dresses exquisitively pretty and the whole pantomime, excellent. An augmented orchestra is under the baton of Mr Hal E. Parker. To-day there will be a matinee at 2.30 in addition to the performances to-night.

div.head: TOBACCO BY AERIAL POST.
div.p: TOBACCO BY AERIAL POST.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN LICENSING SESSIONS.

The annual licensing sessions for the Runcorn division were held on Monday, Mr F Norman presiding. Superintendent Ennion, in his annual report, stated that there were forty-four licensed victuallers, thirty beer sellers, and two others who sold off the premises, giving an average of one licence to 289 of the popula- tion. Two licensed persons were proceeded againat,one of whom was convicted. One hundred and twelve persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness,lo6 of whom were convicted, as compared with seventy-one and seventy-eight respectively. He had received instructions from the chief constable to object to the renewal of the licence of the Duke of Wellington, Percival-lane, on the ground that it had been ill-con- ducted. The present tenant, Thomas Henry Blackwell, was convicted on June 24th last for permitting dranken- ness. Former tenants had also been convicted.

In answer to Mr J W Knowles, Widnes, who appeared for the licensee, Superintendent Eenion said there was nothing against Bleckwell except this conviction, and since then he had conducted the house properly. The Chairman said although it was a pi oper matter to bring before the magistrates they did not consider the offence justified them in talking away the licence, and it would be renewed. All the other licences would be renewed, except the Moulders' Arms, Mill-brow, Foresters' Arms, Canal-street, and the Queen's Arms, High-street. These three would be adjourned until the adjourned sessions with a view to their being referred for compensation.
YOUNG LIBERALISM AT WIDNES. "GOOD FOR HEART AND HEAD."

Keen disappointment was expressed at a well- attenaed meeting of the Young Liberals of Widnes, on Tuesday night at the absence of Sir Edward Russell, who had been announced to speak. Just after eight o'clock a telegram was received stating that be bad got as far as Speke,and could not proceed owing to the density of the fog, but those who had charge of the meeting did not let the opportunity pass while they had an audience and Mr Charles Poole took the chair. Mr Brooke said Liberalism was for the heart as well as the head. In Mr J B Mirtindale, the prospective Liberal candidate for the division, they had a man with a wonderful knowledge of politics. Religion was a matter which ought not to be brought into the sphere of politics. He considered that a chil6l of the present could not be improved until their environs had been made healthier and happier, and to accomplish this, he thought land reform would lend a helping hand. Councillor Baskerville said the Young Liberal League in the town was to be the advance guard among the Liberals of the division. To win Widnes for Liberalism it was necessary to educate the electors, and it was desirous that to accomplish that object the Young Liberal Leaguers should be foremost in the matter of propaganda work. In Mr Martindale they had one of the smartest candidates in the country—(hear, hear)— cud, if they were toil secure his return at the next election, they would have to work very hard and educate the electors of the constituency. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The fortnightly meeting of tbe Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr J Spruce presiding.
ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.
A circular letter from th,> Local Government Board re the election of members of Boards of Guardians fixed the 7tn April as the date for peAling unless such date was varied by the County Couucil.

div.head: RELIEF TO CASUALS.
div.p: RELIEF TO CASUALS.
The Local Government Board wrote with regard to he administration of relief to casuals.

The Assistant Clerk pointed out that the question would come up at the Inter-County Committee meeting on vagrancy on 0,3 28th inst. The Board would be represented by their delegates, It was decided that the matter be referred to the delegates.

RATE OF MAINTENANCE. A communication from the County Asylum, Chester, stated that the rate of maintenance for pauper lunatics had been fixed for the quarter ending 31st March at 93 OM. per head, per 'NOOK.

_ _ THE NEW CHILDREN'S HOME. At a meeting of the Children's Home Committee it was decided that a small opening ceremony take place in regard to the new home, and also that a sub- committee be appointed to consider the details. They recommended the following to constitute the sub- committee : Messrs Spruce, Wood, Baxter and the lady members of the Boarding-out Committee, with the master of the Workhouse and the superintendent of the homes. It was also res.thed that the architect's atten- tion be brought to the condition of the roof and also request that the necessary repairs be carried out as soon as possible. The Chairman replying to a question said the opening ceremony would probably take place in about three weeks.
The minutes were confirmed and the name of Mrs Samuel Taylor was added to the sub-committee.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr Antwiss (vice-chairman) presiding.
WESTON MATTERS.

The minutes of the meeting of the Weston Parochial Committee showed that the questiou of temporary wooden erections and yard sheds had been considered and instructions had been given concerning the action to be taken in each case. A plan showing departures from the deposited plan as made by Mr George S Frith in the erecting of a new house on the Heath was sub- mitted and was recommended to the District Council for approval. The Clerk produced a copy of a resolu- tion passed by the Housing and Town Planning Com- mittee of the Council with respect to Wright's Dock property. It was resolved that it be a request to the Housing, Town Planning, &c; Committee that the terms of the resolution be enforced as quickly as possible and that in the meantime the Sanitary Inspector be asked to take the necessary steps to enforce the abatement o f the existing nuisances. he committee's rfport and recommendations were adopted.

div.head: M.A.NCH ESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: M.A.NCH ESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Urban District Council of Ituucorn wrote as to the appointment of a successor to the late Mr Dean, on the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority. It was explained that Mr Dean's three years of office would have expired in December next and it was decided that Mr G Pilling be appointed until December when the Council would consicer the appointment of a representative for the thrce years.
THE CHEAPEST WATER SCHEME. BOUGHT BY THE COUNCIL.

The Council's cheque for the purchase of Manly water works on the Manley estate, amounting to £267, was passed and Mr Woodward said tnat probably it was the cheapes' water scueme that had ever been purchased. The Clerk intimated that the L,)cal Government Board had not yct written giving their sanction of the purchase. Mr Woodward said that they could not buy it until they had the sanction of the Local Government Board.

div.head: TUBERCULOSIS REGULATIONS.
div.p: TUBERCULOSIS REGULATIONS.

Dr Adams, tne rnedical officer, stated that the new regulations iu regard to tuberculosis were now in operation. Thirteen cases had been reported since the last meeting. There had been live cases of pulmonary tuberculosis, and the remainder were special forms. STOCKTON HEATH OBJECTORS TO THE STREET IMPROVEMENTS.
The Clerk read a letter from Mr K Isherwood of Stockton Ileath,ou behalf of himEelf,Mr F It Isherwood

and Miss PerabBrton. He said be would like an inter- view with the Council re the pavinsz of the back of Ellison-street and a passage adjoining. The Clerk said that the matter had been considered on two occasions by the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee and they had refused to deal further with the matter.

Mr Pilling: It is trying to get out of the street apportionments. Members of the Council had received letters on the matter from those who objected to pay- ing in regard to street improvements. The Clerk : These people will have their proper opportunities under the statute of making their objec- ticns to the magistretes.

Mr Pilling: They have given us all the trouble they possibly could. They are trying to block us in every way. It was decided not to interfere in the matter and that the parties be advised tu make their objections in the proper quarters.

div.head: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.

The first meeting of the Widnes fow-n--deuucil held in the evening within the history of the borough was presided over, on Tuesday, by the Mayer (Alderman F Neil). At 6.i0, the advertised time to start the pro- ceedings, only one alderman and three councillors had taken their seats. When the Mayor took the chair the numbers had increased to four aloermen and twelve councillors. About fifty townsfolk interested in local affairs were present. The recommendation of the Gas and Water Committee to take immediate steps to extend the borough boundaries was altered to a resolution whereby a selected committee should be appointed to reconsider the whole matter, in view of a report from the Liver- pool Council stating that they were considering similar proposals, which would include Netherley where the Widnes waterworks are situated. Councillor D Lewis said the boundaries could be enlarged with advantage, but he wanted to avoid the danger of being carried awiy through the glamour of mere size, and it was wise to move cautiously. He proposed an amendment that a committee consisting of the Mayor, Aldermen CI- Neil, H S S Owens, and Councillor Welding report on the desirability of extension.

Alderman Timmis described the amendment as a milk-and-water one, and said the Council ought to face the position at once. If the time for extension had arrived, why not say so, and if the time had not, why consider it at all ?
The amendment was agreed to. On the motion of Councillor Millar, seconded by Councillor Farghar, the Council adopted the principle of giving their employees one week's holiday with wages per annum.
ST. HELENS. BATHS PROBLEM AT ST. HELENS.

At the St Helens Corporation Water Committee, on Wednesday, the Town Clerk reported that the Council had passed a resolution directing that committee to find a site for the erection of baths convenient for the residents of Hardshaw, Parr, and East Sutton, and to recommend to the Council.
_ Alderman Beecham thought they would have to find bathers as well as baths.
The Chairman (Alderman Dixon-Nuttall) said the, Baths Committee would deal with the matter.

Alderman Foote said he did not agree with wasting public money, and the Mayor said he was of the same opinion. Alderman Foote: Last month there were fifteen adult bathers pr day, and it needs 100 per day to pay even for the upkeep. Alderman Beecham said the people in the neighbonr- hood of the Boundary-road baths did not patronise them. Alderman Foote : And the baths are where the densest part of the population live. The Town Clerk: You have to find a site. '[he question was referred to the Baths Committee, which meets on the 24th inst. Alderman Foote stated later that the cost of the baths last month was £79 and the receipts were £5. MR. RIGBY SWIFT. M.P., ON ST. lIELENS LIBERALS.

The yearly general meeting of the St Helens Con- servative and Unionist Working Men's Association was held on Saturday night at the new Conservative rooms. Mr Rigby Swift, K.C, M.P, presided, and said it had been stated that there were some Liberals in St Helens who might vote on their side. He did not want them to vote on their side. If they had the courage of their convictions, let them bring forward a cannidate and fight them. If they were of opinion that the Liberal party's policy was the correct one let them challenge them in the position they now held. If the Liberals no longer thought they were right, and were not prepared to bring forward a candidate, then let them vote for the party, Conservative or Labour,which they thought right. But they were not going cap in hand to the Liberal party and asking them for support. Let the Liberals come out to declare their position, so that they could see whether there was a Liberal party in the town and what they were intending. (Applause.) He (Mr Swift) bad fought Labour twice, and be did not mind Labour ; it was open and straightforward ; they knew where it was ; but he did not like the Liberal party, which they never heard of and did not know what it was doing except now and then when a suggestion was made that perhaps the Liberal party might vote for them if they did this, that, or the other. Well, he was not going to trim his sails in order to please the Liberal party. The Unionist policy was straight and plain and the Labour party's policy was straight and plain ; let the Liberal party of St. Helens show their policy and fight for it.

div.p: FAIRCLOUGH'S AND THE BRIDGE. BIG CLAIM AGAINST THE CORPORATION.

div.head: Important Arbitration Proceedings.
div.p: Important Arbitration Proceedings.

Important arbitration prcceedings opened at the Town Hall on Thursday in ceunection with the claim lodged by Messrs James Fairclou*h and Sons Ltd in respect of their premises at Bridge Foot which th-, Corporation are acquiring compulsorily under their Act of 10 IL The major pqrt of the property is the building used by Messrs Fairclough as a warehouse, but the arbitration also concerns the adjoining sadist 's shop, cottages and land. It is of cow se, the erection of the new Warrington B idge which makes the demolition cf the buildings—or part of them— a necessity. Great interi st cootred in the aibitra- tion proceedings and there was a large attendance of members I the Council and ratepayers in the Ccuucil Chember. Two days have already been devoted to the case on behalf of Messrs Fairclough and the Coreoration's reply will be made to day. it was stared in the course of yester- day's hearing that the claen originally put in by Messrs Fairclough aracuntr d to £6,900, but the valuations presented in evidence on behalf of the firm totalled only £4,822. Messrs Fairclough are repre- sented by Mr Sanders, n, .K.C.' M.P., and Mr Miller (instiucted by Messrs Wilson eti.d Cowie, of Liver poo)), while Mr Gordon Hewett, K.C. (instructed by the Town Clerk) is appearing for the Corporation. The umpire is Mr J Fowler, cf Sheffield, and the arbitrators sitting with him are Mr Segar Owen, rd Warringtou (on behalf of Messrs Fail clough), and Mr J H Hanson, of Huddersfield (on behalf of the Corporation). 1 HE CLAIM OUTLINED. Mr Sanderson in opeuina the case for Messrs Fejt- dough explained that the firm owned tavo mills, one at Howley 800 y.rds from the prop, rty a ncerned, and the other Bank Quay Mill 1700 3ards oistant from the ware. house. Both mills had access to the river and the valuable part of the consideiaLion as far as the ware- house was concerned was it also bad access to tte river. Of course carriage by river was v,-ry muclicieaper than by rail. The firm had three distrinut leg centres, one at Widnes, where they had a warehouse and quay n the Mersey one at Earlestown wherethey had a warehouse and a rail way eroing and the third was the earehouse at Bridge Foot. The premises were bought by Messrs Fairclough in 1863. The most material matters which influenced the firm in acquiring the premises were that tkey bad access to the river and the position on the roadway. The warehouse occupied an absolutely unique position with regard to the road. VVarrington Brings was practically the chief entrance into Cheshire. There was no bridge on the left hand side within seven miles and en the rigbt hand side there eras not another bridge within six or seven miles. All the main roans and minor roadways passing through Warriugten converged at a point opposite to the warehouse so that the firm got all the traffic which proceeded either from the south-west, the south, the south-east or the east. It was quite obvious that Bridge Foot was a place of vantage because competitors (he instanced Messrs Carters and Mr Gandy) were getting as near to the bridge as possible. The importance of the place was apparent when it was seen that the other bridges on either side of the warehouse were toil bridges aehress Warrington Bridge was free. The premises were not very large but when Messrs Fairclough acquired the property they intended to I develop it by extending it. It might he asked why the premises had not been developed before now. Toere were two very good and obvious reasons. It was not long after the premises were purchased that the project of cutting the Manchester Snip Canal was mooted and in later years the proposal to re-build Warrington Bridge was made. When the Skip Canal Act was passed it was perfectly well known that the cutting of the new waterway would have a considerable effect on the Mersey navigation. Such an effect was experienced and the result was that there was serious litigation. Messrs Fairclough's first took action against the Canal Company for diverting tar more water than they were entitled to do, thereby diminishing the water power at the milts. Their there was further and even more serious litigation undertaken by the Corporation and the traders ot Warrington and carried to the House of Lords. acticn against the Ship Canal Company for interfering with the depth of the river, which silted up, was won by the traders. It would have been most unreasonable on Messrs Fairclough 's part to have put their contemplated extensions in hand when the project of rebuilding the bridge assumed more definite shape because the firm had no desire to put an unnecessary burden on the Corporation. In 1910 application was made to Parlia- ment for the Corporation Act under which the ware- house property was taken in. It was at first proposed to insert a clause in the Act by which the Corporation were to provide other premises but the important point was that those premises should have access to the river. Messrs Fairclough understood that the negotiations had been brought to a successful issue, but unfortunately, not through any fault on the firm's part, the clause was not inserted. Ho supposed the Corporation bad good reason for dropping it and the result was that there was put into the Act a clause which compelled the Corporation to buy all the premises. That was a very material consideration in the arbitration proceedings. It showed conclusively that the tribunal then trying that matter arrived at the conclusion that the most material factor, as far as Messrs Fairclough were concerned, wes that the premises should have access to the river, mei if the Wrpuration wore not in a position to provide other premises with such access then they bad to buy out the firm's interests there altogether because the Corporation's action would amount practically to expelling Messrs Fairclough from the site and from the district. A landing stage was built by the firm at Bridge Foot but was not used, beyond making experiments, because it was found that the warehouse was not sufficiently large to take a large load of grain and in consequence, from a business point of view, it was better to take the material by road as long as the warehouse remained at its present size. He submitted that,in assessing the purchase price of the pro- perty the prospective value and the,potential facilities which it possessed ought to be taken into consideration. The value of land to an owner was enhanced by the probability of more profitable use in the future. The value of the owner's interest was not properly com- pensated by assessing the amount of pecuniary benefits obtained by present user in disregard of possible benefits in future. Messrs Fairclough were in a large way of business and he contended that had circumstances permitted the enlargement of the warehouse, the premises would have become very much more valuable as a receiving centre for Cheshire farmers. Grain then could have been seat down the river to Liverpool to comply with large contracts which the firm had to carry out with the Canadian Government and other customers. The warehouse had a frontage of 152 yards on the river bank and although it was only three storeys high it could be made into a seven or en eight storey building. All the Cheshire farmers went past the very doors of the warehouse and the neighbourhood was increasing. The trams were running past the place and it was only 400 yards from the centre cf Warriugton, which was a large area and the retail business which might be done at a large saving of cost to Messrs. Fairclough would be greatly ineeeaceei if they could only have a larger warehouse with river access. •IHE WIDNES lURNOVER.

The Widnes distributing centre, which was on the river, had a turnover in one year, on an average of two years, of £lOO,OOO on account of the facilities enjoyed there, and there was no reason whatever why the Bridge Foot premises should not be converted into an equally important distributing centre. He sub- mitted that the tribunal must treat the case as one where a trader was compelled to leave his premises entirely. It was so treated by the Act of Parliament under which the arbitration was being held. The Corporation were compelled to buy the whole of the premises although they did not want them because they only wanted to widen the bridge and road. There was a proposal not only to widen the main road but to make a road running along the river edge on the rig ht hand side. Mr Hewart.—There is a mistake about that. Mr Sanderson said that at any rate the Corporation did not want to give the firm tCcPS to the river and that was the point upon the negotitations broke down. In that case the good will was going to be lost entirely and the profits again would be entirely lost. It was obvious that Messrs Fairclough would not be able to get any other premises in the neighbourhood which had river access. Even if that were not an importatant consideration, there was no other site in any shape or form comparable to the site which the firm now possessed. Supposing it were possible to get other premises the firm would miss one of the main objects for which the property was purchased, viz., the traffic passing the point along the main roads. THE BASIS OF THE CLAIM.

In making their claim the valuations had been taken out on the basis that the warehouse was a customer of the firm and the profits bad heen kept entirely dis- tinct. A rent was debited against tbe warehouse but the valuers who were called in found that the figure was not sufficient and in order to be fair to the Cor- poration the rent was i icreased to £6O. The saddler's shop next door which had been vacated and for which the Corporation found other premises was let at a rental of £lO. Taking the rent of the warehouse at £6O that made £lOO for rent and deducting 10 per cent. for outgoings, a sum of £9O was left for rents. In addition to that there was an advertisement hoarding let for £6 per annum, showing a total yearly rental of £96. Mr Hartley, the valuer, had taken twenty years purchase, which worked out at £1,920 Only the land on which stood the buildings at the rear of the warehouse had been taken into account because the buildings were not worth anything. The buildlng3

were left in that state because it was inter:tried to dew-lop the warehouse and the space was now irewed as land. There were 406 square yards, which wfre taken at £4 rer square yard, giving a total of .C 1,624. tie oid nut scppise ausb.dy would be inclined to quarrel wih that price having regard to recent pur- (-oases ,hich had taken place in the immediate neigh- bourhood. Not one single farthing had been taken into consideratic n in respect of the 152 yards of land on the embankment. 1-le hoped the ti iourial would arrive at the conclu,inn that the valuers had not only taken the right principle but had also adopted a fair and re,sonah;e measure of compensation when they as.sebtied the value at 1:4 per square yard having ri gard to the .osition of the laud. Adding together vie items aiready mentioned and putting on a sum of £351 tor c nnpu'sory purchase, a teal of 1:3,898 Et 3 uhtaihed. 'the net p; ont which had been made at the premises on an average of three years was .2.2!3 12a id, hu pntting the rent at the high figure of LOU the profit was £194. Taking that profit at three ) eats' pwchasr., whlob was very reasonable, a or .CSS2 was ohta.ine,i The proa,s which were made in connention with the warehouse were not then exhausted. A p+ of £lO9 his 55.1 for grinning was made in con- nection with the warebi,use at the Mersey 11,ji there as a orniir, worked out on an average of three years, of .ClO 19s 3d rer rumutu on manufactured goods, and a further profit ol 1:50 19s 3d on orders received at Bricte Foot tor the -Mersey Mills. The total claim for loss of business on a two Teals' purchase was 1;921, making a grand total of £4,822

div.head: NI R. JOHN FAIRCLOWIS EVIDENCE.
div.p: NI R. JOHN FAIRCLOWIS EVIDENCE.

Mr iohu Fairclot:ge, ohairmith and manaping oirector of Messrs James itairclotigh and Sons, Ltd., was the first witness called. He bore out Counsel's statement vs to the advantageous position of the Bridge Foot property and stated that when it was purchased the tirm contemplated the c,rection of a largo werehou.se They wa,.ted to do the same ara,tott of inaLs at Bridge Foot as they were doing at Widnes. Mr Miller : Are the facilities which this site would give you, if day-loped, similar to those which you erjoy at Widnes? r Fairciouo : Exqctl y the same. Further questioned be said the river was practically ruined by toe silrinr, caused by the nstruction of the Ship Canal and protract 4 litieation ensued, in which the traders were successful. Witness stated that it vas the cormritction of the Ship Canal and prospect of a new Warringt9n Bridge .eing erected which had stayed the hands of the firm from developing their property. Mr : Have you considered whether you could do the same business elsewhere ? Mr Faircicugn We could not.

Cross-examined by Mr flawart, witness stated that before the firm acquired the premises at Bridge Foot they were used as a shop. Do you represent to this tribunal that the main motive, or one of the main motives that induced you and your father to take these premiss was that. they offered lacilities for transport by river ?—That and the rod as well.

Which do yen say was the more important in your view, the facilities for transport hv river or the con- veniente of access to the road ?—Wall, if we had a largo Once there, I would quite as soon take the river. I am not asking you for any hypothesis. You have stated as a fact that there were two leading motives which induced you to take these premises. lam asking you to say which of those two was the more important in your mind?—l cannot tell yeti which was the more Leportant, to my mind, at that time. I considered one as valuaule as the other.
When 3ou got the premises, as I understand, your object was to develop them ?—Certainly. You have been there fifty years ?—Yes.

Have you developed the ?—No. Have you even developed them to the extent of giving notice to your yearly tenant and taking those premises into your warehouse ?—No. You have done nothing?—No. I have not done any- thing, because if I do anything I want to do it properly For half a century you have had these premises which you took for the primary purpose of developing, and you have not in any respect developed them ?—No, and I have given you the reasons why we have not. How long was it after you got the premises that you made the small landing stage ?—lt was made at the time.

Having taken a second or third barge load in that way, you came to the conclusion that for your ware- house, as it was, the river facilities did not matter ? Well, it did not matter for the moment. But it hasn't mattered for fifty years, has it ?--Yes. What I want to know is this : Why, if in truth and in fact you acquired these premises with a view to developing them, and discovered so early that barge loads were no good for the warehouse as it was, did you not at occe, or at any rate within the next twenty years, make this larger warehouse and get your wharf and river facilitias ?—We wanted to see how the thing would pay in the first instance, and what we were doing. We waited until the Ship Canal came on. You waited a long time, didn't you ?—No. I don't call it a long time. You must bear in mind that we spent a lot of money in building a mill at that time. At any rate, between 1863 and the time when the Macchester Ship Canal was mooted or started, you did nothing ?—No. We did not do anything. When do you say the Manchester Ship Canal began to be seriously discussed ?—lt was in agitation in 1880. The Act was carried in 1885. _ _
Practically, therefore, you had a clear run of twenty years or thereabouts in which you did nothing in order to develop the transport facilities on the river ? Yee.
Do you really suggest that it was apprehensions excited by tho Ship Canal that prevented you for the rext twenty years ?—lt was one of the reasons why we didn't do it. .

Further questioned, Mr Fairclough stated that the litigation with feference to the abstraction of water from the river took place soon after the opening of the Ship Canal in 1894. The proceedings brought by the traders to secure proper dredging followed in 1905. Do you really represent to these gentlemen that it was fears about the Ship Canal which for twenty years after the year 1882, prevented you from developing this wharf or river transport ?—That was arta of the reasons What were the others ?—Ons reason was that we had spent all the money we cared to spend in building a mill. We had just finished it and we wanted to recoup ourselves before we did anything more. In other words, your business was well suited with the facilities you had ?—We have tried to come to terms with the Corporation to go on with this work, but we have been unable to do so. Mr Hewart put questions with a view to showing that the Corporation did not intin ate, so far back as 1900, that they would ri quire the whole of Messrs Fairolough's premises for street improvements. The notice which the Corporation served upon the firm at that time merely prescribed a new line of frontage which would have to be observed in the event of rebuilding. Mr Fairclough said the new line would have cut right across the warehouses. Mr Hewart : I suggest the effe-:t of the notice was simply this : That if you chose tu re-build your premises, there was a new line of frontage which was to be observed—that and nothing more—suhject to compensation for any land of which you were thereby deprived ?—Witness did not answer. Is it not the fact that, your business being what it is, you have never required what you call facilities for water transport ?—We never thought so. You never thought you required them ?—No ; I mean we never thought of it in the way you put it. Have you thought the contrary ?—Yes. Nevertheless, for fifty years, for the reasons you have mentioned, you have held your hand ?—Yes. e'urrher questioned, Mr Fairclough said the firm had not gone so far as to asceitain from a competent authority what the cost of constructing a wharf would be, but they had a good idea of their own. The premises at Widnes, which was the main distributing centre, were immensely larger than those at Bridge Foot. As to the £lOO.OOO turnover at Widnes, there had not been a recent development of the business there. Don't you know that, as originally proposed in their Bill, the Corporation did not intend to take the whole of your present site at Bridge Foot ?—I know they did not. They intended to take about one half of the warehouse. And you objected and said that if they were to take any part of it, you wished them to take the whole ? Certainly. The Warriegton Corporation by their counsel agreed end a clsuee was, by agreement, inserted in the Act, at your request ?—lt may have been. Do you know that, after the notice to treat had been given, the question was mooted with you, and after- wards with your solicitors, as to whether we should take part or the whole of the property, and you insisted upon our taking the whole ?—Yes. Wit:ess added that his brother, who was reore intimately concerned in the negotiations, was unable to attend the arbitration. Asked whether he contended that the acquisition of the warehouse by the Corporation would annihilate the business at Bridge Foot, witness said it would aunihi- late the payin part of it. The firm did not intend to carry on the b'usiness in other premises. Do you suggest that there are no premises in Warrington from which you could carry on the basineis?—None so convenient. I would not erect a warehouse anywhere but on the river-sioe. I suggest that Mr Jeans' premises—the Bridge Mill— are vacant and are excellently suited for your business, at a rent of £4O a year ?—Yes, but there is a street between the building and the river. You have not been getting Your stuff from the river where you are ?—No. I should cart it rather than send it down by boat there. Have you tried to find suitable premises ?—No. And the ease you are putting to this tribunal, so far as your warehouse is concerned, is that the business you have carried on there, so far as it was a paying

business, is tr. ing to kte...extinguished?—Practicaily. Further q testi. ned, Mr harelough said that, so far MI he was a, are, his firm did not make any attempt to acquire Messrs Gaudy's promises fefore that firm entered into occupation of them ahout two years ago. By Mr 6and,rson : The proposa's (.f the Corperatiou to acquire half the premkes. would have reunered the other f elf useless for Luilnens purposes. Au agree- ment was drawn up with the Corporation by which right of access to t lie river was pie.- erved to the firm, but when it was submitted to a Corporation ccmcuittee it was rejected. The proceedings were then adjourned until yesterday morning.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. ROBERT CAMERON M.P. Voted for Home Rule Bill at Eighty-seven.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. ROBERT CAMERON M.P. Voted for Home Rule Bill at Eighty-seven.

We r(gret to ann(,unce the death, which occurred rrom heart failure at one o'clock on Thursday after- noon of Mr Robert Cameron, Liberal M.P. for the Houghtor-le-Spring division of Durham. Born in Perthshire in 1825, Mr Cameron was one of the oldest members of the Hou-e of Commons, which he entered at the age of 69 For 47 years be was headmaster of the Friends' School at Sunderland. He was also a prominent lecturer on literature and science and chairman of the school board.

For practically the whole of the Session Mr Cameron, who was in failing health, had been paired with Mr. Chamberlain, but he insisted on voting on the third readings of the Home Rule and Wel,h Die- establishment Bills. On each occasion he was taken into the division lubby in a chair, but was not required to pass the teller. Mr. Cameron's death necessitates a by-election in the Houghton-le-Spring division, which he had represented since 1895. At the last General Election he was returned unopposed. At the previous election (January, 1910) the figures were: R. Cameron (L), 10,393; Major H S Streatfield (C), 4,382; Liberal majority, 6,011. In 1906 the Liberal majority was 5,750. Mr Cameron had on many occasions appeared as preacher and speaker in Warrington, and further reference to him will be found in another column.

div.head: MISS MAMIE BLACKBURN.
div.p: MISS MAMIE BLACKBURN.

Encou,ager. by the r.runcesS of previous cntc-rpriscs, Messrs Crosfield's op,ratie society have this year hunched out on inure ambitious lines and a full week's perfotimtt:ce of Plauquette's comic opera " Paul Jones " are to be given at the Royal Court Theatre, commtlicing on Monday evening next. The rehearsals, we are jammed, give promise of an entirely affequate production which %yid do the highest credit to these enthusiastic amateurs. Dr Charles D Law is the producer, Mr Richard A 'Moss of Wigan the plofessional conouotor, and Mr G B Dean the stage manager. The dancing tie be-uty and grace of which is ess.ential to the success cf the production— has been taught by Miss Bickford, who has made special j,:urneys to and Irmo Loudon for the purpose.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

When the proceediugs re-opened yesterday Mr John Faitclough mas .gsin cross-examined by Mr Gordon fiewart with regard to the convenience ot the premises tor farmers from the Cheshire side of the Mersey.

By Mr fiewart : You don't suggest that the farmers hring their carts along the:se converging roads at Bridge For:t merely for the purpose of coming to your warehouse ?—Certainly not. I; we buy oats iu the Warrington market from the farmers, they leave them at the warehouse. _ .
Do you represent that they would not take them to your warehouse if it were elsewhere ?—lt woulU not, be so convenient. _ _ . _

Mr H Hartley, of Liverpool gave evidence as to the admirable situation of the premises et Brioge Foot which he characteri-ed as incomparable in Wiirrine,ten for the purposes of Messrs Fairclough's business. With regard to tue construction of a stage on the river bank he had not prepared any details or particulars of such scheme but he felt that a stsge could be con- structed at a small cost ; which in a way would be of the greatest advantage to Messrs Fairclougb. it would economise the cost of carriage between the two mills and this distributing centie and wuuld enable them to make an addition to their existing warehouse. His opinion was that the tents which had been placed on the premises, the smilers shop, and the advertisement hoarding, were under- estimated. His valuation of the lands and buildings, including 10 per cent, for compulsory sale,amounted to £3,898. His valuation of £924 for the claim for loss of business brought the total to £4822 which was extremely reasonable. The purchase price of £582 in respect of the business at the warehouse was a very moderate estimate of the damage which had been sustained through the compulsory disturbance. He had visited the premises of Mr Jeans and in his opinion they were ruinous and dilapidated. By Mr Hewer. : It is a fact that Messrs Fairclough have deposited £3O per year as rent for the warehouse ? —Yes. It was said yesterday that, in fairness to the Corpora- tion, the rent WtlB taken at £6O ?—I don't know who said that, but 1 take it at £6O. I want to see how this fairness to the Corporation works out. The effect of raising the rent for the pur- pose of valuation from £3O to £6O is to diminish by £3O the annual profits of the warehouse. So far as the annual profits for the warehouse are concerned you are asking in this claim for a three years' purchase, but so far as the premises are concerned you are asking for 20 years. So that the fairtinss to the Corporation works out at a2O years' purchase of £3O instead of three.— Witness : 1 don't agree. That is how it works out on the proposition put before me. If you will let me explain, the £3O was not actually the rental of the property. Ii was the rental which the company debited for the purposes of book-keeping. With regard to the premises of Mr Jeans. You don't by a trick of memory in purportiug to describe those premises as ruinous and dilapidated, really describe the condition of the warehouse at Bridge Foot ?—No. The warehouse was, originally built as a house ?—I cannot say. 1 should say it was originally built as a shop. Have wooden pillars been put in to support the floor ?—Yes, that is quite natuial. The cellars are not used in connection with the ware- house ?—No, except as coal cellars. I suggest to you that the building Is about as incon- venient as it could be for the purpose of occupation. —I don't agree with you. Mr Hewart : You have a useless cellar, and only one means of access. Did you notice the condition of the walls when you paid a visit ?—Yss. I suggest to you that the upper storey walls are only nine inches thick ?—They are made in compliance with the bye-laws. What do you say about the stairs ?—They are in fair order. You will appreciate that Messrs. Fairclough have not attempted to improve the premises in view of the disturbance by the Corporation. I suggess that the floors are in had repair.—l don't agree with you. They fulfil the requirements of the trade. In putting £6O on this warehouse you have altogether ignored the fact that it is said to have a river front- age ?—Cerainly. Taking the £6O as rent, you claim to put upon that 20 years purchase, end the builoings being what they are ?—I do. Do you suggest that the L'3s chsried for rent to Mr Wilkinson (who occupies the seddler's shop, was too small ?—I do. - - .

_ Q.estions wore put to Mr Hartley with regard to the area and value of the land. Lie admitted that 76 square 3,2rds of the 1t.6 square yards were occupied by the hoarding. ' Mr Hewart : For the purpose of arriving at sour figures, 3ou have assumed in perpetuity the warehouse and the shop but nevertheless, for the purpose of arriving at the value of the land which is left vacant- -406 square yards—you assume that you would take the warehouse and shop down ?—Certainly. Until you did so, the only means of access to the ' 406 square yards would be this 2ft. 9th. passage ?—No it would be through my own warehouse. By making a door I could get right out on to that land. Questioned as to the possibility of Messrs Fair- dough obtaining suitable premises elsewhere, witness said it would be very difficult, if not impossible for them to find premises with those advantages which would enable him to carry on the business profitably. A large number of their customers would refuse to go out of their way merely because the business was Messrs. Fairclough's, and as the expenses continued the profits would be extinguished Mr Hewart suggested that the introduction of the tramway service into the question of the value of the site was something that was entirely fanciful. Witness : I say you are absolutely wrong. Mr Wallis, valuer, of Manchester, gave similar evidence. He stated that tbe removal of the business would be a very serious matter to Messrs: Fairclough. They might attempt to establish them- selves somewhere else, but they certainly could not find a site 88 good as the present cne. The profit made at Cho warehouse was something less than 2 per cent. of the turnover and it would therefore easily be seen that any dislocation of trade might convert that into a loss. THE ORIGINAL CLAIM.
Mr Ffewart : Your total valuation works out at £4,822 P—Yea.
Do y( u happen to know that the claim made originally WitS tor £6,9C0 ?-1 duo% really know about that.
Yon have nothing to do with that, of course ?—No.

When he vtitneFs had completed his evidence, Mr Sanderson said :Ny learned ti tend asked if the witness knew a hat vvas the amount of our original claim. I don't suppose it will have tha slightest effect upon your minds. Prot:ably it rcay induce yt.o to thick our evidence is very reasonable. The Umpire : Not tt,o slightest effect on mine. Air Sanderson : If tny ieatned triEnd places any reliance upon it, I should lit.° to ask if he knows what. the original offer of the Corporaion was. If in) learned. friend objects I canrot tv.,k it, and I don't propose to do so.

Mr Hewart : I rim sure my learned friend knows perfectly well ti.et evider.ce as to the original offer of the Corporation is inadmissible, It is not relevant to this inquiry. Mr Sancerson : It is just as relevant as the evidence as to our origival claim. Mr Ilewrirt: On the contrary, I respectfully disagree. rlhiengtr,n present thsaitte assro `Mr Alt:art We.rourtop, arceitect, I‘arrington, agreed with the valuation already suhmittfd, lie said there ri nt hea pn rsphoaspees oor f Messrs Fairciough's nusiness. fv'O'arsitinocoLpulpi'acreabinle";::r Mr lietyart questioned witness as to the claim for compensation for loss of business. As an illustration, he said, let, th.rn assume that the Corporation nquired the shop of the Argenta Meat Co, and the company stated " lbs pn.ti!a on our ranch in South Amenca 're going to be affected," would the ,:ipess think it right to compensate them for the loss of proti.s on that ranch ? Wit Less : No, I think not. Why not? Can you gice a reason ?:—No answer. Take another illustration. Supposing it were one of Lipton's shops and they said : " You are com- pensating us for the loss of profits on tea sales at the shop, why not for the loss of profits on our tea gardens in Ceylon " ?—Well, all I can say is that the usual practice is involved bore. Do you suggest it is the u,ual practice think this matter has been dealt with on a tail basis. Mr Sanderson : Let us descend from the realms of comic opera to business. (Laughter). Mr James Lowe, canal and river superintendent, gave evidence in support of Messrs Fairclough's claim as to river frontage. Mr Frank Edward Priest, CE., of Liverpool, said the site was admirably suited for river development. The dredging which would be necessary could not possibly have a detrimental effect upon the main current of the river.

This completed the evidence for Messrs Fairclough Mr. 'Sanderson said it had been stated that after notice to treat had been given, Messrs Fairclough refused to allow the Corporation to take part of the premises. That was not quite correct. Notice to treat was given in November, 1911. Between that time and May,l9l2,negotiations took place and Messrs Faircloug h were quite willing that the Corporation should take part ot the premises, provided that the Corporation could give them premises which had access to the river. Unfortunately the Corporation were not in a position to do that, and therefore Messrs Fairclough said : " You must take the whole of the premises." Mr flowart : I cannot agree. On the contrary Messrs Fairclough were requiring that the Corporation should build them a wharf and dredge the berth at the expense of the Corporation. The proceedings were adjourned until to-day, when the case for the Corporation will he presented.

div.p: MR. BIRRELL'S VISIT.

The Right Hon. Augustine Birrell, K.C., M.P., will address a great Liberal meeting in the Parr Hall, this (Saturday) evening. An exceptional amount of interest is being displayed in the meeting and there has been a heavy demand for tickets, Mr C E Parker will take the chair at 7.30 and the other speakers will include Mr A H Crosfield.

div.head: ANTARCTIC DISASTER.
div.p: THE ANTARCTIC DISASTER.
Local Commemoration of the Dead
Heroes.

Yesterday honoui. was done to the memory of Captain Scott and his fellow victims of the Antarctic disaster. Copies of the Captain's last pathetic yet inspiiing message to the nation were sent round to all the elementary schools in Warrington, with the request that the teachers in the senior departments should read it and draw suitable lessons therefrom. This commemoration took place at the time when the Memortnl Service, attended by the King, was being held in St. Paul's Cathedral. At the Secondary School the message was read and Alderman Bennett delivered an address. Flags were displayed at half- mast on the vazious public buildings.

SANKEY JUNIOR V CROSFIELD'S (TIN siTor). ' Sankey beat Crosfield's nine goals to nil at Sankey on Saturday. This score did nut represent the play, however, Crosfleld's playing pluckily but they were met by a sterling defence, Payne, particularly so. For the winners, Payne, Hicklin and Taylor, played well, and Evans and Ryder were the pick of the visitors. Taylor (two). Plumb (two). Mathor, Knight, Palin and Ellwell were the scorers. Staines also put one through his own goal. ST. HELENS CABLE AND RUBBER CO. V. HELSBY ATHLETIC. An interesting football match took place at Helsby on Saturday last, between the St Helens Cable and Rubber Company's team and the Helsby Athletic A.F.C. which had been arranged by Alr .1 II C Brooking,general manager of the Cable Works. Helsby fully expected to take both points, but the visiting team especially Brooking, Clays and Siddall, played so finely that they inflicted a defeat on the home club by 5 goals to 3. Helsby had the advantage of wind and sun in the first half, but could not penetrate the defence, half time arriving, no score. On resumine, the Cable quickly set about it in a business-like manner, from which point the game was never in doubt. Scorers, Raynor 2, Bradshaw 1, Siddall 1, and Rowlands 1, the latter from a fine piece of work by Brooking. After the match, the team partook of an excellent tea kindly provided for by Mr Brooking, and ably catered for by Mr Seddon. When tea was over, all adjourned to the Robin Hood Hotel, where billiards, and after- wards a concert was held, Mr Stanley officiating in his usual manner at the piano. Mr Brooking's song, ani that of" Nugget " Barton were heartily encored. TO-DAY'S TEAMS. WIDNES AND DISTRICT ALLIANCE. GREAT SANKEY V. FARNWORTII INSTITUTE —At Penketk Recreation to-Jay. Inquiries must he short. concise, and plainly written, and the name and address of the writer given to show that the inquiry is genuine. The section says" Where a woman who has been employed within the meaning of the Act before marriage proves that she continues to be so employed after marriage," &c. As we said last weak our poit,t was that the married woman must prove her continuance in employment. Our correspondent can surely see this. We cannot accept the inter- pretation put upon the section by his company, neither can we agree to argue the point further. SANDY.—The fact that a domestic servant is kept in ' her mistress's house during sickness and is paid wages will not take away her right to sick pay. But if the mistress agrees to give a sick servant board arid lodging (or its value) together with full wages during the first six weeks of illness, then both mistress and servant obtain reduced rates of payment. WAITRESS.—Tips or gratuities which are recognised incidents of the employment must be reckoned as Tart of the employed person's remuneration. L.N.—The validity of a contract or agreement between two parties if properly executed and other- wise in order is not affected by its not having been stamped. But if either party sues the other on the contract it cannot be used in evidence until it has been stamped. The Inland Revenue Authorities will inflict a fine for delay in stamping. ONE WHO WANTS TO KNOW.—If your hersband is still alive his absence from you for seven years does not enable you to contract another legal , marriage. If he plculd turn up you might be prosecuted for bigamy, but if you could prove his absence for seven years' and that you had not heard of him during that time you would be successful in your defence, although of course the second marriage would not be valid.
